It is a leaf in the import graph, not a hub. A god module that both imports and exports widely is the anti-pattern; a foundation module that only exports is a deliberate architectural choice.

The Distributed Monolith

You split the system into services, but they all depend on the same database, deploy together, and fail together. You have the operational overhead of a distributed system with none of the benefits.

Symptom: You cannot deploy one service without deploying all of them. An outage in one service takes down all of them.

Fix: If the components share state, lifecycle, and failure domains, they are one system. Make them one process. Distribute only when you need independent scaling, deployment, or failure isolation.

The Abstraction Inversion

You create an abstract interface between two modules, but the abstraction does not match the real boundary. Callers must work around the abstraction to get the behavior they need, and implementations must jump through hoops to satisfy a contract that does not fit their natural structure.

Symptom: Extensive use of "escape hatches" -- methods like getUnderlying(), raw(), or asSpecificType() that bypass the abstraction.

Fix: The abstraction is in the wrong place. Remove it and let the concrete types flow until you find the real boundary.

Decomposition as Decision

Every decomposition is a decision with long-lasting consequences. Like all architectural decisions, it should be documented with its rationale, considered alternatives, and trade-offs. When you decompose a system, write down:

  1. What you split -- the components and their responsibilities.
  2. Why you split there -- which of the five tests (data flow, change frequency, team boundary, failure domain, independent service) motivated the boundary.
  3. What you considered and rejected -- alternative decompositions and why they lost.
  4. What would change your mind -- the conditions under which you would re-merge or re-split.

This record serves your future self and your team. When someone asks "why is the permission system inside the tool system?" there is a document that explains the reasoning. When requirements change and the boundary no longer makes sense, there is a record of the original rationale to evaluate against the new reality.

Key Principles

  1. Decomposition is not a mechanical process. It requires understanding the forces acting on the system: data flow, change frequency, team boundaries, failure domains, and trust levels.

  2. Natural seam lines run parallel to data flows, not perpendicular. Boundaries that cut across hot data paths create communication overhead on every request.

  3. Split what changes independently. Keep together what changes together. Version history tells you where the real coupling is, regardless of what the module boundaries claim.

  4. The infrastructure layer must import nothing from the layers above it. One-way dependencies prevent circular imports and enable safe initialization ordering.

  5. Three to seven major subsystems. Matches the cognitive limit of working memory. If you cannot draw the architecture on a whiteboard in under a minute, you have too many pieces.

  6. Every boundary spends complexity budget. Too many boundaries over-engineer the system. Too few create a monolith. The art is finding the balance.

Think About It

Exercise 1: The Boundary Audit. Take a system you work on. Draw its current module boundaries on a whiteboard. Now look at the last 50 commits. For each commit, mark which modules were changed. If most commits touch multiple modules, your boundaries do not match your change patterns. Where would you re-draw them?

Exercise 2: The Merge Thought Experiment. Pick two modules in your system that communicate heavily. Imagine merging them into one. What would you gain? (Simpler communication, fewer interfaces, less ceremony.) What would you lose? (Independent testing, separate ownership, clear responsibility.) If the gains outweigh the losses, you should probably merge them.

Exercise 3: The Service Extraction Test. Pick a subsystem in your monolith. Imagine extracting it as a standalone service with an RPC interface. List every piece of shared state it currently accesses. That list is the coupling you would need to eliminate. If the list is short (2-3 items), extraction is feasible. If it is long (10+ items), the boundary is not natural.

Exercise 4: The Layer Violation Hunt. Map your codebase's import graph. Find every import that goes "upward" -- from a lower layer to a higher one. Each such import is a potential circular dependency waiting to happen. For each violation, determine whether it should be eliminated (by moving code to a lower layer), inverted (by introducing a callback or interface), or accepted (by using lazy loading to break the cycle at runtime).

Exercise 5: The Three-Pillar Exercise. Take any application you have built or worked on. Decompose it into exactly three pillars, each described in one sentence. If you cannot find three, the system may be too simple for this exercise. If you find more than three, decide which responsibilities should merge. The constraint of exactly three forces you to find the highest-level decomposition -- the one that explains the system to a new engineer in thirty seconds.

Chapter 6: Interface Design

The most expensive lines of code in any system are the interfaces between its components. Not because they are hard to write -- interface definitions are often short -- but because they are hard to change. An implementation can be rewritten in a weekend. An interface that ten modules depend on cannot be changed without modifying all ten. The implementation is the house; the interface is the foundation. You can renovate the house. Replacing the foundation means tearing everything down first.

Chapter 5 showed how to decompose a system into manageable pieces. This chapter addresses the harder question: how do those pieces talk to each other? The contracts between components determine how easily the system can evolve, how independently teams can work, and whether adding a new capability takes one file or forty.

The case study is Claude Code's tool interface -- a single contract that 52 tools implement. It is, arguably, the most important design decision in the entire 500K-line codebase. This chapter explains why, and extracts principles you can apply to any system.

Contracts Before Code

The natural instinct is to write the implementation first and extract the interface later. You build the file-reading tool, then the bash-execution tool, then the search tool. When you have three tools, you notice their common shape and factor out an interface.

This is backwards.

When you extract an interface from existing implementations, you get an interface shaped by the accidents of those implementations. The file reader returns strings. The bash executor returns a struct with exit code, stdout, and stderr. The search tool returns a list of matches. Your extracted interface must accommodate all three return types, so it becomes a union type or a generic blob. The interface does not guide the implementations; it merely describes what already exists.

When you design the interface first, every implementation is shaped by the contract. The file reader, bash executor, and search tool all return the same result type because the contract requires it. Differences that seemed essential in a bottom-up extraction turn out to be accidental -- there is no reason the file reader cannot return a structured result with a type field, just like the bash executor.

The Discipline of Pre-Design

Designing the interface first requires answering three questions before writing any implementation:

1. Who is the caller, and what do they need? The interface exists for the caller, not the implementer. If the agent loop needs to dispatch tool calls, the interface should be shaped around dispatching, not around individual tool mechanics. If the permission system needs to check whether a tool is safe, the interface should declare safety properties, not bury them in implementation details.

2. What is the minimum information that must cross the boundary? Every field in the interface is a commitment. Once callers depend on it, removing it is a breaking change. Start with the minimum and add fields only when a concrete use case demands them.

3. What should be impossible to express? A good interface makes illegal states unrepresentable. If a tool cannot be both read-only and destructive, the type system should prevent it. If a tool result must include either data or an error (never both, never neither), a discriminated union enforces this at compile time.

An Example of Contract-First Thinking

Consider designing a tool system. The bottom-up approach starts with one tool:

// Bottom-up: shaped by the first implementation
class FileReadTool {
  async readFile(path: string): Promise<string> { ... }
}

Then you add another:

class BashTool {
  async execute(command: string): Promise<{
    exitCode: number; stdout: string; stderr: string
  }> { ... }
}

Now you need a common interface. The two implementations have different signatures, different return types, and different parameter shapes. The extracted interface is awkward:

// Extracted: awkward union of two different shapes
interface Tool {
  run(input: unknown): Promise<unknown>
}

The contract-first approach starts differently. Before writing any tool, you ask: what does the agent loop need?

// Contract-first: shaped by the caller's needs
interface Tool {
  name: string
  inputSchema: Schema
  call(input: ValidatedInput): AsyncGenerator<Progress, Result>
}

The agent loop needs to know a tool's name (for dispatch), its input schema (for validation), and a way to call it (for execution). Every tool implements this. The file reader does not get to define its own signature. The bash executor does not get to return a custom struct. They both conform to the contract.

Why Interfaces Matter More Than Implementations

An implementation can be wrong and fixed in a day. An interface can be wrong and unfixable for years.

This asymmetry exists because interfaces create coupling. Every module that depends on an interface is coupled to its shape. Changing the shape requires changing every dependent module. In a system where 52 tools implement one interface, changing that interface means modifying 52 tool implementations, plus every consumer of the interface (the registry, the executor, the permission system, the UI renderer, the context compactor, the search system).

Implementations create no external coupling. The bash tool's internal parsing logic can change completely without affecting any other module, as long as it still satisfies the tool interface. This is the fundamental value proposition of interfaces: they allow independent evolution of the pieces on each side.

The Cost of Interface Changes

Claude Code's tool interface has approximately 20 methods and properties. Changing any method's signature affects:

  • 52+ tool implementations that must update their conformance
  • The tool registry that queries the method
  • The executor that calls the method
  • The permission system that checks the method
  • The UI that renders the method's output
  • The compactor that summarizes the method's results
  • The test harness that mocks the method

A single interface change can cascade to 60+ files. This is why Claude Code's tool interface uses fail-closed defaults with a factory function -- new methods are added with default implementations, so existing tools do not need to change:

const DEFAULTS = {
  isReadOnly: () => false,
  isDestructive: () => false,
  isConcurrencySafe: () => false,
  maxResultSizeChars: undefined,
}

function buildTool<I, O>(def: ToolDefinition<I, O>): Tool<I, O> {
  return { ...DEFAULTS, ...def }
}

When a new behavioral property is needed (say, canRunInBackground()), it is added to DEFAULTS with a conservative default (false). No existing tool must change. Only tools that want to opt into the new behavior override the default. This is the practical cost of a 52-implementation interface: every addition must be backward-compatible by construction.

The Power of Narrow Interfaces

A narrow interface is one that exposes the minimum surface area needed by its callers. The narrower the interface, the less coupling, the more freedom for implementations, and the easier it is to test.

What "Narrow" Means

Narrow does not mean "few methods." It means "each method carries the minimum information necessary." Consider two designs for a tool's permission check:

// Wide: exposes the tool's internals to the permission system
interface Tool {
  getPermissionRules(): Rule[]
  getRequiredCapabilities(): Capability[]
  getSandboxProfile(): SandboxConfig
  getFileAccessPatterns(): GlobPattern[]
}

// Narrow: the tool answers a single question
interface Tool {
  checkPermissions(input: ValidatedInput,
                   context: PermissionContext): PermissionResult
}

The wide interface leaks implementation details. The permission system must understand rules, capabilities, sandbox profiles, and file access patterns. If any of these concepts change, the permission system changes too.

The narrow interface hides all of that. The tool receives the input and context, consults its own rules internally, and returns a verdict: allow, deny, or ask. The permission system does not know how the tool makes the decision. It only knows the result.

Claude Code uses the narrow approach. Each tool's checkPermissions() method encapsulates the full permission logic for that tool. The Bash tool checks the parsed command against security rules. The Read tool checks the file path against deny lists. The Edit tool checks whether the file has been read first. Each tool knows its own domain-specific rules. The permission system orchestrates the check without understanding any tool's internals.

The Information Hiding Principle

David Parnas formulated this in 1972, and it remains the most important principle in interface design: each module hides a design decision that is likely to change. The interface exposes only what other modules need to know.

In Claude Code's tool system, the design decisions hidden behind the tool interface include:

Hidden Decision What the Interface Exposes
How the Bash tool parses commands inputSchema: z.object({ command: z.string() })
How the Edit tool finds text to replace call(input): AsyncGenerator<Progress, Result>
How the Read tool handles binary files mapToolResultToAPIBlock(result): ContentBlock
How each tool evaluates permissions checkPermissions(input, ctx): PermissionResult
How tools render in the terminal renderToolUseMessage(input): ReactNode

Every tool can change how it parses, searches, renders, and checks permissions without affecting any other tool or any consumer of the interface. The implementation is free to evolve because the interface is stable.

Designing for the Caller, Not the Implementer

The most common interface design mistake is shaping the interface around the implementer's convenience rather than the caller's needs. The implementer knows their internals and creates methods that expose them. The caller must then map their needs onto the implementer's model.

The Agent Loop as the Primary Caller

Claude Code's tool interface was designed around the agent loop's needs. The agent loop needs to:

  1. Discover tools -- know what tools exist and their schemas
  2. Dispatch calls -- route a tool call to the right implementation
  3. Check permissions -- determine whether a call is allowed
  4. Execute calls -- run the tool and get results
  5. Handle progress -- show the user what is happening
  6. Format results -- convert results to the API's message format
  7. Summarize calls -- compress old tool calls during context compaction

Each need maps to one or two methods on the tool interface:

interface Tool<Input, Output> {
  // Discovery (need 1)
  name: string
  description: string | ((ctx: ToolUseContext) => string)
  inputSchema: z.ZodType<Input>

  // Dispatch (need 2)
  aliases?: string[]

  // Permissions (need 3)
  checkPermissions(input: Input, ctx: PermissionContext): PermissionResult
  isReadOnly(): boolean

  // Execution (need 4)
  call(input: Input, ctx: ToolUseContext): AsyncGenerator<Progress, Output>

  // Progress (need 5)
  renderToolUseProgressMessage(progress: Progress): ReactNode

  // Formatting (need 6)
  mapToolResultToAPIBlock(result: Output): ContentBlock
  renderToolUseMessage(input: Input): ReactNode
  renderToolResultMessage(result: Output): ReactNode

  // Summarization (need 7)
  getToolUseSummary(input: Input, result: Output): string
}

Notice what is absent from this interface. There is no initialize() method -- the agent loop does not need to initialize tools. There is no getState() method -- the agent loop does not need tool-internal state. There is no configure() method -- tools are configured through their constructors, not through the interface. The interface contains exactly what the callers need and nothing more.

Multiple Callers, One Interface

The tool interface has six callers, each using a different subset:

graph LR
    subgraph "Tool Interface"
        N["name"]
        S["inputSchema"]
        C["call()"]
        P["checkPermissions()"]
        RO["isReadOnly()"]
        CS["isConcurrencySafe()"]
        R1["renderToolUseMessage()"]
        R2["renderToolResultMessage()"]
        R3["renderToolUseProgressMessage()"]
        SUM["getToolUseSummary()"]
        MAP["mapToolResultToAPIBlock()"]
        EN["isEnabled()"]
        PR["prompt()"]
    end

    LOOP["Agent Loop"] --> N & S & C
    PERM["Permission System"] --> P & RO
    EXEC["Executor"] --> C & CS
    UIL["UI Layer"] --> R1 & R2 & R3
    COMP["Compactor"] --> SUM
    REG["Registry"] --> EN & PR & N & S

    style LOOP fill:#e94560,color:#fff
    style PERM fill:#0f3460,color:#fff
    style EXEC fill:#16213e,color:#fff
    style UIL fill:#533483,color:#fff
    style COMP fill:#2d132c,color:#fff
    style REG fill:#0a4c2e,color:#fff

Each caller uses 2-4 methods out of the ~20 available. No caller uses the full interface. This is typical of well-designed interfaces -- they serve multiple consumers, each using a different facet.

An alternative design would create separate interfaces for each consumer: Dispatchable, Permissioned, Renderable, Summarizable. Some languages encourage this (Go's small interfaces, Rust's traits). But in a TypeScript codebase with 52 implementations, each tool would need to satisfy 4-6 separate interfaces. The cognitive overhead of understanding which interface provides which method outweighs the purity benefit. One interface with good defaults is more practical than five interfaces with perfect separation.

The Uniform Contract

The most powerful aspect of Claude Code's tool interface is its uniformity. Every tool -- from the simple Glob tool (find files by pattern) to the complex Bash tool (4,400-line parser, security analysis, sandboxing) -- implements the same contract. This uniformity has profound consequences.

What Uniformity Enables

Generic infrastructure. The tool executor does not need a switch statement to handle different tools. It calls tool.call(input, context) on every tool, regardless of what the tool does. The permission system calls tool.checkPermissions(input, context) on every tool. The UI calls tool.renderToolUseMessage(input) on every tool. No special cases, no type checks, no "if this tool, do this" branching.

// Generic execution -- works for any tool, past or future
async function executeTool(tool: Tool, input: unknown, ctx: ToolUseContext) {
  const validated = tool.inputSchema.parse(input)
  const permission = tool.checkPermissions(validated, ctx)
  if (permission === 'denied') return errorResult(permission)

  const generator = tool.call(validated, ctx)
  for await (const progress of generator) {
    renderProgress(tool.renderToolUseProgressMessage(progress))
  }
  return generator.return
}

This function works for 52 tools today and will work for tool 53 without modification. The tool interface is a protocol -- the executor speaks it fluently without knowing the specifics of any tool.

Adding a tool is a self-contained change. When Claude Code adds a new tool, the change touches exactly one directory: the new tool's directory. No registry file to update (the tool registers itself). No executor switch to extend. No permission rules to add (the tool defines its own via checkPermissions). No UI code to modify (the tool provides its own render methods). The uniform interface means every subsystem adapts automatically.

Testing is generic. Test utilities can verify that any tool conforms to the contract without knowing what the tool does:

// Generic conformance test -- applicable to all 52 tools
function testToolConformance(tool: Tool) {
  expect(tool.name).toBeDefined()
  expect(tool.inputSchema).toBeDefined()
  expect(typeof tool.call).toBe('function')
  expect(typeof tool.checkPermissions).toBe('function')
  expect(typeof tool.isReadOnly).toBe('function')
  expect(typeof tool.isConcurrencySafe).toBe('function')
}

What Uniformity Costs

Uniformity has costs, and acknowledging them is honest engineering.

Lowest common denominator risk. The uniform interface must accommodate the simplest tool (Glob: takes a pattern, returns paths) and the most complex (Bash: takes a command, parses it into an AST, runs security analysis, spawns a process, captures output, enforces timeout). The interface must be flexible enough for the complex case without imposing unnecessary burden on the simple case. The factory defaults solve this -- simple tools implement name, inputSchema, and call; everything else uses defaults.

Semantic mismatch. The isReadOnly() method makes sense for filesystem tools but is awkward for web tools. Is WebFetch read-only? It does not modify the local filesystem, but it makes a network request that could have side effects on the remote server. The interface forces a boolean answer to a non-binary question. Claude Code resolves this pragmatically: WebFetch returns true for isReadOnly because the relevant question for the permission system is "does this modify the user's local environment?"

Evolution pressure. Adding a new method to the interface requires every tool to either implement it or accept a default. Over time, the interface accumulates methods that most tools use the default for. Claude Code's tool interface has ~20 methods. A typical tool overrides 5-8 of them. The rest use defaults. This is acceptable -- the defaults handle the common case, and the methods exist because at least one caller needs them.

API Ergonomics

Interface design is not just about what information crosses the boundary. It is about how easy it is for the implementer to get right and how hard it is to get wrong.

The Pit of Success

A good API makes the correct usage the easiest usage. Incorrect usage should require extra effort -- ideally, it should not even compile.

Claude Code's tool factory function embodies this principle:

const ReadTool = buildTool({
  name: 'Read',
  description: 'Read file contents',
  inputSchema: z.object({
    file_path: z.string(),
    offset: z.number().optional(),
    limit: z.number().optional(),
  }),
  isReadOnly: () => true,
  isConcurrencySafe: () => true,
  async *call(input, context) {
    // Implementation
  },
})

The buildTool factory:

  1. Requires only the essential fields. name, inputSchema, and call are mandatory. Everything else has a default.
  2. Sets safe defaults. isReadOnly: false, isConcurrencySafe: false. A tool that forgets to declare itself read-only is treated as mutating -- the permission system checks it more carefully. This is fail-closed: the safe assumption is the default.
  3. Validates at construction time. If the schema is invalid or the name conflicts with another tool, the error occurs when the tool is built, not when it is first used.
  4. Provides type inference. The input type for call is inferred from inputSchema. The implementer does not need to manually declare the input type -- it is derived from the schema definition.

Making Wrong Things Hard

The interface design prevents several classes of errors:

Error: Forgetting to handle permissions. Every tool call passes through checkPermissions before call. The executor enforces this, not the tool. A tool cannot accidentally skip the permission check because the executor calls it externally.

Error: Returning unformatted results. The mapToolResultToAPIBlock method converts tool results to the API format. The executor calls this after call returns. A tool cannot accidentally return raw data to the API because the formatting step is external.

Error: Running unsafe tools in parallel. The executor checks isConcurrencySafe before parallelizing. The default is false. A new tool cannot be accidentally parallelized because it must explicitly opt in.

Error: Allowing a write to an unread file. The Write and Edit tools check readFileState in their checkPermissions method. The agent loop cannot bypass this because the permission check is part of the standard execution pipeline.

Each of these protections works because the interface puts the enforcement in the caller (the executor), not the implementer (the tool). The tool does not need to remember to check permissions, format results, or prevent parallelism. The infrastructure does it.

The Zod + JSON Schema Dual

A particularly elegant ergonomic decision is the dual-schema pattern. Tools define their input schemas using Zod (a TypeScript-native schema library):

inputSchema: z.object({
  command: z.string().describe('The command to execute'),
  timeout: z.number().optional().describe('Timeout in milliseconds'),
})

This one definition serves two consumers:

Consumer Format Needed How
Agent process Runtime validation schema.parse(input)
Model API JSON Schema for generation constraint Auto-converted from Zod

The implementer writes one schema. The system derives both validation and API constraint from it. The auto-conversion is cached per session for performance and stability (the same bytes on every request preserve the prompt cache key). The implementer does not need to know that JSON Schema exists, that it is cached, or that it affects caching economics. The interface hides all of it.

Case Study: 52 Tools, One Contract

Let us trace how the uniform tool interface plays out across the full tool system. Claude Code has tools ranging from trivially simple to extraordinarily complex:

Tool Complexity Lines Key Methods Overridden
Glob Simple ~200 name, schema, call, isReadOnly, isConcurrencySafe
Read Medium ~800 + deduplication, format dispatch, token limits
Edit Complex ~1,200 + staleness check, atomic write, read-before-write
Bash Very complex ~12,000 + AST parser, security analysis, sandboxing
Agent Complex ~600 + subagent spawning, result aggregation

The Bash tool is 60x larger than the Glob tool, yet both implement the same interface. The Bash tool's complexity is entirely internal. From the executor's perspective, BashTool.call(input, ctx) and GlobTool.call(input, ctx) are identical invocations. The 4,400-line parser, the security analyzer, the sandbox configuration -- all invisible to the caller.

This is the payoff of the uniform contract. The system's most complex component (Bash) and its simplest (Glob) participate in the same infrastructure without the infrastructure knowing the difference.

How New Tools Are Added

The process for adding tool number 53 to Claude Code:

  1. Create a directory: src/tools/NewTool/
  2. Define the tool using buildTool():
export const NewTool = buildTool({
  name: 'NewTool',
  description: 'Does something new',
  inputSchema: z.object({ /* fields */ }),
  async *call(input, context) {
    // Implementation
    yield { type: 'progress', message: 'Working...' }
    return { type: 'success', data: result }
  },
})
  1. Register it in the tool list (one line).

That is it. The registry picks it up. The executor dispatches to it. The permission system checks it (using defaults -- it is treated as mutating and non-concurrent until declared otherwise). The UI renders it (using default renderers). The compactor summarizes it (using the default summarizer). The schema is auto-converted and cached. No other file needs modification.

This is the measure of a good interface: how many files must change to add a new implementation? If the answer is "one," the interface is doing its job.

How the Interface Evolved

The tool interface was not born with 20 methods. It started with 4: name, inputSchema, description, call. Every additional method was added when a concrete use case demanded it:

Method Added When Why
checkPermissions Permission system was built Tools needed to define their own permission logic
isReadOnly Auto-mode classifier needed to know which tools are safe Could not classify without this signal
isConcurrencySafe Parallel tool execution was implemented Needed to know which tools could run simultaneously
getToolUseSummary Context compaction needed shorter representations Full tool results wasted context tokens
prompt Some tools needed to inject context into the system prompt The system prompt builder needed tool-specific content
renderToolUseMessage UI needed tool-specific rendering Generic rendering was too verbose for some tools

Each addition followed the same process: a caller needed information that the interface did not provide, a new method was added with a default implementation, and only tools that needed non-default behavior overridden it. The interface grew by accretion, driven by real needs, not by speculation.

Interface Design Principles

1. The Dependency Rule

Interfaces should point in the direction of stability. Stable components should not depend on volatile components. In practice, this means the interface is defined by the more stable side of the boundary.

In Claude Code, the tool interface is defined by the infrastructure (executor, registry, permission system), not by the tools. The infrastructure is stable -- it changes rarely. The tools are volatile -- new tools are added, existing tools are modified. The dependency points from volatile (tools) toward stable (infrastructure). This is correct.

If the tools defined their own interfaces and the infrastructure adapted to each one, every new tool would require infrastructure changes. The system would become harder to evolve, not easier.

2. The Uniformity Principle

Treat different things the same way when possible. Uniformity reduces the cognitive load on everyone who works with the system. The developer adding tool 53 does not need to understand how tools 1-52 work. They need to understand one interface.

The cost of uniformity is semantic mismatch -- some tools fit the interface more naturally than others. The benefit is that every piece of infrastructure (executor, registry, permission system, UI, compactor) works with every tool without special cases. In a system with 52 tools, the benefit overwhelms the cost.

3. The Default Direction Principle

When a property has a safe default and a dangerous override, the default should be the safe option. This is the fail-closed principle applied to API design:

Property Safe Default Override
isReadOnly false (mutating) true (read-only)
isConcurrencySafe false (serialized) true (parallelizable)
isDestructive false (non-destructive) true (destructive)
strict false (flexible schema) true (strict validation)

A tool that forgets to declare itself read-only gets extra permission checks -- annoying but safe. A tool that is falsely declared read-only skips permission checks -- dangerous. The default must be the one that fails safely.

4. The Composition Principle

Design interfaces so that tools compose naturally. In Claude Code, tool composition happens through the conversation: the output of one tool becomes context for the next model response, which may invoke another tool. This implicit composition works because:

  • Output formats are consistent. Every tool returns structured results that the model can parse.
  • Path formats are normalized. A file path returned by Grep is valid input to Read. A path returned by Glob is valid input to Edit. No translation needed.
  • Errors are visible. When a tool fails, the model sees the error and can adapt. Silent failures break the composition chain.

5. The Evolution Principle

Interfaces will change. Design for change by:

  • Using factory functions with defaults (new methods do not break existing implementations)
  • Preferring additive changes (new optional methods) over breaking changes (modified signatures)
  • Documenting the rationale for each method (so future engineers know whether it can be removed)

The Anti-Patterns

The Leaky Abstraction

The interface exposes implementation details that callers become dependent on. When the implementation changes, callers break.

Example: A tool interface that exposes getProcessId() because one caller needs it. Now every implementation must have a process concept, even tools that do not spawn processes. The interface is shaped by one implementation's internals, not by the callers' actual needs.

Fix: If one caller needs implementation-specific information, provide it through a separate, narrower interface -- not through the universal tool interface.

The Kitchen Sink Interface

The interface accumulates every method any caller might ever need. It grows to 50 methods. New implementations are a burden because they must satisfy a massive contract.

Example: renderToolUseMessage, renderToolUseCompactMessage, renderToolUseOneLineMessage, renderToolUseIconMessage, renderToolUseDarkThemeMessage...

Fix: Ask whether each method is used by more than one caller. If a method serves only one caller, it may belong in a separate, caller-specific interface rather than the universal contract.

The Over-Specific Interface

The interface is so specific to current requirements that it cannot accommodate future needs without a breaking change.

Example: execute(command: string): string -- works for bash but cannot accommodate tools that return structured data, images, or streaming results.

Fix: Design the interface for the category of operations, not for specific operations. call(input: Validated): AsyncGenerator<Progress, Result> accommodates bash commands, file reads, web fetches, and anything else that produces progressive output.

The Phantom Abstraction

An interface exists between two components, but only one implementation exists for one side. The interface adds ceremony without providing any of the benefits of abstraction (substitutability, testing isolation, independent evolution).

Fix: Remove the interface. Use the concrete type directly. Add the interface when a second implementation actually appears. The premature interface costs maintenance today with no benefit until the second implementation arrives -- which may never happen.

Key Principles

  1. Design the interface before the implementation. The interface shapes every implementation; extracting it after the fact shapes the interface around implementation accidents.

  2. Design for the caller, not the implementer. The agent loop's needs determine the tool interface, not the bash tool's internals.

  3. Narrow interfaces reduce coupling. Each method should carry the minimum information necessary. Hide implementation decisions behind single-method queries (checkPermissions returns a verdict, not the rules).

  4. Uniformity beats specificity at scale. 52 tools implementing one contract means zero special cases in the infrastructure. The cost (semantic mismatch for edge cases) is overwhelmed by the benefit (generic executor, generic permissions, generic rendering).

  5. Defaults must fail safely. Every boolean property defaults to the restrictive option. A forgotten override causes extra caution, not a security hole.

  6. Adding an implementation should be a one-file change. If adding tool 53 requires modifying the registry, the executor, the permission system, and the UI, the interface is not doing its job.

Think About It

Exercise 1: The Caller Inventory. Pick an interface in your codebase. List every caller. For each caller, list which methods it actually uses. Draw the diagram (as shown in this chapter). If every caller uses all methods, the interface is well-factored. If most callers use 2 out of 20 methods, consider whether the interface should be split.

Exercise 2: The Default Audit. Find every boolean property in your interfaces. What is the default value? Is it the safe option or the convenient option? For each property where the default is the dangerous option (e.g., allowParallelExecution: true), consider whether the default should be inverted.

Exercise 3: The New Implementation Test. Imagine adding a new implementation of your most important interface. How many files must you touch? Write down every file. If the number is greater than 3, the interface is leaking implementation coupling into the infrastructure. Identify which infrastructure components have hard-coded knowledge of existing implementations and refactor them to query the interface instead.

Exercise 4: The Contract-First Rewrite. Take a module you built bottom-up. Imagine you are starting over, but this time you must write the interface first -- before any implementation. What would change? Would the interface be narrower? Would the method signatures be different? Would some methods disappear entirely? This exercise reveals the gap between your current interface (shaped by implementation accidents) and the ideal interface (shaped by caller needs).

Exercise 5: The Evolution Simulation. Take your system's most stable interface. Imagine three new requirements: (a) a new implementation with different performance characteristics, (b) a new caller that needs a property the interface does not currently expose, (c) a requirement to remove a method that is now obsolete. For each requirement, trace the ripple: how many files change? If adding a property requires touching 50 files, you need a factory-with-defaults pattern. If removing a method is impossible because too many callers depend on it, you have a coupling problem to address before it gets worse.

Chapter 7: The Architecture of Decisions

Every production system is a fossil record of decisions. The code you ship is the sum of thousands of choices — some deliberate, some accidental, some brilliant, some desperate. The difference between a system that ages gracefully and one that collapses under its own weight is not the quality of individual decisions, but the process by which decisions are made, recorded, and revisited.

This chapter is about that process. We will examine Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) as thinking tools, not bureaucratic artifacts. We will build trade-off matrices that force rigor on decisions that intuition alone cannot resolve. We will distinguish reversible decisions from irreversible ones and calibrate our decision-making process accordingly. And we will study one of the most instructive decisions in Claude Code's architecture: the choice to use global mutable state instead of dependency injection — a decision that violates every textbook recommendation and is exactly right.

7.1 Decisions Are the Architecture

Junior engineers think architecture is about boxes and arrows. Senior engineers know architecture is about decisions. The boxes and arrows are consequences.

When someone asks "what's the architecture?", they are really asking three questions:

  1. What decisions were made? Global state or DI? Monolith or microservices? REST or gRPC?
  2. Why were those decisions made? What constraints existed? What trade-offs were accepted?
  3. Are those decisions still valid? Have the constraints changed? Should we revisit?

A system with clear architectural documentation answers all three. A system without it can only answer the first — and only by reading the code, which tells you what but never why.

The Cost of Lost Context

Every engineer has experienced this: you open a file, see a pattern that looks wrong, and "fix" it. Three days later, tests fail in production because the "wrong" pattern was load-bearing. The original developer had a reason for it, but that reason existed only in their head, and they left the company two years ago.

This is the cost of undocumented decisions. Not the cost of the decision itself — the decision might have been excellent — but the cost of losing the reasoning. Without the reasoning, every future engineer must either:

  • Reverse-engineer the intent from the code (expensive, error-prone)
  • Ask someone who was there (impossible after turnover)
  • Assume it was arbitrary and change it (dangerous)

Architecture Decision Records exist to prevent this. They are not bureaucracy. They are engineering memory.

7.2 ADRs as Thinking Tools

Michael Nygard's lightweight ADR format has four sections. Each one forces a specific kind of thinking:

# ADR-0042: Use Global Mutable State for Application State

## Status
Accepted

## Context
[What forces are at play? What constraints exist?]

## Decision
[What did we decide?]

## Consequences
[What are the trade-offs? What becomes easier? What becomes harder?]

Why This Format Works

The format is valuable not because of what it captures, but because of what it forces you to articulate before you write code.

Context forces constraint discovery. Writing the Context section requires you to enumerate the forces shaping the decision. Most engineers skip this step. They jump from "we have a problem" to "here's my solution" without mapping the constraint space. The Context section is where you discover that the real constraint is not technical but organizational, or that the constraint you assumed was fixed is actually flexible.

Decision forces commitment. Vague decisions produce vague architectures. "We'll use some kind of caching" is not a decision. "We will use a session-scoped in-memory cache with LRU eviction and a 500ms debounce on invalidation" is a decision. The Decision section forces you to be specific enough that another engineer could implement it without asking questions.

Consequences forces honesty. Every decision has costs. The Consequences section forces you to enumerate them. This is where you write "Test isolation will require a manual reset function in beforeEach" instead of pretending global state has no downsides. Honesty in the Consequences section is what separates architectural documentation from marketing.

When to Write an ADR

Not every decision needs an ADR. The heuristic: write an ADR when the decision is hard to reverse or when reasonable engineers would disagree.

Decision ADR? Why
Use TypeScript for a new TypeScript project No No reasonable alternative exists in context
Use global state vs. dependency injection Yes Reasonable engineers disagree strongly
Name a variable userId vs user_id No Trivially reversible
Use a monolithic binary vs. CLI + daemon Yes Structural, expensive to reverse
Choose between two logging libraries Maybe Depends on how deeply integrated
Cache API headers for prompt cache stability Yes Non-obvious, has financial implications

The threshold is roughly: if you would need to explain your decision in a code review comment of more than two sentences, it deserves an ADR.

7.3 The Trade-Off Matrix

Some decisions resist intuition. When you are choosing between three database engines, four caching strategies, or two fundamentally different architectural patterns, the number of factors exceeds what you can hold in your head. This is where the trade-off matrix earns its place.

Structure

A trade-off matrix is a table where rows are options and columns are evaluation criteria, each weighted by importance:

Criterion Weight Option A Option B Option C
Startup speed 5 4 (20) 2 (10) 3 (15)
Test isolation 3 2 (6) 5 (15) 3 (9)
Code simplicity 4 5 (20) 2 (8) 3 (12)
Refactoring ease 2 2 (4) 5 (10) 4 (8)
Total 50 43 44

Scores are 1-5 (5 = best). The weighted score is in parentheses. The total tells you which option wins across all criteria.

Why the Matrix Works

The matrix does three things that gut-feel decision-making cannot:

  1. Surfaces hidden criteria. Building the column list forces you to articulate all the things you care about, not just the loudest one. Engineers naturally anchor on whichever criterion they thought of first. The matrix corrects for this.

  2. Makes weights explicit. Two engineers might agree that "test isolation" matters but disagree on how much. Making weights explicit turns implicit disagreements into explicit ones that can be resolved.

  3. Separates scoring from weighting. You might score Option B highest on test isolation (5/5) but still reject it because test isolation has low weight relative to startup speed. The matrix keeps these two judgments separate.

When the Matrix Lies

The matrix is a tool for structured thinking, not a decision algorithm. It can lie in three ways:

Criteria are not independent. If "startup speed" and "binary size" are both columns, and they correlate strongly (smaller binary = faster startup), you are double-counting the same underlying factor. Fix: identify correlated criteria and merge them or reduce one's weight.

Scores are fabricated precision. Is Option A really a 4 on startup speed, or could it be a 3? The difference between 3 and 4 at weight 5 is 5 points — enough to swing the total. Fix: use only three values (1, 3, 5) instead of five. Less precision, but the rankings are more robust.

The matrix cannot capture non-linear effects. Option B might score well on every criterion but have a fatal flaw that the matrix averages away. A database that is fast, cheap, and well-documented but loses data under network partitions gets a reasonable total score despite being unusable. Fix: add "deal-breaker" criteria that are pass/fail, not scored.

Use the matrix to structure your thinking. Then use your judgment to make the decision.

7.4 Reversible vs. Irreversible Decisions

Jeff Bezos calls them one-way doors and two-way doors. The concept is simple: some decisions can be undone cheaply, others cannot.

One-Way Doors (Irreversible)

These decisions are expensive or impossible to reverse once made:

  • API contract published to external clients. Once third parties build against your API, removing or changing a field breaks them. You can add, but you cannot subtract.
  • Data format committed to storage. Once you write billions of records in format A, migrating to format B is a multi-month project with risk of data loss.
  • Architectural topology. Switching from monolith to microservices (or vice versa) after two years of development is a rewrite, not a refactor.
  • The serialization format of session persistence. Claude Code chose JSONL for session files. Once millions of sessions exist on disk, changing the format requires a migration path that supports both old and new formats indefinitely.

One-way doors deserve maximum deliberation. ADRs, trade-off matrices, prototype implementations, team reviews. The cost of getting it wrong is measured in months, not hours.

Two-Way Doors (Reversible)

These decisions can be undone cheaply:

  • Which linter to use. Switching from ESLint to Biome requires updating config files and running the new linter. A day of work, not a month.
  • Default values. Changing a timeout from 2 seconds to 5 seconds is a one-line change with a deploy.
  • Internal function signatures. Renaming parameters, reordering arguments, splitting functions — these are refactors, not rewrites.
  • Runtime feature flags. Claude Code's GrowthBook integration lets behavior change without redeployment. A runtime flag is, by definition, a two-way door.

Two-way doors deserve speed, not deliberation. Make the decision with 70% of the information you wish you had, ship it, and adjust based on feedback.

The Meta-Decision

The most important decision is deciding which kind of decision you are making. Engineers over-deliberate two-way doors (spending a week choosing between two equivalent libraries) and under-deliberate one-way doors (committing to a database schema in an afternoon).

A useful rule of thumb: if you can reverse the decision in less time than you would spend deliberating it, just decide. If reversing takes longer than deciding would have, slow down and use the full toolbox — ADRs, matrices, prototypes, reviews.

7.5 Decision Fatigue and the Power of Defaults

Herbert Simon's concept of "satisficing" — choosing an option that is good enough rather than optimal — is the antidote to decision fatigue. In engineering, satisficing manifests as defaults.

Why Defaults Matter

Every configurable system is a collection of decisions deferred to the user. Each configuration option says: "I couldn't decide, so you decide." Too many options and the user is paralyzed. Too few and the system is inflexible.

Claude Code's configuration cascade (Chapter 5 covered this in detail for the architecture book) has seven layers of configuration. But the critical design insight is not the layers — it is the defaults. A fresh installation with zero configuration works correctly. The model defaults to Sonnet. The permission mode defaults to "ask for writes." Auto-compaction is enabled. The context window is 200K tokens.

These defaults are not arbitrary. Each one is a decision made by the engineering team on behalf of all users who will never touch a config file. Most users never will. The defaults are the architecture for 90% of users.

The Default as a Decision Record

Every default should be justified:

Setting Default Justification
Model Sonnet Best cost/quality balance for typical development tasks
Permission mode Default (ask for writes) New users should see what the agent does before trusting it
Auto-compaction Enabled Prevents context overflow; no sane reason to disable
Startup flag fetch timeout 2 seconds p99 network latency with margin; fail-open on timeout
Max output tokens 8,000 (with escalation) p99 actual output is ~5K; saves 4-8x GPU reservation

Look at the last row. The default of 8,000 max output tokens seems wrong — the model can produce 32,000. But the engineering team analyzed the output distribution: p99 is 4,911 tokens. Setting the default to 32,000 wastes 6.5x GPU capacity globally. Setting it to 8,000 with automatic escalation to 64,000 when needed serves 99%+ of requests efficiently and handles the tail with one retry per 100 requests. The default encodes a sophisticated engineering decision that most users will never see.

Decision Fatigue in API Design

Tool design for AI agents is particularly susceptible to decision fatigue — not for the user, but for the LLM. Claude Code has 35+ tools. Each tool call is a decision the model makes. If each tool has ten parameters, the model faces a combinatorial explosion of possibilities.

The antidote: tools with good defaults. The BashTool requires only command. The optional timeout, description, and run_in_background parameters have sensible defaults. The model makes one decision (what command to run) instead of four. The principle of least surprise (Chapter 6 of the outline) applies here: a tool that does the obvious thing with minimal parameters reduces the decision load on both the model and the user.

7.6 Case Study: Global State vs. Dependency Injection

This is the most instructive decision in Claude Code's architecture because it violates conventional wisdom and is exactly right. Understanding why it is right teaches more about architectural decision-making than any textbook.

The Decision

Claude Code uses a global mutable singleton for application state: a single object with 250+ fields, accessed through approximately 130 typed accessor functions. Not dependency injection. Not a service container. Not event sourcing.

Every senior engineer reading this just flinched. Global mutable state is the first thing you learn to avoid. It makes testing hard. It creates implicit dependencies. It resists refactoring. The entire dependency injection ecosystem exists to solve the problems that global state creates.

And yet, for this system, global state is the correct choice.

The Constraints That Change Everything

Three constraints specific to Claude Code's domain make DI the wrong choice:

Constraint 1: Single process, single thread. A CLI agent runs as one process with one user. There is no concurrent mutation. The primary argument for DI — isolating dependencies to manage concurrency — does not apply. There is no race condition to prevent because there is only one execution context.

Constraint 2: Deep call stacks. The path from a user prompt to tool execution to permission evaluation to bash security analysis traverses 15+ function calls. With DI, every function in that chain needs a context parameter:

// With DI: context parameter in every signature
function handlePrompt(ctx: AppContext, prompt: string): Promise<Response> {
  const assembled = assembleContext(ctx, prompt);
  const response = await callApi(ctx, assembled);
  for (const tool of response.toolCalls) {
    const result = await executeTool(ctx, tool);
  }
}

// With global state: clean signatures
function handlePrompt(prompt: string): Promise<Response> {
  const assembled = assembleContext(prompt);
  const response = await callApi(assembled);
  for (const tool of response.toolCalls) {
    const result = await executeTool(tool);
  }
}

Across hundreds of functions, the ctx parameter becomes noise. It appears in every signature but most functions only read one or two fields. The signal-to-noise ratio of the code degrades measurably.

Constraint 3: Cross-cutting concerns. Telemetry, cost tracking, session identity, model usage, and feature flags are accessed from every architectural layer. In a DI framework, these become "singleton-scoped" services — which is global state with an abstraction layer on top. The abstraction buys you nothing in a single-process application. It is complexity without benefit.

The Trade-Offs Accepted

The engineering team did not pretend global state has no costs. They enumerated them and designed mitigations:

Test isolation. Every test must start with a clean state. The solution: a resetStateForTests() function that overwrites every field with fresh defaults, called in beforeEach. This is boilerplate, but it is straightforward boilerplate.

Implicit dependencies. When a function calls getSessionId(), the dependency on global state is invisible in the function signature. The mitigation: accessor functions are grep-able. getSessionId() finds every consumer. setSessionId() finds every mutation point.

Refactoring difficulty. Removing a state field requires finding all accessor calls. The mitigation: the accessor pattern (not exporting the raw state object) means field renames require changing one accessor, not 50+ direct property accesses.

The Guard Rails

Global state without discipline is a disaster. Three patterns prevent it:

  1. No direct export of the state object. Only accessor functions are exported. STATE.sessionId = "oops" cannot appear in arbitrary files.

  2. Atomic update functions. Fields that must change together have a single update function. switchSession() atomically updates sessionId, sessionProjectDir, and emits a signal. There is no separate setSessionId().

  3. Import DAG leaf constraint. The state module has zero imports from the rest of the codebase. An ESLint rule enforces this. The state module can be imported by any module without creating circular dependencies.

The Decision Through the ADR Lens

Let us write the ADR for this decision:

# ADR-001: Global Mutable State for Application State

## Status
Accepted

## Context
Claude Code is a single-process, single-user CLI agent. Call stacks
reach 15+ levels from prompt to tool execution. Cross-cutting concerns
(telemetry, cost tracking, session state, feature flags) are accessed
from every layer. The team considered dependency injection, service
locators, and event sourcing.

## Decision
Use a global mutable singleton accessed through ~130 typed accessor
functions. No direct export of the state object. Atomic update
functions for fields that must change together. ESLint rule enforcing
zero imports in the state module.

## Consequences
- POSITIVE: Clean function signatures (no ctx threading)
- POSITIVE: No abstraction overhead for cross-cutting concerns
- POSITIVE: Simple mental model (one state, one source of truth)
- NEGATIVE: Test isolation requires manual resetStateForTests()
- NEGATIVE: Implicit dependencies (invisible in function signatures)
- NEGATIVE: Cannot easily switch to multi-process without rewrite
- MITIGATED: Accessor pattern makes dependencies grep-able
- MITIGATED: Import DAG constraint prevents circular dependencies

What This Decision Teaches

The decision teaches three principles:

Principle 1: Constraints determine correctness. DI is not universally "better" than global state. It is better under specific constraints (concurrent processes, large teams, multiple implementations). Change the constraints (single process, single user, deep call stacks) and the calculus inverts. The textbook answer is wrong when the textbook's assumptions do not match your reality.

Principle 2: Accept trade-offs explicitly. The team did not choose global state because they did not know about DI. They chose it after evaluating the alternatives and accepting the costs. The costs are documented. The mitigations are implemented. This is deliberate engineering, not negligence.

Principle 3: Guard rails make dangerous patterns safe. Global state is dangerous in general. Global state with accessor functions, atomic updates, ESLint enforcement, and test-reset discipline is safe in this specific context. The pattern is not "use global state." The pattern is "use global state with these five guard rails."

7.7 The Decision Cascade

Individual decisions do not exist in isolation. They form a cascade where each decision constrains or enables subsequent ones.

graph TD
    A["Single-process CLI agent"] -->|enables| B["Global mutable state"]
    A -->|requires| C["400ms startup budget"]
    A -->|justifies| D["Monolithic binary"]

    B -->|simplifies| E["Deep call stacks"]
    B -->|requires| F["Test reset discipline"]
    B -->|enables| G["Cache latching"]

    C -->|drives| H["Parallel I/O in bootstrap"]
    C -->|drives| I["Compile-time flag elimination"]

    D -->|enables| J["Shared types, no schema drift"]
    D -->|combined with| I

    G -->|driven by| K["Prompt cache economics"]

    style A fill:#e94560,stroke:#1a1a2e,color:#fff
    style K fill:#e94560,stroke:#1a1a2e,color:#fff

The root decision — "this is a single-process CLI agent" — cascades through the entire architecture. It enables global state (no concurrency concerns), requires fast startup (CLI users expect responsiveness), and justifies a monolith (one user, one binary). Global state enables cache latching (simple boolean fields in a singleton). The startup budget drives compile-time flags (smaller binary = faster load). Cache economics shape context compaction strategy (preserve the cached prefix, compact the middle).

This cascade is what coherent architecture looks like. Not a collection of independent "best practices" applied in isolation, but a web of decisions that reinforce each other because they all derive from the same root constraints.

Identifying Root Decisions

When analyzing any system, look for the root decisions — the ones from which everything else follows. In Claude Code:

  • "Single-process CLI" is a root decision. Everything about state management, startup, and deployment follows from it.
  • "Global state" is a derived decision. It follows from the root, enabled by the single-process constraint.
  • "Cache latching" is a leaf decision. It follows from global state and cache economics.

Changing a leaf decision is cheap. Changing a root decision is a rewrite. Know which is which before you start.

7.8 Making Decisions Under Uncertainty

Most real decisions happen with incomplete information. You do not know the future traffic pattern. You do not know which feature will be most popular. You do not know whether the third-party API will change its rate limits.

The 70% Rule

Make the decision when you have 70% of the information you wish you had. At 50%, you are guessing. At 90%, you have wasted time gathering information that will not change the outcome. The 70% threshold is the sweet spot where you have enough data to make a defensible choice without analysis paralysis.

Reversibility as a Decision Accelerator

The 70% rule has a corollary: lower the threshold for reversible decisions. If you can undo it in an afternoon, decide at 50%. If undoing it takes six months, wait until 85%.

Claude Code's dual feature flag system embodies this principle:

  • Runtime flags (GrowthBook): Reversible in seconds. No deployment needed. Decide fast, adjust based on data.
  • Compile-time flags: Reversible only with a new release. Decide carefully, because rolling back requires a deploy cycle.

The system design itself encodes the reversibility of each decision type.

Documenting Uncertainty

The most valuable thing you can add to an ADR is an explicit statement of what you did not know:

## Unknowns at Decision Time
- We do not know if the model output distribution will change with
  future model versions. The 8K default assumes p99 < 5K tokens.
  If future models produce longer output, the escalation will fire
  more frequently, adding latency.
- We do not know if cache economics will change. The 7x cost
  difference between cache hit and miss drives cache latching.
  If pricing changes, this optimization may become unnecessary.

These unknowns are the most useful part of the ADR two years later. When the model does produce longer output and the escalation fires on 10% of requests instead of 1%, the unknown statement tells the future engineer exactly which assumption changed and what to revisit.

Key Principles

1. Architecture is decisions, not diagrams. The boxes and arrows are consequences of decisions. Document the decisions, and the diagrams draw themselves.

2. ADRs are thinking tools, not compliance artifacts. The value is in writing them (forcing clarity), not in reading them (though that helps too).

3. Use trade-off matrices when intuition fails. When the decision space is too large for gut feel, structure it. Then override the matrix with judgment if it misses something important.

4. Calibrate deliberation to reversibility. One-way doors deserve ADRs, matrices, and reviews. Two-way doors deserve a quick decision and a willingness to course-correct.

5. Constraints determine correctness. The "right" pattern depends on the constraints. Global state is wrong in general and right for a single-process CLI. Know your constraints before reaching for conventions.

6. Document what you don't know. The most valuable line in an ADR is the one that says "we assumed X, and if X changes, revisit this decision."

7. Decisions cascade. Root decisions constrain derived decisions. Know which decisions are root (expensive to change) and which are leaf (cheap to change).

Think About It

Exercise 1: Identify the Root Decision Take a system you work on. List ten architectural decisions. For each, trace it back: does it derive from another decision on the list? Which decisions are roots (nothing else forces them) and which are derived? What would change if you reversed a root decision?

Exercise 2: Write the ADR for a "Wrong" Decision Find a decision in your codebase that violates conventional wisdom (a large file that "should" be split, a pattern that "should" be different, a dependency that "should" be abstracted). Write an ADR for it. Can you articulate why it is right in context? If you cannot, it might actually be wrong — and now you have the framework to fix it.

Exercise 3: The Reversibility Audit List five decisions you made in the last month. For each, estimate the time to reverse it (hours, days, weeks, months). For each, estimate the time you spent deliberating. Did you spend proportionally more time on the harder-to-reverse decisions? If not, recalibrate.

Exercise 4: Build a Trade-Off Matrix Choose a decision you are currently facing (library choice, API design, infrastructure selection). Build a trade-off matrix with at least five criteria. Weight the criteria. Score the options. Does the matrix agree with your intuition? If not, examine why — did you weight a criterion incorrectly, or is your intuition wrong?

Exercise 5: The Decision Cascade Draw the decision cascade for your system, following the format in Section 7.7. Start with the root decisions (deployment model, language, single/multi-tenant) and trace how they constrain everything downstream. Find one derived decision that conflicts with its root — a place where the architecture is internally inconsistent. What would it take to resolve the inconsistency?

Chapter 8: Managing Complexity

Complexity is the only enemy that never surrenders. Features ship, bugs get fixed, requirements evolve, deadlines pass — but complexity only grows. Every line of code, every configuration option, every integration point adds to the complexity budget. And unlike a financial budget, there is no explicit ledger. The balance is invisible until the day an engineer opens the codebase and cannot understand what it does.

This chapter provides that ledger. We will distinguish essential complexity (inherent to the problem) from accidental complexity (introduced by the solution). We will model complexity as a budget that every feature withdraws from. We will examine state — the root cause of most complexity — and the tools that tame it: immutability, isolation, and encapsulation. We will confront the hardest question in software design: when to add abstraction and when to tolerate duplication. And we will dissect Claude Code's permission system, a subsystem that manages extraordinary complexity — six permission modes, eight rule sources, a three-tier AI classifier — through clear layering that keeps each piece comprehensible even as the whole system is vast.

8.1 Essential vs. Accidental Complexity

Fred Brooks drew this distinction in "No Silver Bullet" (1986), and forty years later it remains the most useful lens for evaluating any system's design.

Essential complexity is what the problem demands. A shell parser must handle every quoting rule, every heredoc variant, every pipe syntax. A permission system that serves solo developers, enterprise teams, and CI pipelines must handle diverse configuration sources. This complexity cannot be reduced without reducing the problem's scope.

Accidental complexity is what the solution introduces. A shell parser that also has a plugin system for adding custom syntax rules that nobody uses. A permission system that stores its state in three different formats because two engineers built it at different times. This complexity can be eliminated without affecting the problem's coverage.

The Diagnostic Question

When examining any component, ask: "If I built this from scratch today, knowing everything I know now, would this piece exist?"

If the answer is yes, the complexity is essential. The piece exists because the problem demands it.

If the answer is no, the complexity is accidental. The piece exists because of historical accidents, premature optimization, or a misunderstanding of the requirements.

Most systems are 30-50% accidental complexity. The ratio rarely improves over time because each new feature introduces both essential complexity (the feature itself) and accidental complexity (integration with existing accidental complexity). It compounds.

Essential Complexity in Claude Code

Claude Code's Bash parser is 4,400 lines. This seems excessive until you enumerate what it must handle:

  • Single quotes (no escaping, no variable expansion)
  • Double quotes (escaping, variable expansion, command substitution)
  • Heredocs (<<EOF, <<'EOF', <<-EOF — three variants with different semantics)
  • Command substitution ($(...) and backticks, including nesting)
  • Process substitution (<(...) and >(...))
  • Piping (|, |&)
  • Redirections (>, >>, 2>, &>, 2>&1, and many more)
  • Semicolons, &&, ||, subshells, brace expansion
  • Security analysis of each construct (is this command safe?)

Each of these is a real shell feature that real users type. The parser must handle all of them because a security tool that misses a case creates a vulnerability. The 4,400 lines are essential complexity. You cannot build a secure shell parser in fewer lines without leaving holes.

The question "could this file be split into smaller files?" misses the point. Splitting the tokenizer, parser, and AST builder into three files would not reduce complexity. It would scatter related logic across files and add inter-file coordination — accidental complexity introduced by the "solution" of splitting.

The Cohesion Test

A file should be large when splitting it would increase total complexity. The heuristic from the Claude Code architecture: if you can draw a line through the file such that the code above the line never calls the code below the line, the file should be split at that line. If every section calls every other section, the file is a cohesive unit and should remain whole.

The REPL screen is 5,000 lines with 80+ React hooks. Each hook depends on several others: the scroll hook depends on the output hook, the permission dialog hook depends on the tool execution hook, the input hook depends on the model state hook. Extracting hooks into separate files would create 80+ files with complex interdependencies — more files, but no less complexity. The file is cohesive. It stays whole.

The 3,000-line utility file with string formatting, date parsing, and HTTP helpers? Split it. Those concerns are independent. The code above the line does not call the code below it.

8.2 The Complexity Budget

A financial budget works because it is explicit: you have $100,000 and every purchase subtracts from it. Complexity does not come with a natural ledger, but you can create one.

The Model

Imagine every feature in your system has a complexity cost:

Feature Complexity Cost Justification
Core agent loop 30 units Essential: the system's reason for existing
Permission system 25 units Essential: safety is non-negotiable
Tool architecture 20 units Essential: extensibility is a core requirement
Configuration cascade 15 units Mixed: 7 layers serve 4 stakeholders (essential), dual settings systems (accidental)
Context compaction 10 units Essential: without it, sessions die at context limits
Session persistence 5 units Essential but bounded: JSONL append-only log
Cache latching 3 units Essential: 7x cost savings justify 3 units of complexity
Custom Ink fork 15 units Mixed: flexbox and virtual DOM essential, but forking adds maintenance burden

The numbers are relative and subjective — the point is not precision but discipline. Every new feature proposal should estimate its complexity cost and justify the withdrawal:

"Adding webhook notifications costs 8 complexity units (new subsystem, configuration, retry logic, credential management). It is justified because it enables enterprise CI/CD integration, which 30% of enterprise customers have requested."

Versus:

"Adding a fifth log level costs 1 complexity unit. It is not justified because four log levels already cover all use cases, and the fifth adds a distinction that nobody will consistently maintain."

The Budget Limit

Every system has an implicit complexity budget. Exceed it and the system becomes unmaintainable — not in a dramatic collapse, but in a gradual erosion of development velocity. The symptoms:

  • New features take 3x longer than they "should"
  • Bug fixes introduce new bugs
  • Onboarding takes months instead of weeks
  • Engineers avoid touching certain subsystems
  • The test suite takes so long that developers skip it

The budget is roughly proportional to the team's cognitive capacity. A team of 5 senior engineers can maintain a system of, say, 300 complexity units. A team of 20 can maintain 1,000. A solo developer can maintain about 100.

When Claude Code tolerates a 5,000-line file, it is spending less budget, not more. Five thousand lines in one cohesive file costs less cognitive overhead than twenty 250-line files with complex import graphs. The complexity is the same — the cognitive overhead of navigating it differs.

Deposits and Withdrawals

Most engineering discussions focus on complexity withdrawals (adding features). Equally important are complexity deposits — activities that reduce the system's complexity:

Withdrawal Deposit
Adding a new feature Removing a feature nobody uses
Supporting a new platform Dropping support for an old platform
Adding a configuration option Choosing a sensible default and removing the option
Integrating a new dependency Inlining a dependency that provides one function
Adding a new tool to the registry Marking rarely-used tools as deferred (progressive disclosure)

Claude Code's deferred tool loading is a complexity deposit. Instead of sending all 35+ tool schemas (12,000+ tokens) in every API request, it sends just the tool names for rarely-used tools. The model knows they exist. It pays the full token cost only when it needs one. The system became simpler to reason about (fewer tool schemas in context) and cheaper to run (fewer tokens processed).

8.3 State: The Root of All Complexity

If you trace most bugs, most confusion, and most architectural headaches to their root cause, you find state. Not algorithms. Not interfaces. Not data structures. State — mutable values that change over time and must be kept consistent with each other.

Why State Is Hard

A stateless function is trivially correct: same input, same output, every time. Add one piece of mutable state and you have doubled the complexity: the function's behavior now depends on both its input and the state, and the state can change between calls. Add ten pieces of mutable state and you have a combinatorial explosion: the function's behavior depends on the interaction of ten independent variables.

Claude Code's global state has 250+ fields. In theory, that creates 2^250 possible states — more than atoms in the universe. In practice, most combinations are impossible (you cannot be in session and not in session simultaneously), but the point stands: state creates combinatorial complexity that grows exponentially.

The Three Tools for Managing State

Three strategies tame state complexity:

Immutability

Make data read-only after creation. An immutable value cannot be corrupted by a concurrent reader, cannot be accidentally modified by a helper function, and cannot drift out of sync with a related value because it never changes.

Claude Code's session persistence uses JSONL — an append-only log where each line is a JSON message. Messages are written once and never modified. Replaying the session is just reading the file line by line. There is no "update in place" operation that could corrupt the log. The replay algorithm is a pure function from the log contents to the session state: same file, same session, every time.

Immutability is not free. It costs memory (you keep old versions) and sometimes performance (you create new objects instead of modifying existing ones). But for data that crosses boundaries — function arguments, API responses, cached values — immutability eliminates entire categories of bugs.

Isolation

Limit who can see and modify each piece of state. The fewer components that access a state variable, the fewer opportunities for inconsistency.

Claude Code's accessor pattern is isolation applied to global state:

// NOT exported: nobody can access directly
const STATE = { sessionId: '', model: 'sonnet', ... };

// Exported: controlled read access
export function getSessionId(): string { return STATE.sessionId; }

// Exported: controlled write access with validation
export function switchSession(id: string, projectDir: string): void {
  STATE.sessionId = id;
  STATE.sessionProjectDir = projectDir;
  emitSignal('session-changed');
}

There is no setSessionId() function. The only way to change the session ID is through switchSession(), which atomically updates the session ID, the project directory, and emits a notification. This isolation prevents a bug where the session ID changes but the project directory does not — a state inconsistency that would be invisible until a tool reads a file from the wrong directory.

Encapsulation

Hide the representation of state behind an interface. The consumer knows what the state provides (a session ID), not how it is stored (a field on a global object, a database row, an environment variable).

The permission system's session memory cache illustrates this. To the rest of the system, the cache is simple: "has the user approved this pattern?" How the cache stores the approval (a Map<string, Decision>), how it generalizes patterns (exact match vs. prefix match), and how it invalidates entries (on mode change, on /clear, on session end) are all hidden behind a single checkSessionMemory(toolCall) function.

This encapsulation means the cache implementation can change entirely — from a map to a trie, from in-memory to persisted — without affecting any caller. The complexity of the cache is contained within the cache module.

8.4 Layering: The Master Strategy

When essential complexity is large, the only viable strategy is layering: organizing the system so that each layer deals with one level of abstraction, each layer has a clear contract with its neighbors, and understanding any single layer does not require understanding the whole system.

What Makes a Good Layer

A layer is effective when it satisfies three properties:

  1. Internal consistency. Everything within the layer uses the same abstractions, the same terminology, and the same conventions.

  2. Narrow interface. The layer communicates with adjacent layers through a small, well-defined contract. The more you can hide behind the layer boundary, the less the rest of the system needs to know.

  3. Independent comprehensibility. A new engineer can understand the layer by reading its code and its contract with adjacent layers. They do not need to understand the layers above or below to work within this layer.

The TCP/IP stack is the canonical example: each layer (physical, data link, network, transport, application) is independently comprehensible. An engineer working on HTTP does not need to understand Ethernet frame encoding. An engineer working on TCP does not need to understand HTTP semantics.

Layering Applied to Claude Code's Configuration

The configuration cascade from the architecture book has seven layers, but conceptually it is three:

graph TB
    subgraph "Layer 3: Resolution"
        R["Merge algorithm<br/>Schema validation<br/>Hot-reload watcher"]
    end

    subgraph "Layer 2: Sources"
        S1["Built-in defaults"]
        S2["MDM / Enterprise policy"]
        S3["User settings"]
        S4["Project settings"]
        S5["Local settings"]
        S6["Environment variables"]
        S7["CLI arguments"]
    end

    subgraph "Layer 1: Consumption"
        C["getModel(), getPermissionMode(),<br/>getEffortLevel(), ..."]
    end

    R --> S1 & S2 & S3 & S4 & S5 & S6 & S7
    C --> R

    style R fill:#16213e,stroke:#0f3460,color:#fff
    style C fill:#533483,stroke:#e94560,color:#fff
