Input chunkₙ → Process → Output chunkₙ

Streaming is harder but delivers lower latency. The user sees the first word of the response within 500ms, rather than waiting 10 seconds for the complete response. For a CLI tool where responsiveness determines the user experience, this latency advantage is decisive.

The Hybrid: Batch Boundaries in a Streaming Pipeline

Claude Code's streaming pipeline is streaming at the token level but batch at the block level. Text deltas stream to the renderer immediately — every token appears as the model generates it. But tool-use deltas accumulate in a buffer until the entire JSON input is received, then get parsed and dispatched as a batch.

graph TB
    subgraph "Streaming Path (text)"
        TD1["text_delta: 'Let me '"] --> R1["Render immediately"]
        TD2["text_delta: 'check '"] --> R2["Render immediately"]
        TD3["text_delta: 'that.'"] --> R3["Render immediately"]
    end

    subgraph "Batch Path (tool use)"
        JD1["json_delta: '{\"file_'"] --> BUF["Buffer"]
        JD2["json_delta: 'path\":\"'"] --> BUF
        JD3["json_delta: 'src/main.ts\"}'"] --> BUF
        BUF --> PARSE["Parse complete JSON"]
        PARSE --> EXEC["Dispatch tool"]
    end

This hybrid exists because text and tool-use data have different requirements. Text can be rendered incrementally — displaying half a sentence is useful (the user reads along). But half a JSON object is useless and cannot be parsed. The data's nature dictates the processing mode.

The principle generalizes: use streaming when partial data is useful, batch when partial data is meaningless. Log entries can be streamed (each line is independent). SQL transactions must be batched (a partial transaction is worse than no transaction). Image data can be streamed for progressive display. Cryptographic signatures must be batched (you need the complete message to verify).

Choosing the Processing Mode

Criterion Streaming Batch
Latency requirement Low (interactive) Tolerant (background)
Partial data value Useful Useless or dangerous
Memory constraint Tight (can't hold all data) Relaxed
Processing complexity Simple per-item logic Complex cross-item logic
Error recovery Per-item retry Full restart
Ordering guarantee Natural (arrival order) Requires explicit sort

Backpressure: The Hidden Architecture

When a producer generates data faster than a consumer can process it, something must give. That "something" is backpressure — the mechanism by which a slow consumer signals a fast producer to slow down. Backpressure is invisible in working systems and catastrophic in broken ones.

The Problem Concrete

Claude Code's streaming pipeline has an explicit backpressure scenario. The language model generates tokens at roughly 100 tokens per second. The terminal renderer must parse markdown, apply syntax highlighting, and write to stdout. On a slow terminal — an SSH session over a satellite link, a terminal with complex ligature rendering, a screen reader processing output — rendering takes longer than token generation.

Without backpressure, the pipeline buffers tokens in memory. A 64K-token response generates roughly 16,000 delta events. If the renderer processes 1,000 per second and the model produces 3,000 per second, the buffer grows by 2,000 events per second. Over a 30-second generation, 60,000 events accumulate in memory. The process eventually runs out of memory or the user sees a frozen terminal followed by a flood of text.

Pull vs. Push

Two fundamental approaches to flow control:

Push-based: The producer pushes data to the consumer. The consumer must process it or buffer it. Flow control requires explicit signals — the consumer tells the producer "pause" and "resume." This is the observer pattern, event emitters, and callback-based architectures.

Pull-based: The consumer pulls data from the producer when it is ready. The producer blocks until the consumer pulls. Flow control is implicit — the producer simply cannot produce faster than the consumer pulls.

Claude Code's streaming pipeline uses the pull-based approach via async generators:

async function* processStream(
  rawStream: AsyncIterable<RawSSEEvent>
): AsyncGenerator<ProcessedEvent> {
  for await (const raw of rawStream) {
    const processed = processEvent(raw)
    yield processed  // Pauses until consumer pulls
  }
}

The yield statement is the backpressure mechanism. When the consumer (the terminal renderer) has not pulled the next event, the generator pauses at yield. This pause propagates through the async iterable chain to the HTTP response stream, which signals TCP flow control to the server. The model's token generation is not affected (it continues into a server-side buffer), but the byte delivery to the client slows down, keeping the client's memory bounded.

Batching Under Pressure

Pure pull-based backpressure has a visual problem: when the renderer is slow, tokens arrive in bursts instead of smoothly. The user sees nothing for 100ms, then a chunk of text, then nothing again. This stuttering is distracting.

The solution is frame-rate batching — accumulate text deltas during a frame budget (16ms for 60fps) and render them as a single chunk:

// Batch deltas into 16ms frames for smooth display
if (elapsed > 16) {
  yield { type: 'batched_text_delta', text: pendingText }
  pendingText = ''
  lastYieldTime = performance.now()
}

This trades individual token latency (each token arrives up to 16ms late) for visual smoothness (the user sees steady text flow). The 16ms budget is not arbitrary — it matches the display refresh cycle. Humans cannot perceive latency below 16ms, so the delay is invisible while the batching eliminates stutter.

Backpressure as Architecture

Backpressure is not an optimization you add later. It is a fundamental architectural property that must be designed from the start. A pipeline without backpressure is a pipeline with an implicit unbounded buffer — and unbounded buffers always fill up eventually.

The design checklist for every pipeline stage:

  1. What is my input rate? The maximum rate at which the upstream stage produces data.
  2. What is my processing rate? The rate at which I can transform and emit data.
  3. What happens when input rate exceeds processing rate? Buffer (bounded), drop, slow the producer, or error.
  4. Who controls the flow? The producer, the consumer, or an external coordinator.

System Prompt Assembly: A Pipeline Case Study

Claude Code's system prompt assembly is one of the most architecturally significant data pipelines in the system. Before every API call, the system assembles a prompt from 10+ sections, each drawn from a different source. The design of this pipeline determines prompt cache hit rates, context window utilization, and — ultimately — the quality of the model's responses.

The Stability Gradient

The system prompt blocks are ordered by stability — how frequently they change:

graph LR
    subgraph "Stable (rarely change)"
        B1["Identity Block"]
        B2["Tool Definitions (52 tools)"]
        B3["Model-Specific Instructions"]
    end

    subgraph "Semi-stable (change across sessions)"
        B4["Project Rules (.claude/rules/)"]
        B5["Memory (CLAUDE.md, auto-memory)"]
    end

    subgraph "Dynamic (change between turns)"
        B6["Active Skills"]
        B7["Session Context (cwd, git status)"]
        B8["MCP Server Descriptions"]
    end

    subgraph "Volatile (change every turn)"
        B9["Custom Instructions"]
        B10["Plan Context"]
    end

    B1 --> B2 --> B3 --> B4 --> B5 --> B6 --> B7 --> B8 --> B9 --> B10

    B10 --> CACHE["Cache Control Marker"]

This ordering is not about logical grouping. It is about cache economics. The prompt cache matches on byte-identical prefixes. Everything before the first changed byte is cached. Everything after is re-processed. By placing the most stable blocks first, the maximum prefix is cacheable.

A concrete example: the identity block and tool definitions are roughly 15,000 tokens. If these are stable across turns, the cache saves 15,000 tokens of input processing on every API call. At $3 per million input tokens, a session with 50 API calls saves $2.25 from this single optimization. Multiply by millions of sessions and the economics are decisive.

The design constraint this creates: no block can depend on a block after it in the ordering. If the identity block referenced the current active skill, it would change every time a skill was invoked, breaking the cache for all subsequent blocks. Dependencies must flow forward (later blocks can reference earlier ones), never backward.

Deterministic Assembly

The assembly pipeline is a pure function: given the same inputs, it produces the same output byte for byte. This determinism enables three things:

  1. Snapshot testing. Record the assembled prompt for a set of inputs, store it as a test fixture, and assert future assemblies match. Any drift indicates a bug or an intentional change that needs review.

  2. Cache stability analysis. Compare the assembled prompts from consecutive turns. If only the last two blocks differ, the cache prefix covers blocks 1-8. If an early block changed unexpectedly, investigate why.

  3. Debugging model behavior. When the model produces unexpected output, dump the assembled prompt. The prompt is what the model saw. If the prompt is wrong, the output is a symptom, not the problem.

Determinism requires discipline. Tool definitions must be sorted by name (not hash-order, which varies between runs). Feature flags must be latched at session start (not re-evaluated per turn, which could change mid-session). MCP tool schemas must be placed after core tools (so adding an MCP server does not shift core tool bytes).

The Rendering Pipeline: Data Flow to the User's Eyes

The final stage of the data flow pipeline transforms structured data into pixels on a terminal. This is not a trivial serialization step — it is a complex incremental parser that must handle markdown formatting, syntax highlighting, code blocks, and ANSI escape codes, all while tokens arrive one at a time.

Incremental Markdown Parsing

Markdown is not designed for incremental parsing. A ** token could be the start of bold text or the end of bold text, depending on what comes later. A ` could be the start of an inline code span or a literal backtick. The renderer must make provisional decisions and revise them as more tokens arrive.

The state the renderer maintains:

- Am I inside a code block? (``` ... ```)
- Am I inside an inline code span? (` ... `)
- Am I inside bold? (** ... **)
- Am I inside italic? (* ... *)
- Am I inside a heading? (# ...)
- What indentation level am I at?
- Is the current line a list item?

Each text delta updates this state. Most updates are simple (append text to the current context). Some require retrospective correction (a * that looked like italic turns out to be a bullet point at the start of a new line).

The rendering pipeline handles this by separating parsing from rendering:

Text delta → Incremental parser → Parse tree update → Renderer → ANSI output → Terminal

The parser maintains a mutable parse tree. Each delta extends the tree (append a text node, open a formatting span, close a code block). The renderer walks the updated portions of the tree and produces ANSI escape sequences for the terminal. Only the changed portions are re-rendered — the renderer does not reprocess the entire output on every delta.

This incremental approach is what makes streaming feel instant. The user sees each word appear with correct formatting as the model generates it. A batch approach (wait for the complete response, then render) would be simpler but would destroy the responsiveness that makes a CLI agent feel alive.

Data Flow Reveals Component Boundaries

One of the most powerful consequences of data flow thinking: the natural component boundaries in a system align with the transformation boundaries in the data flow.

In Claude Code's message pipeline, the natural components are:

Component Input Output Boundary
REPL Keystrokes User prompt string Human-machine interface
Context injector Prompt string + env state Enriched user message Context assembly
System prompt assembler Rules, skills, memory, tools System prompt blocks Static → dynamic
API client Request params SSE event stream Network boundary
Stream state machine Raw SSE events Typed content blocks Protocol parsing
Text renderer Text deltas ANSI terminal output Data → presentation
Tool dispatcher Tool-use blocks Tool results Computation boundary
Conversation manager New messages Updated history State management

Each component exists because the data transformation at that point is fundamentally different from the transformations before and after. The context injector combines data from multiple sources (working directory, git status, user preferences) into a single message — that merging operation defines the component. The stream state machine parses a byte-level protocol into typed events — that parsing operation defines the component.

When engineers struggle with "where should I put this code?", the data flow answer is: put it at the stage where the data transformation happens. If you are adding a feature that transforms tool results before they enter the conversation, it belongs in the conversation manager. If you are adding a feature that modifies the system prompt based on the current file, it belongs in the system prompt assembler.

Anti-Pattern: Cross-Cutting Data Access

The worst violation of data flow architecture is when a component reaches across stages to access data it should not know about. A renderer that queries the conversation history to decide how to format text. A tool dispatcher that modifies the system prompt. An API client that reads user preferences directly.

These cross-cutting accesses create invisible dependencies. When you change the conversation history format, the renderer breaks. When you refactor the system prompt assembly, the tool dispatcher produces different results. The data flow diagram shows clean pipeline stages; the actual code is a web of hidden connections.

The fix is strict interface enforcement: each stage receives data only from its input and produces data only through its output. If a stage needs additional data, it must arrive as an explicit input, not as a side-channel read from shared state.

Error Propagation in Pipelines

Errors in a pipeline can originate at any stage. The question is not whether errors will happen but how they propagate. Three strategies:

Strategy 1: Fail Fast

The error halts the pipeline immediately. No downstream stages execute. The error propagates to the caller.

Use when: The error makes downstream processing meaningless. If the API client cannot connect, there is no stream to parse, no tool to dispatch, no text to render. Fail fast.

Strategy 2: Error as Data

The error becomes a datum in the pipeline. Downstream stages process it as a special case of their normal input.

Use when: The error is recoverable at a later stage. In Claude Code, a malformed SSE event becomes an Error state in the streaming state machine. The state machine does not crash — it logs the violation, stays in its current state, and waits for the next valid event. The error is absorbed rather than propagated.

Strategy 3: Parallel Error Channel

Errors flow through a separate channel from normal data. This is the Result<T, E> pattern — every stage returns either a success value or an error, and the pipeline branches on which it is.

Use when: Error handling logic is complex and should not pollute the normal data path. Claude Code's streaming pipeline uses this for partial response recovery: when a disconnect occurs mid-stream, the error channel carries information about what was received (which complete content blocks exist, whether the JSON buffer is parseable), while the normal channel carries the successfully-received data.

Recovery at Pipeline Boundaries

The most effective recovery happens at pipeline boundaries — the points where data changes form. If the API client fails (network boundary), retry at the network level. If the JSON parser fails (protocol boundary), retry parsing with error-tolerant mode. If the renderer fails (presentation boundary), fall back to plain text.

Recovery at non-boundary points is usually wrong. Retrying a single token in the middle of a stream does not make sense. Retrying a single block in the system prompt assembly creates an inconsistent prompt. Recovery is a stage-level operation, not a datum-level operation.

Monitoring Data Flow

You cannot optimize what you cannot measure. For data flow architectures, the critical metrics are:

Throughput

How many data units per second pass through each stage. In Claude Code's streaming pipeline, the key throughput metrics are:

  • Time to first token (TTFT): Latency from API request to first message_start event. This measures network latency plus model initialization time.
  • Token rate: Tokens per second through the text rendering pipeline. This is the user-perceived speed.
  • Tool dispatch latency: Time from content_block_stop (tool JSON complete) to tool execution start.

Queue Depth

How much data is waiting between stages. A growing queue indicates backpressure failure — the upstream stage is producing faster than the downstream stage consumes.

In Claude Code, the text delta buffer is the primary queue. The batching processor accumulates deltas during each 16ms frame. If the buffer grows beyond a frame's worth of text, the renderer is falling behind.

Error Rate Per Stage

Which stage produces the most errors reveals which transformation is the most fragile. In a typical API streaming session, the SSE parser has the highest error potential (network issues), while the system prompt assembler has the lowest (it operates on local data with no I/O).

Key Principles

  1. Follow the data. Trace every datum from entry to exit. The data flow diagram is the architecture diagram.

  2. Design stages, then components. The data transformations define the natural component boundaries. Do not force data into pre-conceived component shapes.

  3. Use streaming when partial data is useful, batch when it is not. Text renders incrementally. JSON parses in batch. Match the processing mode to the data's nature.

  4. Backpressure is architectural. A pipeline without explicit flow control has an implicit unbounded buffer. Unbounded buffers always fill.

  5. Order by stability for caching. In any assembled output (prompts, configurations, documents), place the most stable content first. This maximizes cache prefix length.

  6. Keep stages independent. Each stage knows only its input type and output type. No cross-cutting data access. No reaching around stages to read shared state.

  7. Recovery happens at boundaries. Retry at the stage level, not the datum level. Network errors retry at the network boundary. Parse errors retry at the protocol boundary.

Think About It

  1. Map a data flow you own. Pick a feature in your current system. Trace a single user action from input to final output. How many transformations does the data undergo? Where are the resting points? Where could data be corrupted? Did you find any cross-cutting accesses that violate stage independence?

  2. Batch-streaming boundary. You are building a system that receives a stream of financial transactions. Each transaction must be validated against the user's current balance (which requires querying a database). Where do you place the batch boundary? What are the tradeoffs of validating each transaction individually (streaming) versus collecting a batch and validating the set?

  3. Backpressure audit. Examine a producer-consumer relationship in your codebase. What happens when the consumer is 10x slower than the producer? Is there explicit flow control? What is the maximum memory consumed by the intermediate buffer? What happens when that maximum is exceeded — does the system degrade gracefully or crash?

  4. Cache stability analysis. Take a configuration or prompt that is assembled from multiple sources and sent repeatedly. Are the sources ordered by stability? Could you reorder them to improve caching? What is the cost of a cache miss, and how often does it happen?

  5. Error channel design. You have a 5-stage pipeline where stage 3 occasionally produces invalid output. The current behavior is to crash the pipeline. Design an alternative: should the error become data (skip the bad item), trigger a retry (re-run stage 3), or flow through a parallel error channel? What information does each downstream stage need about the error to make correct decisions?

Chapter 14: State Machines Everywhere

Most bugs are state bugs. Not off-by-one errors, not null pointer dereferences, not syntax mistakes — state bugs. A variable that should be true is false. A connection that should be open is closing. A session that should be active is paused but the UI thinks it is running. Two fields that must change together get updated one at a time, and another thread reads the intermediate state.

State bugs are the hardest to reproduce, the hardest to diagnose, and the hardest to fix, because the system's behavior depends not on what it is doing now but on everything it has done before. The current state is the accumulation of every transition since initialization. When the state is wrong, you must trace backward through every transition to find the one that went astray.

Explicit state machines eliminate entire categories of these bugs. When you model your system as a finite set of states with defined transitions between them, three things happen: illegal states become unrepresentable, invalid transitions become compile-time errors, and the system's behavior becomes a diagram you can stare at on a whiteboard. Claude Code models its streaming pipeline, session lifecycle, and permission resolution as explicit state machines. The bugs they prevent are the bugs you never see — and never have to debug at 2 AM.

The Cost of Implicit State

Before we discuss explicit state machines, consider what happens without them. Implicit state is state that exists in the code but has no formal model — it lives in boolean flags, enum-like strings, and conditional chains that implicitly encode what the system is "doing."

Here is an implicit state model for a streaming connection:

// Implicit state — scattered across variables
let isConnected = false
let isStreaming = false
let hasError = false
let isRetrying = false
let buffer: string[] = []

This looks reasonable. Five booleans, a buffer. But how many states can this represent? Five booleans give 2^5 = 32 possible combinations. How many of those combinations are valid?

  • isConnected=false, isStreaming=true: Streaming without a connection? Invalid.
  • isRetrying=true, isStreaming=true: Retrying and streaming simultaneously? Invalid.
  • hasError=true, isConnected=true, isStreaming=true: Error but still connected and streaming? Maybe valid — depends on the error type.
  • isConnected=true, isStreaming=false, isRetrying=true: Connected but retrying? Invalid.

Of 32 possible states, perhaps 6-8 are valid. The other 24-26 are illegal states that the code does not prevent. Every bug in this system is a path that reaches one of those illegal states. And every if statement that checks these flags is an implicit transition that may or may not maintain the invariants.

Now count the transitions. With 5 booleans, each of which can be set or cleared independently, there are 10 possible mutations per step. With 8 valid states and 10 mutations, you have 80 possible transitions — most of which are invalid but not prevented.

This combinatorial explosion is why implicit state produces bugs. The developer cannot hold 80 transitions in their head. They write code that handles the common paths and hope the uncommon ones never happen.

The Explicit State Machine

An explicit state machine replaces scattered booleans with a single state variable and a defined transition table. Here is the same streaming connection modeled explicitly:

type StreamState =
  | 'Idle'
  | 'Connecting'
  | 'Streaming'
  | 'Error'
  | 'Recovering'
  | 'Done'

type StreamEvent =
  | { type: 'connect' }
  | { type: 'message_start' }
  | { type: 'data'; payload: string }
  | { type: 'disconnect' }
  | { type: 'error'; error: Error }
  | { type: 'retry' }
  | { type: 'complete' }

function transition(state: StreamState, event: StreamEvent): StreamState {
  switch (state) {
    case 'Idle':
      if (event.type === 'connect') return 'Connecting'
      break
    case 'Connecting':
      if (event.type === 'message_start') return 'Streaming'
      if (event.type === 'error') return 'Error'
      break
    case 'Streaming':
      if (event.type === 'data') return 'Streaming' // self-transition
      if (event.type === 'disconnect') return 'Error'
      if (event.type === 'complete') return 'Done'
      break
    case 'Error':
      if (event.type === 'retry') return 'Recovering'
      break
    case 'Recovering':
      if (event.type === 'connect') return 'Connecting'
      if (event.type === 'error') return 'Error'
      break
    case 'Done':
      break // terminal state — no transitions
  }
  throw new InvalidTransitionError(state, event)
}

Count the differences from the implicit model:

  1. 6 states instead of 32. Every state is named and meaningful. There is no combination like "connected but not streaming but retrying."

  2. 13 transitions instead of 80. Every valid transition is listed explicitly. Everything else throws an error.

  3. One variable instead of five. The current state is a single discriminated value. There is no way to have inconsistent flags.

  4. The transition function is the specification. Reading the switch statement tells you exactly what the system can do from any state. No hunting through scattered if chains to reconstruct the state model.

Visualizing the Machine

The transition function can be rendered as a diagram — and it should be. State diagrams are the most effective specification format for stateful systems because they show both the states and the transitions in a single visual:

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Idle
    Idle --> Connecting : connect
    Connecting --> Streaming : message_start
    Connecting --> Error : error
    Streaming --> Streaming : data
    Streaming --> Error : disconnect
    Streaming --> Done : complete
    Error --> Recovering : retry
    Recovering --> Connecting : connect
    Recovering --> Error : error
    Done --> [*]

This diagram is the design. Not a documentation artifact generated after the code was written — the design that precedes the code. When a new requirement arrives ("support pause/resume"), you add states and transitions to the diagram first, then update the transition function.

Making Illegal States Unrepresentable

The most powerful technique in state machine design is ensuring that invalid states cannot exist at all — not that they are checked at runtime, but that the type system prevents them from being constructed.

The Boolean Trap

Consider a session with three properties: whether the user has authenticated, whether the session has a valid token, and whether the session is active. The boolean representation:

interface Session {
  isAuthenticated: boolean
  hasValidToken: boolean
  isActive: boolean
}

This allows { isAuthenticated: false, hasValidToken: true, isActive: true } — an active session with a valid token but unauthenticated? That should never happen. But the type system permits it.

The Discriminated Union Solution

Replace the booleans with a discriminated union that only contains valid combinations:

type Session =
  | { state: 'anonymous' }
  | { state: 'authenticating'; challenge: Challenge }
  | { state: 'active'; token: Token; user: User }
  | { state: 'expired'; lastToken: Token; user: User }
  | { state: 'terminated'; reason: string }

Now the token field only exists when the session is active. The user field only exists when the session is active or expired. The challenge field only exists during authenticating. There is no combination of fields that represents an illegal state because each state variant declares exactly which fields exist.

This is what "making illegal states unrepresentable" means in practice. It is not a runtime check ("assert that if isAuthenticated is false then hasValidToken is also false"). It is a compile-time guarantee: the type Session cannot hold an illegal combination.

Claude Code's Session State

Claude Code's session lifecycle (as discussed in Chapter 6's source material) uses this pattern. The session is not a bag of booleans (isCreating, isActive, isPaused, isShuttingDown). It is a discriminated state with explicit transitions:

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Creating : claude invoked

    Creating --> Initializing : UUID generated, transcript opened
    Initializing --> TrustCheck : Config loaded, auth resolved

    TrustCheck --> Active : Directory trusted
    TrustCheck --> Restricted : Trust declined

    Active --> Active : User prompts, tool calls, responses
    Restricted --> Restricted : Limited functionality

    Active --> Resuming : --resume invoked
    Resuming --> Active : Transcript replayed

    Active --> Switching : switchSession() called
    Switching --> Active : New session + project dir

    Active --> Compacting : Context window full
    Compacting --> Active : Conversation summarized

    Active --> ShuttingDown : User exits
    Active --> Crashed : Unexpected termination

    ShuttingDown --> Ended : Cleanup complete
    Crashed --> Ended : No cleanup

    Ended --> Resuming : claude --resume
    Ended --> [*] : No resume

    Restricted --> ShuttingDown : User exits

Each state carries specific data. The Active state has a conversation history, a cost accumulator, and a transcript path. The Resuming state has the session ID being resumed and the transcript being replayed. The Crashed state has no cleanup data — that is the point; cleanup did not happen.

The transition from Active to Switching uses the Atomic Switch Pattern — a single function that updates both sessionId and sessionProjectDir together, with no separate setters exposed. This prevents the invariant violation where one field is updated but the other is not.

State Transition Diagrams as Design Tools

State diagrams are not just documentation. They are design tools that reveal problems before code is written.

Finding Missing Transitions

Draw the state diagram for your system. Then ask for every state: "What happens if [unexpected event] occurs while in this state?" The diagram makes missing transitions visible.

Example: In the streaming state machine, what happens if a disconnect event occurs during the Recovering state? If the diagram does not show this transition, the code probably does not handle it either. Adding the transition to the diagram (Recovering → Error on disconnect) makes the code fix obvious.

Finding Unreachable States

A state with no incoming transitions (except from the initial state) is either the initial state or a dead state that can never be reached. A state with no outgoing transitions is a terminal state — which may be intentional (Done) or a design bug (the system gets stuck).

Walk the diagram from the initial state. Every state should be reachable through some sequence of events. Every non-terminal state should have at least one outgoing transition. Violations indicate either a design error or an unnecessary state that should be removed.

Finding Missing States

The most valuable insight from state diagrams: discovering states that the system implicitly enters but has not formally defined.

In Claude Code's session lifecycle, the Compacting state was not in the original design. Sessions went from Active to Active when compaction happened — it was treated as an operation within the active state. But compaction temporarily changes the session's behavior: new messages cannot be added while compaction is in progress, the model sees a different conversation history (the summary), and certain operations (like session resume) must wait for compaction to complete.

Making Compacting an explicit state with explicit transitions (Active → Compacting on context pressure, Compacting → Active when summarization completes) made these constraints visible and enforceable. Without the explicit state, the code used a boolean flag (isCompacting) that created the same scattered-boolean problems described earlier.

Event Sourcing and State Reconstruction

An event-sourced system stores the sequence of events that caused state transitions, rather than the current state itself. The current state is reconstructed by replaying the event sequence. This pattern has a natural relationship with state machines: the events are the transition triggers, and replaying them walks the state machine from its initial state to the current state.

The JSONL Transcript as Event Log

Claude Code's session transcript is an event log. Every conversation message, tool call, tool result, and state change is recorded as a JSONL entry with a timestamp:

{"type":"session_start","sessionId":"abc-123","timestamp":1712956800000,"cwd":"/project"}
{"type":"message","role":"user","content":"Fix the login bug","timestamp":1712956801000}
{"type":"tool_use","name":"Read","input":{"path":"auth.ts"},"timestamp":1712956802000}
{"type":"tool_result","toolUseId":"tu_01","output":"...","timestamp":1712956803000}
{"type":"message","role":"assistant","content":"Found the issue...","timestamp":1712956810000}
{"type":"session_end","timestamp":1712957000000,"totalCost":0.42,"reason":"user_exit"}

This event log enables session resume. When the user runs claude --resume, the system reads the transcript line by line, reconstructs the conversation history, recomputes accumulated metrics (cost, token counts), and continues from where it left off.

The reconstruction is a state machine replay:

function reconstructSession(transcript: TranscriptEntry[]): SessionState {
  let state: SessionState = initialState()

  for (const entry of transcript) {
    state = applyEvent(state, entry)
  }

  return state
}

function applyEvent(state: SessionState, entry: TranscriptEntry): SessionState {
  switch (entry.type) {
    case 'session_start':
      return { ...state, sessionId: entry.sessionId, cwd: entry.cwd }
    case 'message':
      return {
        ...state,
        messages: [...state.messages, entry],
        messageCount: state.messageCount + 1,
      }
    case 'tool_use':
      return {
        ...state,
        pendingToolCalls: [...state.pendingToolCalls, entry],
      }
    case 'tool_result':
      return {
        ...state,
        pendingToolCalls: state.pendingToolCalls.filter(
          t => t.id !== entry.toolUseId
        ),
        toolResults: [...state.toolResults, entry],
      }
    case 'session_end':
      return { ...state, totalCost: entry.totalCost, ended: true }
  }
}

Why Event Sourcing Over State Snapshots

The alternative to event sourcing is state snapshots — periodically saving the current state to disk. Claude Code's designers chose event sourcing (the JSONL transcript) for three reasons:

Crash safety. Each JSONL entry is an atomic append — if the process crashes mid-write, at most one line is corrupted. All previous entries survive. A state snapshot that corrupts mid-write can lose the entire session.

Auditability. The event log answers "what happened" — not just "what is the current state" but "how did we get here." When debugging a session, the transcript shows every tool call, every response, every state change in chronological order. A state snapshot shows only the end result.

Cheap writes. Appending a single line to a file is O(1) regardless of file size. Writing a full state snapshot is O(n) in the state size, which grows throughout the session.

The tradeoff: reconstruction is O(n) in the event count. Resuming a long session (thousands of events) takes measurable time. Claude Code accepts this tradeoff because resume is infrequent (once per session at most) while writes are constant (every message, every tool call).

The Dual Write Pattern

In practice, Claude Code uses a hybrid approach. The transcript is the source of truth (event sourcing), but the in-memory state is the working copy (state snapshot). Writes go to both:

Event occurs
  ├── Update in-memory state (fast, used for all operations)
  └── Append to transcript file (durable, used for recovery)

This dual write means the in-memory state can drift from the transcript if a write fails. The recovery strategy is to trust the transcript: if the process crashes and restarts, the in-memory state is rebuilt from the transcript, not from a cached snapshot.

Coupled State: The Atomic Switch Pattern

The most dangerous state bugs occur when two fields must change together but can be observed in an intermediate state where one has changed and the other has not.

The Problem

Claude Code's session has two fields that are semantically coupled: sessionId (which session this is) and sessionProjectDir (which project directory this session belongs to). These fields determine where the transcript file is stored:

~/.claude/projects/{hash(sessionProjectDir)}/sessions/{sessionId}.jsonl

If sessionId changes but sessionProjectDir does not, the system looks for the transcript in the wrong directory. If sessionProjectDir changes but sessionId does not, it stores new entries in the wrong project's session list.

With separate setters, this race is trivial to introduce:

// DANGEROUS: Non-atomic update
setSessionId(newId)
// <-- Other code reads sessionId here
//     but sessionProjectDir still points to old directory
//     → reads wrong transcript → corrupt state
setSessionProjectDir(newDir)

The Solution

Expose a single function that updates both fields. Do not expose individual setters:

function switchSession(
  sessionId: SessionId,
  projectDir: string | null = null,
): void {
  // 1. Clean up outgoing session
  STATE.planSlugCache.delete(STATE.sessionId)

  // 2. Atomically update both fields
  STATE.sessionId = sessionId
  STATE.sessionProjectDir = projectDir

  // 3. Notify listeners
  sessionSwitched.emit(sessionId)
}

There is no setSessionId(). There is no setSessionProjectDir(). The only way to change either field is through switchSession(). This is not a convention documented in a style guide. It is a structural constraint: the setter functions do not exist, so they cannot be called.

Generalizing the Pattern

The Atomic Switch Pattern applies whenever you have coupled state — fields that must maintain a mutual invariant:

Coupled Fields Invariant Atomic Function
sessionId + projectDir Point to same session switchSession()
userId + permissions Permissions belong to user switchUser()
host + port Form a valid endpoint setEndpoint(host, port)
minValue + maxValue min <= max setRange(min, max)
width + height Maintain aspect ratio resize(w, h)

The implementation pattern is always the same:

  1. Identify the invariant between the fields.
  2. Create a single function that updates all fields.
  3. Remove individual setters (or make them private).
  4. Emit a signal so observers react to the change as a unit.

Guard Transitions, Not States

A common mistake with state machines is putting validation logic in the wrong place. Engineers check "am I in state X?" before performing an action. The correct approach is to guard the transition, not the state.

Wrong: Guarding the State

function processMessage(msg: Message) {
  if (state !== 'Active') {
    throw new Error('Cannot process messages when not active')
  }
  // process the message
}

This check is scattered everywhere that messages are processed. Every call site must remember to check the state. Missing one check means processing a message in an invalid state.

Right: Guarding the Transition

function transition(current: State, event: Event): State {
  const allowed = TRANSITION_TABLE[current]
  const next = allowed?.[event.type]

  if (!next) {
    throw new InvalidTransitionError(current, event)
  }

  return next
}

The transition function is the single point of control. It does not matter who calls it or from where — invalid transitions are rejected at the gate. There is no way to reach state Processing from state Idle without going through the transition function, which enforces the valid transition path (Idle → Active → Processing).

This centralization has a second benefit: logging. Every transition can be logged in one place:

function transition(current: State, event: Event): State {
  const next = TRANSITION_TABLE[current]?.[event.type]

  if (!next) {
    log.warn('invalid_transition', { current, event })
    return current // graceful degradation
  }

  log.info('state_transition', { from: current, to: next, event: event.type })
  return next
}

This log is invaluable for debugging. When a system is in an unexpected state, the transition log shows exactly how it got there — every event that triggered every transition, in order.

Graceful Degradation in State Machines

Production systems must decide what to do when an invalid transition is attempted. Two strategies:

Strict: Throw on Invalid Transitions

if (!next) {
  throw new InvalidTransitionError(current, event)
}

Use strict mode during development and testing. Invalid transitions are bugs — they should fail loudly so they are found and fixed. A state machine that silently accepts invalid transitions provides no guarantees.

Lenient: Ignore Invalid Transitions

if (!next) {
  log.warn('unknown_transition', { current, event })
  return current // stay in current state
}

Use lenient mode in production for forward compatibility. Claude Code's streaming state machine uses lenient mode because the API server may introduce new event types in future versions. A strict state machine would crash on new_event_type; a lenient one ignores it and continues working.

The choice depends on the source of invalid transitions:

Source Strategy Reasoning
Internal code bug Strict (throw) Bugs should be caught, not hidden
External protocol evolution Lenient (ignore) New events should not crash old clients
User input Lenient (reject with message) Users should not crash the system
Race conditions Lenient (log and continue) Races are transient; crashing makes them permanent

Hybrid: Strict Internally, Lenient Externally

The best approach is a hybrid: strict validation for internally generated events (where invalid transitions are definitely bugs) and lenient validation for externally generated events (where invalid transitions may be protocol evolution or network artifacts).

Claude Code's streaming pipeline applies this: if the internal code attempts an invalid transition (e.g., emitting a text_delta event while processing a tool-use block), it throws. If the external SSE stream delivers an unknown event type, it logs and ignores.

Hierarchical State Machines

Simple state machines have flat states. But real systems have states within states — an Active session contains sub-states like Idle, Processing, WaitingForTool. Hierarchical state machines (also called statecharts) model this nesting.

The Nesting Problem

Consider Claude Code's active session. Within the Active state, the system cycles through a sub-machine:

stateDiagram-v2
    state Active {
        [*] --> WaitingForInput
        WaitingForInput --> SendingToAPI : user submits prompt
        SendingToAPI --> Streaming : first token arrives
        Streaming --> ProcessingTools : tool_use detected
        ProcessingTools --> SendingToAPI : tool results ready
        Streaming --> WaitingForInput : response complete
        ProcessingTools --> WaitingForInput : response complete
    }

    state Streaming {
        [*] --> InTextBlock
        InTextBlock --> InTextBlock : text_delta
        InTextBlock --> BetweenBlocks : content_block_stop
        BetweenBlocks --> InToolBlock : content_block_start(tool_use)
        BetweenBlocks --> InTextBlock : content_block_start(text)
        BetweenBlocks --> InThinkingBlock : content_block_start(thinking)
        InToolBlock --> InToolBlock : input_json_delta
        InToolBlock --> BetweenBlocks : content_block_stop
        InThinkingBlock --> InThinkingBlock : thinking_delta
        InThinkingBlock --> BetweenBlocks : content_block_stop
    }

The Streaming state itself contains a sub-machine with its own states (InTextBlock, InToolBlock, InThinkingBlock, BetweenBlocks). Events like Disconnect at the outer level apply regardless of which inner state the streaming sub-machine is in — the entire Streaming state transitions to Error, taking the sub-machine with it.

Benefits of Hierarchy

Shared transitions. The Active → ShuttingDown transition applies regardless of the inner state. Without hierarchy, you would need separate transitions: WaitingForInput → ShuttingDown, SendingToAPI → ShuttingDown, Streaming → ShuttingDown, ProcessingTools → ShuttingDown. Four transitions encoding the same logic.

Encapsulation. The streaming sub-machine's internal states (InTextBlock, InToolBlock) are invisible to the outer machine. The outer machine knows only that the session is Streaming — the details of which content block type is currently active are encapsulated within the sub-machine.

Manageable complexity. A flat state machine with all states at one level might have 12+ states and 50+ transitions. A hierarchical machine with 3 levels of 4 states each has the same expressiveness but is far easier to understand because each level has only 4 states to reason about.

State Machines in Shutdown Sequences

Shutdown is where state machines prove their worth most dramatically. A system that shuts down correctly from any state is a system that never loses data, never leaves zombie processes, and never corrupts shared resources.

The Shutdown State Machine

Claude Code's graceful shutdown is an ordered sequence of operations, each dependent on the previous:

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> StopInput : shutdown signal received
    StopInput --> AbortRequests : input disabled
    AbortRequests --> FlushTelemetry : in-flight requests cancelled
    FlushTelemetry --> RunCleanups : telemetry flushed
    RunCleanups --> WriteEndMarker : cleanup handlers complete
    WriteEndMarker --> Deregister : session_end written
    Deregister --> RestoreTerminal : active_sessions updated
    RestoreTerminal --> [*] : terminal restored

Each state has a clear precondition (the previous state completed) and a clear action. The ordering is not arbitrary:

  1. StopInput before AbortRequests. If you abort requests before stopping input, the user could start a new request during shutdown, which would then be aborted, creating a confusing experience.

  2. AbortRequests before FlushTelemetry. In-flight requests might generate telemetry events. Aborting them first ensures the telemetry flush captures their abort status.

  3. RunCleanups before WriteEndMarker. Cleanup handlers (stopping language servers, killing subagents, disconnecting MCP servers) might update the cost counter. The end marker must record the final cost.

  4. WriteEndMarker before Deregister. The end marker in the transcript must be written before the session is deregistered. If deregistration happens first, another process might see "no active session" and start a new one, while the old session is still writing its end marker.

Error Isolation in Shutdown

Each cleanup step is wrapped in a try/catch:

for (const cleanup of registeredCleanups) {
  try {
    await cleanup()
  } catch (err) {
    logError('Cleanup handler failed', err)
    // Continue — other cleanups must still run
  }
}

A failed cleanup step transitions to the next step, not to an error state. This is a deliberate violation of the "fail fast" principle — during shutdown, the goal is to complete as many cleanup steps as possible, even if some fail. A language server that fails to stop should not prevent the transcript from being written.

The Transition Table as Documentation

A transition table is the most compact and precise documentation of a stateful system. It is more complete than prose (which tends to omit edge cases) and more precise than diagrams (which tend to omit events).

Example: Streaming State Machine

Current State Event Next State Side Effect
Idle message_start MessageActive Record TTFT
MessageActive content_block_start(text) InTextBlock Initialize text buffer
MessageActive content_block_start(tool_use) InToolUseBlock Initialize JSON buffer, record tool name
MessageActive content_block_start(thinking) InThinkingBlock Initialize thinking buffer
MessageActive message_delta MessageComplete Record stop_reason, merge usage
InTextBlock text_delta InTextBlock Append to buffer, yield to renderer
InTextBlock content_block_stop MessageActive Finalize text block
InToolUseBlock input_json_delta InToolUseBlock Append to JSON buffer
InToolUseBlock content_block_stop MessageActive Parse JSON, create tool request
InThinkingBlock thinking_delta InThinkingBlock Append to thinking buffer
InThinkingBlock content_block_stop MessageActive Finalize thinking block
MessageComplete message_stop Done Release resources
Any timeout Error Start stall detection
Any network_error Error Record partial state for recovery
Error retry_allowed Recovering Initialize retry with backoff

This table has 15 rows. It completely specifies the streaming pipeline's behavior. Any event-state combination not in the table is an invalid transition. A developer reading this table can answer any question about "what happens when X occurs during Y" in seconds.

Compare this to the hundreds of lines of if/else code that implement the same logic. The table is both the specification and the test oracle — generate tests that exercise every row, and you have complete coverage of the state machine.

When Not to Use State Machines

State machines are powerful but not universal. Three cases where they are the wrong tool:

1. When State Is Continuous

A progress bar that fills from 0% to 100% is not a state machine — it is a continuous value. Modeling it as discrete states (0-25%, 25-50%, 50-75%, 75-100%) adds artificial boundaries. Use a numeric variable with bounds checking.

2. When Transitions Are Unstructured

A free-form text editor does not have meaningful states. The user can type any character at any position in any order. There is no useful transition table because every "state" (the current document content) can transition to any other "state" (the document with one character changed). Use data structures, not state machines.

3. When the State Space Is Too Large

A chess game has approximately 10^44 legal states. Modeling this as an explicit state machine is absurd. Use rules and constraints (legal move generation) rather than enumerated states.

The rule of thumb: use state machines when you have fewer than ~20 states and the transitions between them carry important semantics. Beyond 20 states, consider hierarchical state machines. Beyond 100 states, consider a different modeling approach.

Testing State Machines

State machines are among the easiest code to test because the specification (the transition table) directly maps to test cases.

Transition Coverage

For every row in the transition table, write a test:

test('Idle + message_start → MessageActive', () => {
  const next = transition('Idle', { type: 'message_start' })
  expect(next).toBe('MessageActive')
})

test('InTextBlock + text_delta → InTextBlock', () => {
  const next = transition('InTextBlock', { type: 'text_delta', text: 'hello' })
  expect(next).toBe('InTextBlock')
})

This gives you one test per valid transition. For a 15-row table, that is 15 tests — comprehensive coverage of the state machine's behavior.

Invalid Transition Coverage

For every state, test at least one invalid event:

test('Idle + text_delta → throws', () => {
  expect(() => transition('Idle', { type: 'text_delta', text: 'x' }))
    .toThrow(InvalidTransitionError)
})

test('Done + any event → throws', () => {
  expect(() => transition('Done', { type: 'message_start' }))
    .toThrow(InvalidTransitionError)
})

Sequence Tests

Beyond individual transitions, test sequences that exercise meaningful paths through the machine:

test('complete happy path: Idle → Streaming → Done', () => {
  let state: StreamState = 'Idle'
  state = transition(state, { type: 'message_start' }) // → MessageActive
  state = transition(state, { type: 'content_block_start', blockType: 'text' }) // → InTextBlock
  state = transition(state, { type: 'text_delta', text: 'Hello' }) // → InTextBlock
  state = transition(state, { type: 'content_block_stop' }) // → MessageActive
  state = transition(state, { type: 'message_delta', stopReason: 'end_turn' }) // → MessageComplete
  state = transition(state, { type: 'message_stop' }) // → Done
  expect(state).toBe('Done')
})

Sequence tests verify that the machine's states compose correctly — that the end state of one transition is a valid start state for the next.

Key Principles

  1. Most bugs are state bugs. When behavior depends on accumulated history, scattered boolean flags create an exponential space of possible states. Most combinations are invalid. Bugs are paths that reach invalid combinations.

  2. Make illegal states unrepresentable. Use discriminated unions instead of boolean flags. If a field only makes sense in certain states, it should only exist in those states.

  3. The transition function is the specification. A single function that maps (current state, event) to next state is both the implementation and the documentation. If you cannot write the transition table, you do not understand the system.

  4. Guard transitions, not states. Put validation in the transition function, not scattered across call sites. One gate, not many.

  5. Coupled state requires atomic transitions. When two fields must change together, expose a single function that changes both. Remove individual setters.

  6. Strict internally, lenient externally. Throw on invalid transitions from internal code (they are bugs). Ignore or log invalid transitions from external protocols (they may be forward-compatible events).

  7. Event sourcing pairs naturally with state machines. Store the events (transitions), derive the state (by replay). Crash safety, auditability, and cheap writes — all from one design decision.

Think About It

  1. Boolean audit. Find a class or module in your codebase with three or more boolean flags that interact. How many total state combinations do the flags create? How many are actually valid? Could you replace the flags with a discriminated union that only allows valid combinations?

  2. Draw the diagram. Pick a stateful component you work with (a connection pool, a request handler, a workflow engine). Draw its state diagram on paper. Did you discover states or transitions you had not considered? Did you find states that are unreachable?

  3. The shutdown test. Your system is in the middle of processing (any state except idle or terminated). The process receives SIGTERM. Walk through your shutdown sequence. Is it ordered? Does each step depend on the previous? What happens if step 3 of 6 fails — do steps 4-6 still run?

  4. Atomic coupling. Find two fields in your codebase that must always change together (they maintain a mutual invariant). Is there a single function that updates both, or can they be updated independently? If they can be updated independently, what happens when another thread reads between the two updates?

  5. Transition table exercise. Write the complete transition table for a traffic light controller (green, yellow, red, with a pedestrian crossing request button). How many states? How many transitions? What happens if the pedestrian presses the button during yellow? Is there a state for "flashing red" (power failure mode), and if so, how does the system enter and leave it?

Chapter 15: Concurrency and Coordination

Parallel execution is easy. You call Promise.all(), spawn threads, or fork processes. Any junior engineer can make things run at the same time. The hard part -- the part that separates production systems from demos -- is coordination: making parallel work converge into correct results, handling partial failures, and knowing when parallelism helps versus when it makes everything worse.

This chapter is about thinking concurrently. Not the syntax of async/await or the mechanics of mutexes, but the engineering discipline of decomposing work into parallel streams, designing coordination points, and reasoning about the failure modes that concurrency introduces. The patterns are universal: fork-join, pipeline, event-driven, actor model. The traps are also universal: race conditions, deadlocks, the coordination tax that eats the performance gains you thought you were getting.

We will use Claude Code's multi-agent orchestration as the running case study -- a system where the "threads" are independent AI agents, each with its own context window, tool permissions, and failure modes. The coordination challenges are the same ones you face in any concurrent system: how to dispatch work, how to collect results, how to handle the case where one worker fails while others succeed.

15.1 The Concurrency Decision

The first question is not "how do I parallelize this?" but "should I parallelize this at all?"

Parallelism has costs. Every concurrent operation requires coordination overhead: dispatching work, synchronizing results, handling partial failures. If the overhead exceeds the time saved, parallelism makes your system slower, more complex, and harder to debug -- all at once.

The Break-Even Analysis

Consider a task that takes 100ms sequentially. You split it into two parallel subtasks of 50ms each. Sounds like a 2x speedup. But add the real costs:

Cost Time
Dispatch overhead (spawning, context setup) 5ms
Coordination (collecting results, merging) 10ms
Synchronization (waiting for the slower subtask) varies
Error handling (what if one fails?) complexity, not time

Your "50ms parallel" execution actually takes 65ms (50ms work + 15ms overhead), compared to 100ms sequential. A 35% improvement, not 50%. And you have added error handling complexity that did not exist before.

Now consider the case where the two subtasks are not balanced: one takes 20ms and the other takes 80ms. Your parallel execution takes 95ms (80ms + 15ms overhead). You saved 5ms and added a failure mode. This is worse than not parallelizing.

The break-even rule: parallelism helps when the coordination overhead is small relative to the work, and the work is roughly balanced across workers. Unbalanced parallelism is the most common trap -- you pay the full overhead but only save the difference between the longest and second-longest task.

Claude Code's Decision Framework

When Claude Code encounters a task that could benefit from delegation to subagents, it evaluates five thresholds before spawning parallel work:

flowchart TD
    A[New task identified] --> B{Single tool call?}
    B -->|Yes| C[Execute directly]
    B -->|No| D{Independent of current context?}
    D -->|No| E{Would pollute context?}
    D -->|Yes| F{Can parallelize with other work?}
    E -->|No| C
    E -->|Yes| G[Delegate to subagent]
    F -->|Yes| H[Delegate to parallel subagents]
    F -->|No| I{Exceeds 10 tool calls?}
    I -->|Yes| G
    I -->|No| C

The key insight embedded in this tree: delegation is primarily about context management, not capability. The parent agent could theoretically do everything a subagent does. The value of delegation is keeping the parent's working memory clean, restricting the blast radius of errors, and enabling parallelism for independent analyses.

This is a general principle. In any system, the decision to parallelize should be driven by the characteristics of the work, not by the availability of concurrency primitives. Just because you can run things in parallel does not mean you should.

15.2 The Four Fundamental Patterns

Every concurrent system, regardless of implementation technology, uses one or more of four fundamental patterns. Understanding them as thinking tools -- not just as code patterns -- is the key to designing correct concurrent systems.

Fork-Join

Dispatch N independent tasks. Wait for all to complete. Aggregate results.

graph TB
    D["Dispatch"] --> A1["Worker 1"]
    D --> A2["Worker 2"]
    D --> A3["Worker 3"]

    A1 --> J["Join Point"]
    A2 --> J
    A3 --> J

    J --> S["Aggregate Results"]

    style D fill:#e8f4f8,stroke:#2196F3
    style J fill:#fff3e0,stroke:#FF9800
    style S fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#4CAF50

Fork-join is the workhorse of concurrent programming. It is appropriate when:

  • All tasks are independent (no data flows between workers)
  • All results are needed before proceeding
  • The tasks are roughly balanced in duration

Claude Code example: When reviewing a pull request, Claude Code spawns a code-reviewer agent and a security-reviewer agent in parallel. Each operates in its own context window with its own system prompt. The parent waits for both to complete, then synthesizes a unified review. The two analyses are independent -- neither needs the other's findings to do its work.

The critical design question: What happens at the join point when one worker fails? Three strategies:

Strategy Behavior When to Use
All-or-nothing Cancel remaining workers if any fails Financial transactions, atomic operations
Collect-all Wait for all, report successes and failures Analysis tasks, reviews
Best-effort Return whatever succeeded Non-critical enrichment, telemetry

Claude Code uses collect-all for PR reviews. If the security review times out, the code review results are still valuable. The parent notes the partial failure: "Security review was incomplete -- agent reviewed 2 of 4 modules."

Pipeline

Output from Stage N becomes input for Stage N+1. Each stage transforms or enriches the data.

graph LR
    S1["Stage 1: Investigate"] -->|"File list"| S2["Stage 2: Analyze"]
    S2 -->|"Root cause"| S3["Stage 3: Fix"]
    S3 -->|"Changes"| S4["Stage 4: Verify"]

Pipelines are sequential by definition -- each stage depends on the previous. The "concurrency" comes from two sources:

  1. Pipelining across items: If you have multiple items to process, Stage 1 can work on item N+1 while Stage 2 works on item N.
  2. Internal parallelism: Each stage can internally parallelize its work.

Claude Code example: Bug fixing follows a pipeline: an explore agent investigates the codebase (cheap, fast, read-only), then a debugger agent analyzes the evidence (expensive, Opus-class reasoning), then a general-purpose agent implements the fix. Each stage's output feeds the next. The explore agent is deliberately cheap -- Haiku or Sonnet model, read-only tools. The debugger is expensive -- Opus model, full bash access. This is the "start cheap, escalate if needed" principle applied to a pipeline.

The critical design question: What happens when a pipeline stage produces empty or invalid output? A robust pipeline validates at each stage boundary. If the explore agent finds nothing relevant, the parent agent does not blindly dispatch the debugger with empty input -- it reports the investigation came up empty.

Event-Driven

Components react to events as they arrive, rather than polling for results.

Event-driven concurrency is appropriate when:

  • The timing of work completion is unpredictable
  • Multiple independent event sources produce work
  • You need responsiveness -- the system should react immediately when something happens, not at the next polling interval

Claude Code example: MCP server connections use event-driven notification handlers. When a connected server changes its tool list, it sends a ToolListChangedNotification. The client reacts immediately -- invalidating tool caches, re-fetching the new tool set, and updating the UI. No polling. No wasted cycles checking "has anything changed?"

// Three notification types, each driving cache invalidation
client.on(ToolListChangedNotification, () => {
  fetchToolsForClient.cache.delete(name);
  refreshTools();
});

client.on(PromptListChangedNotification, () => {
  fetchCommandsForClient.cache.delete(name);
  refreshCommands();
});

client.on(ResourceListChangedNotification, () => {
  fetchResourcesForClient.cache.delete(name);
  refreshResources();
});

The event-driven model composes well with fork-join. When parallel workers complete at different times, the join point can be implemented as an event counter: each completion event increments the counter, and when it reaches N, the aggregation runs.

Actor Model

Independent actors with private state communicate through message passing. No shared memory. No locks.

The actor model is the most restrictive concurrency pattern and the most resistant to bugs. Each actor:

  • Has its own state (no shared mutable data)
  • Processes one message at a time (no internal concurrency)
  • Can send messages to other actors (but not access their state)
  • Can create new actors

Claude Code example: Subagents are actors. Each has its own context window (private state), processes one API call at a time, and communicates with the parent through structured messages. The parent cannot reach into a subagent's context -- it can only send delegation prompts and receive results. The isolation is enforced by the architecture: subagents literally operate in separate API conversations.

graph TB
    subgraph Parent["Parent Actor"]
        PS["Parent State:<br/>Conversation history,<br/>user context"]
    end

    subgraph Agent1["Subagent Actor"]
        AS1["Agent State:<br/>Fresh context,<br/>specialized prompt"]
    end

    subgraph Agent2["Subagent Actor"]
        AS2["Agent State:<br/>Fresh context,<br/>specialized prompt"]
    end

    Parent -->|"Task prompt<br/>(message)"| Agent1
    Parent -->|"Task prompt<br/>(message)"| Agent2
    Agent1 -->|"Result<br/>(message)"| Parent
    Agent2 -->|"Result<br/>(message)"| Parent

    Agent1 -.-x|"Cannot access"| Agent2

    style Parent fill:#e8f4f8,stroke:#2196F3
    style Agent1 fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#4CAF50
    style Agent2 fill:#fff3e0,stroke:#FF9800

The actor model's constraints -- no shared state, message-only communication -- eliminate entire categories of concurrency bugs. Race conditions cannot exist when actors do not share memory. Deadlocks cannot exist when there are no locks. The trade-off is performance: message passing is slower than shared memory access. For AI agents, where each "message" is an API call taking seconds, the overhead is irrelevant.

Pattern Comparison

Pattern Communication Failure Handling Best For
Fork-join None between workers Join-point decision Independent parallel work
Pipeline Sequential data flow Stage-boundary validation Dependent multi-step work
Event-driven Asynchronous events Per-event error handlers Reactive, timing-unpredictable work
Actor model Message passing only Actor-level isolation Complex state, strong isolation

Most real systems combine patterns. Claude Code's multi-agent orchestration uses actors (subagents with isolated state), fork-join (parallel dispatch with join-point aggregation), and pipelines (sequential investigation-to-fix chains).

15.3 Race Conditions: When Timing is Destiny

A race condition occurs when the correctness of your system depends on the relative timing of concurrent operations. The operation that "wins the race" determines the result, and different executions can produce different results.

Race conditions are the most common and most insidious concurrency bug. They are common because they arise naturally whenever concurrent operations access shared state. They are insidious because they often work correctly in testing -- the race only manifests under specific timing conditions that are hard to reproduce.

The General Pattern

Every race condition follows the same structure:

  1. Two or more operations access shared state
  2. At least one operation modifies the state
  3. The operations are not synchronized
  4. The outcome depends on which operation executes first

A Concrete Example: Concurrent Compaction

Claude Code's context window management system (discussed in Chapter 9 of this book's companion architecture volume) maintains a compaction state tracker:

@dataclass
class AutoCompactTracking:
    last_token_count: int
    consecutive_failures: int
    last_compact_turn: int
    compaction_in_progress: bool  # The race condition guard

The compaction_in_progress flag exists to prevent a specific race condition: if two concurrent API calls both detect high context pressure, they might both trigger compaction simultaneously. Two concurrent compactions would produce two conflicting summaries, corrupting the conversation state.

Without the flag:

Thread A: checks token count → above threshold → starts compaction
Thread B: checks token count → above threshold → starts compaction
Thread A: completes, replaces messages with summary A
Thread B: completes, replaces messages with summary B (overwrites A)
Result: Summary B is based on pre-compaction messages, not on summary A
         Information from summary A is lost

With the flag:

Thread A: checks token count → above threshold → sets flag → starts compaction
Thread B: checks token count → above threshold → flag is set → skips compaction
Thread A: completes, clears flag
Result: Single compaction, consistent state

The MCP Connection Cache Race

A subtler race condition exists in MCP connection management. When a connection closes, all associated caches must be invalidated:

client.onclose = () => {
  fetchToolsForClient.cache.delete(name);
  fetchResourcesForClient.cache.delete(name);
  fetchCommandsForClient.cache.delete(name);
  connectToServer.cache.delete(key);
};

Without this invalidation, a reconnected client would serve stale tools from the previous connection -- tools whose call() closures reference a dead MCP SDK client instance. The call would either hang (waiting for a response from a dead process) or throw with a confusing error about a closed transport.

The race: if a reconnection starts before all caches are invalidated, the new connection might be served the stale cache. The solution is not more locking -- it is ensuring that cache invalidation runs synchronously on connection close, before any reconnection logic can access the cache.

Thinking About Races

The discipline for preventing race conditions is not "add locks everywhere." It is:

  1. Identify all shared mutable state. Draw a diagram of what state exists and which concurrent operations access it.
  2. For each piece of shared state, determine the invariant. What must always be true? (e.g., "at most one compaction runs at a time")
  3. Ensure the invariant is enforced. Use the simplest mechanism that works: a boolean flag, an atomic operation, a queue, or -- as a last resort -- a lock.
  4. Prefer eliminating shared state over synchronizing access. The actor model's power comes from making shared mutable state impossible, not from managing it carefully.

15.4 The Coordination Tax

Every concurrent system pays a coordination tax: the overhead of dispatching work, synchronizing results, and handling the interactions between concurrent operations. This tax is paid in three currencies.

Time Tax

Coordination takes time. Spawning workers, passing messages, waiting at join points -- all of this adds latency that does not exist in sequential execution.

In Claude Code's multi-agent system, each subagent delegation incurs:

Overhead Time
Delegation prompt construction ~5ms
Subagent context initialization ~50ms
System prompt injection ~20ms
Tool schema filtering ~5ms
Result collection and parsing ~10ms
Total coordination overhead ~90ms

This is dwarfed by the subagent's actual execution time (typically 10-60 seconds). But the overhead exists, and it matters at the margins. If you are delegating a task that takes 200ms, the 90ms coordination overhead makes delegation a bad trade.

Complexity Tax

Concurrent code is harder to reason about than sequential code. Every concurrent operation introduces new failure modes: what if the worker hangs? What if it produces a partial result? What if it succeeds but the parent has already moved on?

The complexity compounds when concurrent operations interact. Consider three parallel subagents reviewing different aspects of a PR. Each might flag the same line of code. The parent must deduplicate findings across agents -- a task that does not exist in sequential execution. The parent must handle the case where one agent's recommendation contradicts another's. The parent must decide what to do when one agent finishes in 10 seconds and another takes 2 minutes.

Token Tax

In AI agent systems, there is a third tax: tokens. Each subagent operates in a fresh context window. It must re-read files the parent already read. It must re-establish context that the parent already has. A subagent reviewing auth.ts does not know that the parent already read auth.ts and identified the relevant functions -- it must discover this independently.

Claude Code mitigates this through context stripping -- subagents skip CLAUDE.md, memory entries, skill prompts, and most project context. The parent digests project context and passes only what the subagent needs in the delegation prompt. This saves 500-2,000 tokens per subagent invocation. Over a session with 10 delegations, that is 5,000-20,000 tokens saved.

But the fundamental tax remains: isolated workers duplicate discovery. The trade-off is worth it when the alternatives -- shared context that enables pollution and prompt injection -- are worse. As discussed in Chapter 12 of this book, the defender's asymmetry means that correctness and security constraints often dominate performance considerations.

15.5 When Parallelism Hurts

The most important concurrency skill is knowing when not to parallelize. Three scenarios consistently produce worse outcomes with parallelism than without.

Scenario 1: Sequential Dependencies Disguised as Parallel Tasks

A developer looks at a workflow -- investigate, analyze, fix, test -- and says "let's run investigate and analyze in parallel." The problem: analyze depends on investigate's output. Running them in parallel means the analyzer starts with no information and wastes its early work discovering what the investigator already knows.

Claude Code's delegation decision tree explicitly checks for this: "Independent of current context?" If the answer is no -- if the task needs information that only the current conversation has -- delegation loses more than it gains.

The engineering heuristic: if you must include more than 2 paragraphs of context in the delegation prompt to make the subtask self-contained, the task is probably not independent enough for parallel execution.

Scenario 2: Resource Contention

Parallel tasks that compete for the same resource can actually serialize themselves through contention, producing worse throughput than sequential execution.

Claude Code encounters this with local MCP server spawning. Each stdio MCP server requires spawning a subprocess, which involves process creation, file descriptor allocation, and environment setup. Spawning 20 servers simultaneously overwhelms the OS process table. The solution: batch local server connections at 3 concurrently, while remote HTTP connections (which are cheap) batch at 20.

await Promise.all([
  processBatched(localServers, 3, processServer),    // Subprocess-heavy
  processBatched(remoteServers, 20, processServer),  // Network I/O only
]);

The batching numbers were determined empirically. The general principle: match concurrency to resource constraints, not to task count. Having 100 tasks does not mean you should run 100 in parallel.

Scenario 3: The Thundering Herd

When multiple workers wake up simultaneously in response to the same event, they stampede through the same critical section. Classic examples: cache invalidation causing all workers to regenerate the cache, all reconnection timers firing at once after a network outage.

Claude Code's MCP reconnection uses exponential backoff (1s, 2s, 4s, 8s, 16s, capped at 30s) specifically to prevent thundering herds. If 10 MCP servers disconnect simultaneously, staggered backoff ensures they do not all reconnect at the same time and overwhelm the authentication service.

15.6 The Principle of Least Authority for Delegated Work

When you dispatch work to a concurrent worker, the worker should have exactly the tools and permissions it needs -- no more. This is the principle of least authority (POLA), adapted from security to concurrency.

POLA is not just a security principle. It is a correctness principle. A worker with access to tools it does not need will occasionally use them. A code-review agent with write access will sometimes "helpfully" fix the issues it finds, corrupting the review's objectivity. A research agent with bash access might try to install packages instead of reporting findings.

Claude Code enforces POLA through three layers of defense:

graph TB
    subgraph Layer1["Layer 1: System Prompt"]
        SP["Role definition:<br/>'You are a read-only reviewer.<br/>You will NOT modify code.'"]
    end

    subgraph Layer2["Layer 2: Tool Schema"]
        TS["Tool allowlist:<br/>Only Read, Grep, Glob available.<br/>Write, Bash not in schema."]
    end

    subgraph Layer3["Layer 3: Permission Rules"]
        PR["Runtime enforcement:<br/>Even if tool is somehow called,<br/>permission system blocks it."]
    end

    Layer1 --> Layer2 --> Layer3

    style Layer1 fill:#e8f4f8,stroke:#2196F3
    style Layer2 fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#4CAF50
    style Layer3 fill:#fff3e0,stroke:#FF9800

Layer 1 (System Prompt) is a soft constraint -- the model might ignore it. But it handles 95% of cases.

Layer 2 (Tool Schema) is a hard constraint at the API level. If the Write tool is not in the schema, the model cannot generate a valid tool-use request for it. The model literally does not know the tool exists.

Layer 3 (Permission Rules) catches anything that slips through Layers 1 and 2. Even if a tool is in the schema (because the agent type needs limited bash access), the permission rules can restrict which specific commands are allowed.

The result is a taxonomy of agent types, each with a different authority profile:

Agent Type Read Write Bash Web Typical Use
explore Yes No Read-only No Fast codebase investigation
code-reviewer Yes No No No Code quality review
security-reviewer Yes No Analysis only No Security audit
debugger Yes No Yes No Root cause analysis
researcher Yes No No Yes Information synthesis
doc-writer Yes Yes (docs only) No No Documentation
general-purpose Yes Yes Yes Yes Full autonomy

The general-purpose agent is the only type that can itself spawn subagents. This enables hierarchical delegation -- but also enables exponential cost growth. Which brings us to the next section.

15.7 Error Propagation Across Boundaries

In sequential code, error propagation is simple: an exception bubbles up the call stack. In concurrent code, errors propagate across boundaries -- from worker to coordinator, from subagent to parent. The boundary crossing makes error handling fundamentally different.

The Five Failure Modes

Every delegated concurrent task can fail in five ways:

Failure Mode Cause Is Result Usable?
Timeout Worker exceeded time/turn limit Partial (what it produced before timeout)
Infrastructure error Network failure, API error No
Resource exhaustion Context window full, memory exhausted Partial (what fit)
Tool error Individual operation failed Depends (usually recoverable)
